#2842. Young state star impresses in his UWM debut as the Panthers fall to USC

For a mid-major team looking to bounce back from a miserable 2025-26 season, starting on the road against a ranked opponent with 7-footers in the middle was a tough ask.

That's what the Milwaukee Panthers did, though, on opening night of college basketball season Nov. 2 and they suffered the sort of fate one might expect, a 95-63 loss to Southern California at the Galen Center in Los Angeles in the teams' first meeting.

The Trojans, ranked 22nd in USA Today coaches poll, used a size advantage that included 7-foot freshmen Adonis and Darius Ratliff, sons of former NBA player Theo Ratliff, and pulled away with a 19-2 run in the first half.

"Anybody that wasn't here live, you don't understand is how much length and positional size they have," UWM coach Bart Lundy said in his postgame radio interview. "It's basically an NBA team. There's gonna be five guys on that team that are gonna play in the NBA, and a couple might be really good NBA players.

"The combination of athleticism, size, and skill is pretty amazing. … That's an unusual team. They're better than 21st in the country."

Adonis Ratliff led the Trojans with 25 points as well as six rebounds and went 5 of 7 from 3-point range. Sophomore guard Alijah Arenas, son of Gilbert Arenas, had 21 points and a team-high eight rebounds.

Freshman guard Amare Hereford was a bright spot for Milwaukee, which is looking to bounce back from an injury-plagued 12-20 season. The top scorer in Wisconsin high school basketball last season and Beloit Memorial's all-time leader led the Panthers with 14 points in 26 minutes.

Marquette transfer guard Tre Norman added all 13 of his points in the second half for the Panthers and Isiah Dorceus, one of five returning Panthers, scored 10 in 15 points.

"Those three figured out they could get downhill and make plays for themselves and for others," said Lundy, who began his fifth season at UWM. "And that's what we've seen in practice.

"It's just … we were in a huge deficit, and then the 3s. ... I really thought for a little bit that we were going to make a comeback run."

Jake Hansen, a Wauwatosa West graduate who played three games at Oklahoma last season, hit a pair of 3-pointers in the first half and scored eight points but was limited by foul trouble.

For UWM, USC marked the first of five nonconference opponents who are ranked or received votes in preseason polls. The Panthers stay in California for a Nov. 4 matchup at Santa Clara.

#2837. The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

The outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds.

The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term.

There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.

Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy.

"It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."

Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats.

For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031.

"The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.

It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.

If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities.

"It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.

Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close.

"Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said.

Other voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply.

Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said.

Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election.

"That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said.

Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted.

The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said.

"There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."

Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.

For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.

"At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.

Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."

Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds.

"The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

#2833. Preview: Warriors take on Suns in Chase Center with Curry, Green back

The last time the Phoenix Suns and the Golden State Warriors met, the Suns got the Warriors' backups. Steve Kerr rested Steph Curry, Draymond Green, Al Horford and Brandin Podziemski on the second night of a back-to-back, and Devin Booker went berserk. He dropped 43 points, seven rebounds and seven assists in a 131-122 Phoenix win that dropped Golden State to 0-3, its worst start in almost two decades. He set a Suns record for points in a home opener, a historic performance against a limping Warriors squad.

Let's see what he does tonight. But for those who haven't been following Suns basketball, here's a quick refresher for you this season.

Opening night was a disaster. Portland jumped out to a 21-0 lead and won 124-83, with Phoenix trailing by as many as 52. Damian Lillard scored 25 in his Blazers return. That's the seventh-largest margin in opening-night history,.

Then came the big game against GSW. After scoring 43, Booker said the bench had more chemistry than his own starting group.

Since then, two more losses. Phoenix lost 125-114 in Oklahoma City and 127-120 at home to Denver. Through four games, the Suns rank dead last in defensive rating at 126.3 points allowed per 100 possessions. Their offense sits right in the middle at 15th. SI's Suns site summed up the start in one word: consistency.

How they play. Phoenix runs at the fourth-slowest pace in the league and ranks near the top in pull-up points. Translation: lots of Booker and Green creating their own shots late in the clock. When those shots fall, the Suns can beat anyone. When they don't, you get Portland. That's a tough formula against Golden State, which leads the league in threes made and passes per game. The Warriors will move the ball until Phoenix's league-worst defense breaks somewhere, while Booker has to manufacture tough looks possession after possession.

Who's missing. Mark Williams is out after surgery on a torn labrum in his left shoulder. Oso Ighodaro, who missed the first meeting, is available this time.

On the other side, the Warriors (4-3) haven't lost since Phoenix. Curry and Green sat Sunday's 124-112 win over the Clippers and are expected back tonight. Curry scored 99 points over the three wins before that, and rookie Yaxel Lendeborg dropped 37 on the Clippers. Golden State is still without Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody, Kristaps Porziņģis and Gui Santos, but this group has proven it can win while shorthanded.

The Suns have real talent and a star who can win a game by himself. But let's see if he can put the team on his back again against a Warriors lineup that will be more fortified than in these two teams' last battle. Phoenix got its only win of the season against a Warriors team without Steph and Draymond. Tonight it has to earn one against both of them, plus a rookie who's been playing like a headliner since the last time these teams met.

#2832. ‘Matter of days’ – Harry Kane shares Bayern contract update

Harry Kane has made everyone at Bayern Munich proud by winning the prestigious 2026 Ballon d'Or last week.

The 33-year-old joined Bayern in the summer of 2023, and he has been simply phenomenal for the Bavarian giants.

Kane has scored 156 goals in 160 games across all competitions, and he is showing no signs of slowing down.

The striker scored 61 goals across all competitions for Bayern, but his contribution to the side goes beyond goals and assists.

Kane drops deep and often acts as a playmaker. Against Borussia Dortmund, he even dropped too deep to act as a defender, making some good clearances.

He has already scored 10 goals across all competitions, and he is invaluable to the Bayern side.

The former Tottenham Hotspur striker has repeatedly suggested that he is enjoying his life in Germany and wants to win more trophies with Bayern.

Kane has a contract at the German club until the end of the season. The striker has confirmed that his deal will be signed in a "matter of days".

The striker said to the reporters: "I'd say it's a matter of days. There's been a good conversation over this weekend, and today as well, so yeah, I know I keep saying we're close, but we are extremely close now, details are just details in every contract.

"A lot of the bigger stuff has been ironed out, and we're happy with, but in every contract there's loads of little things that go into it, and small details that in the end the lawyers have to figure out. So yeah, all in all, I'd say it's more days than weeks. The conversations have gone well again today, and hopefully we'll be in a place to do something within the next few days."

Christian Falk has exclusively told CFBayern Insider that Kane's contract will not have any release clause, which can be activated by specific clubs.

Kane will sign a new contract until 2029. Talks are progressing smoothly and only minor details are left to be ironed out.

Falk said: "It is NOT TRUE: Harry Kane will get a release clause in his new contract that can be activated by specific clubs. There are final details to clear – that's what we've been hearing from Bayern Munich. But the two parties are in total agreement otherwise; Kane will sign a new contract until 2029.

"There are small details and clauses to be cleared but things are accelerating now. Before the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, Bayern were always asking, 'Could we talk about the contract?' And the answer was always that Kane was focusing on the ceremony. I'm now hearing that there could be talks next week, and from there we could hear about a new contract being signed very soon."

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

This week's first stock pick is Datadog, an AI-powered observability and security platform. The company will announce its results for the third quarter on Nov. 4. Datadog is seeing strong demand for its offerings, thanks to cloud migration and rapid AI adoption. TipRanks' KPIs tool for DDOG shows the growth in its customer base over the past few years amid increasing market penetration and growing adoption of its products.

Heading into Q3 FY26 earnings, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Datadog stock and raised his price target to $335 from $305. The analyst noted that industry checks and data indicate that infrastructure software demand is strengthening, with AI increasingly driving usage and growth.

Ikeda called Datadog and Atlassian his top picks, saying that companies that can show that AI is a tailwind to growth could see their valuation rerate, even at premium multiples. He added that the total addressable market for observability is growing faster than anticipated, driven by accelerated growth of enterprise AI and the rapid ramp of consumer AI agents.

The five-star analyst believes that focus will be on revenue growth, which he estimates to be 28.7% for Q3 FY26 versus the Street's consensus of 29.1%. Ikeda thinks that the market is underestimating the growth prospects of DDOG's security products. Meanwhile, he cautioned investors about concentration risk related to large customers.

"We think results will be supportive of our long-term thesis that Datadog is a strong share gainer in the rapidly expanding observability opportunity," said Ikeda.

With demand outpacing supply, Moore said that focus is on closing the gap. In this regard, he highlighted the supply chain deals on substrate, packaging and testing. While the analyst continues to view TSMC 3 nm wafer supply as the biggest challenge, he expects it to ease over time.

#2827. DeForest Buckner, 49ers realize their best chance at Super Bowl glory is with each other

The last time DeForest Buckner stood behind the lectern that he did Monday afternoon, he was a lot younger — some six years — and a whole lot poorer, say by $140 million or so.

With age comes wisdom, and over his time away Buckner seemed to have learned a lesson.

There's always green in the bag, but that doesn't always apply to the other side of the grass.

The only person happier than the 49ers Faithful and the existing inhabitants of their locker room in Santa Clara to hear the news of their trade for Buckner might have been Buckner himself.

DeForest Buckner of the Indianapolis Colts looks on after a game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images

"I'll be honest, I just fell to my knees and started praying," the current and former 49ers defensive tackle said of his reaction to the trade that sent him from the Colts, where he signed in free agency back in 2020, to San Francisco, the only other organization he has known.

"It's just crazy the way everything happened. God, he'll open doors you thought were closed, and he was able to open this one back up for me."

When Buckner left for the Colts, the 49ers were coming off their first trip to the Super Bowl under Kyle Shanahan, a run fueled in large part by a dominant defensive line. San Francisco thought it could reallocate the money and replace Buckner through the draft.

In Indianapolis, Buckner saw a team that "obviously wanted me" and "invested in me." He "gave that organization my heart and soul," earning first-team All-Pro honors in his first season and appearing in all but two of a possible 68 games over his first four years there.

Yet, Buckner had one playoff game to show for it — a wild-card round loss in his first season. At 2-6 this season, his frustrations seemed to grow in each of his postgame sessions this season.

DeForest Buckner of the Indianapolis Colts runs onto the field before a game against the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, in Kansas City, Mo. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

As was the specific request he made to principal owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon and interim general manager Ed Dodds.

"When everything kind of unfolded, I made it pretty – I mean, I stated it – that I wanted to come here," Buckner said. "I didn't want to go anywhere else."

Buckner's inner circle of football friends basically makes up a map of the prominent stalls in the 49ers' locker room: Fred Warner, George Kittle, Kyle Juszczyk, Nick Bosa, Dre Greenlaw, Deebo Samuel. They stayed in touch, and Buckner never stopped tuning in.

San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner (54) celebrates a defensive stop against the Atlanta Falcons in Atlanta, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Brynn Anderson

"I've been keeping up with the games over the years," he said. "Just watching the standard of football they play at, the winning football they play – this is where I wanted to be. …

"Over the years they'd be like, 'Come back home, bro. Come back home.' I had my own things that I needed to do out in Indy. Lo and behold, I'm here."

While Buckner agonized over ultimately requesting his trade from the Colts, there was a certain standard that he had become accustomed to with the 49ers that was absent in Indianapolis.

"I know the standard here," Buckner said. "It's very high. It's Super Bowl or bust."

To be clear: It's not like the Niners won the breakup, either.

San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (85) takes the field before a game against the Washington Commanders in Santa Clara, Calif., Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Not unlike Samuel and Greenlaw, whose sabbaticals lasted only one season, the 49ers tried to move on from Buckner and never quite filled the hole created by his departure.

With their first selection that spring, they drafted Javon Kinlaw 14th overall. Injuries prevented him from playing more than 200 snaps in two of his four seasons before the 49ers let him walk.

They signed Javon Hargrave, who gave them one Pro Bowl season in 2023 before getting injured and eventually released the following year. After going back to the well for Alfred Collins and C.J. West in last year's draft, they seem to have accepted reality:

They couldn't do better than Buckner. And there's no place Buckner would rather be.

Both sides realized their best chance at achieving the ultimate goal was together.

He watched them make a return trip to the Super Bowl in 2023, only to come up short against the same opponent that snuffed out their dreams three seasons earlier.

Now, back together again, Buckner said, "there is unfinished business."

"We definitely talked about it," he said. "Me coming back and everything like that, it's great, a little nostalgic and things like that, but there's still a job to do."

That work has already gotten under way. Upstairs, general manager John Lynch continues to work the phones to further bolster the 49ers roster ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch looks on during warmups before a game against the Atlanta Falcons in Atlanta, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. Getty Images

In the facility, it hasn't taken Buckner long to get back into his long-held routines.

Just earlier Monday morning, he was catching up with Warner over a coffee.

"He's been preaching about how you want to continue to be a team on the rise, which I really love," Bucker said. "This is the part of the season where teams start falling off and the really select group continues to rise and get better every single week."

"That's what I'm still trying to do," Buckner said. "Everything happens for a reason. Life just came full circle and I'm back. I'm a Niner again."

Dave Portnoy accuses 76ers' LeBron James of setting a poor example with mid-game wine sip appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

LeBron James is approaching the age of 42 and is enjoying every single second he has left on an NBA court. On Monday night, in the third quarter of the Philadelphia 76ers' 126-107 victory over the Chicago Bulls, he continued his quirky era by taking a sip of wine from a fan's cup in the middle of the game after he ran all the way to the baseline on a botched possession.

This was a lighthearted moment that drew some laughter at Xfinity Mobile Arena, as it is becoming very evident that James is playing loose and carefree and does not care that much at all anymore about what other people think. However, this wine-sipping "incident", so to speak, has become a reason for some, including Barstool Sports owner Dave Portnoy, to dish out some criticism the 76ers star's way.

Drinking while on the job is a frowned-upon practice in workplaces, so it's a bit understandable as to where Portnoy is coming from. If a regular employee drank while on the job in a corporate setting, he might have been on the unemployment line the next morning.

However, the NBA isn't exactly a regular job, and no one could get drunk from a single sip of an alcoholic beverage. Portnoy is being a bit overdramatic by insinuating that the 76ers star could get anywhere close to being inebriated after taking that little amount of wine.

This just proves that James, no matter what he does, is always going to be one of, if not outright the most divisive superstar of his generation.

#2818. Rams PFF grades: Offensive line pancakes Chargers in win

The Los Angeles Rams defeated the Los Angeles Chargers 24-9 to move to 4-4 on the season.

The Rams have two winnable games on deck against the Washington Commanders and Arizona Cardinals to potentially put together a four-game win streak and move to 6-4.

But before we get ahead of ourselves, let's put a cap on the team's win over the Chargers. These are the Pro Football Focus (PFF) grades from the game with important notes.

PFF counted four pressures on Matthew Stafford across 26 dropbacks. The quarterback was sacked only a single time. The offensive line was credited with only one of these pressures, which suggests Stafford was inviting pressure with his play.

Steve Avila did not allow a single pressure. He was also effective in the run game with a grade of 82.9.

Dotson also did not allow a pressure. He posted a run grade of 79.9. This was by far his best grade of the season, which is encouraging because he has not looked like himself. Dotson has strung together two positive performances and could be trending in the right direction.

The offense runs through Puka Nacua. He caught 11 of 12 targets for 80 yards with a score. 65 of his yards came after the catch point, and he averaged nearly six additional yards per catch. With a 1.5 average depth of target (ADOT), Nacua was doing the hard work for nearly every yard he gained.

Shelton received a poor pass protection grade of 57.5 with no pressures allowed. He shined in the run game at 79.5.

McClendon is the only lineman to allow a pressure. Still, he finished with a strong pass protection grade of 70.8 with even better marks in the run game at 74.6.

The Rams had 110 yards after the catch point in the passing game. Matthew Stafford had 157 passing yards on the day. Just 30% of his yardage total on the game were "air yards", which underscores how suffocated the passing game felt at times. Stafford finished with an ADOT of just 3.8 yards down field with a 2.26 second time to throw. That is about as short and fast as it gets.

McDuffie intercepted Justin Herbert and nearly returned for a defensive scheme. He made five defensive run stops from the secondary with nine total tackles. Herbert looked his way often with eight targets. McDuffie allowed six receptions for 47 yards, of which 45 came after the catch with a long of 30.

Speights' best work came this week in pass coverage with a grade of 91.5. He allowed three catches on four targets for 14 yards.

Nate Landman is still the starter in the middle of the defense. He played 42 snaps, and that suggests his role as an every-down player is diminishing. Quentin Lake was the "green d0t" guy. Speights played 35 snaps.

The interior defensive line continues to step up without Poona Ford and Kobie Turner. Tyler Davis was the emerging player this week, and he ranked third on the defense in run grade behind McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. He also added two pressures as a pass rusher.

Lake snatched the first of two Justin Herbert interceptions on the day. In total he allowed three catches on four targets for 30 yards. Lake did not miss a tackle on six attempts. He rushed the passer on three occasions.

Jaylen Watson suffered a shoulder injury and played 41 of the total 61 defensive snaps. Forbes was the biggest recipient of this additional playing time with 17 snaps. The corner was targeted one time and allowed just one catch for a yard, including five yards after the catch.

Aaron Donald, Braden Fiske, and Byron Young were the three lowest graded defenders this week at 54.9, 53.1, and 49.7, respectively. That doesn't happen often. It's still encouraging that someone other than the usual suspects stepped up in a stifling defensive performance.

#2817. Cavs fall at home to the Thunder 117-112

On a night when both teams were missing key rotational pieces, it was the Oklahoma City Thunder who found a way to win, beating the Cleveland Cavaliers 117-112. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander dropped 40 points and hit the go-ahead three-pointer with 32 seconds to go to clinch the game. Donovan Mitchell and Maleek Thomas, who was starting for Peyton Watson, led the Cavs with 17 points apiece.

Cleveland was without Watson (hamstring) and Jaylon Tyson (ankle), depleting an already thin wing room. Oklahoma City was without stars Jalen Williams (ankle) and Chet Holmgren (knee).

The Cavs had an exceptionally well-rounded effort with seven players in double-figures, but the Thunder had the better star down the stretch. All of Cleveland's starters had at least 14 points, and Mario Hezonja and Tyrese Proctor had 12 and 10 points off the bench respectively. But while the box score looks good, the Cavs' inability to finish defensive possessions ended up dooming them. In a tightly-contested game, the little things reared their ugly heads.

As has been the case to start the season, the Cavs' inability to close out games in high-pressure situations continues to be a glaring issue. Cleveland briefly held the lead, but then gave up key buckets to Ajay Mitchell — who himself was thrust into a bigger role — and Gilgeous-Alexander. After Sam Merrill's three-pointer tied things up with 91 seconds to go, the Cavs never scored again.

The Cavs trailed the Thunder by 11 at the break, but fought back hard in the third quarter and made it a game. But the difference ended up being determined by the the Thunder's star point guard. James Harden's last bucket came with 8:51 left in the third quarter, and his last points scored period were on free throws with eight minutes left in the game. The rookie Thomas attempted six more shots than Harden on a night the Cavs could have used boost.

Players like Gilgeous-Alexander are going to get their buckets, that's why he is an MVP candidate and one of the best in the league. But the Cleveland fought back hard, had a solid team effort, and came up short at home because its stars were not able to get them over the hump in crunch time.

#2815. Georgia Fans Better Hope Rick Jackson Wins, Because Keisha Lance Bottoms Could Become Kirby Smart’s Worst Nightmare

ATHENS, Ga. — Georgia football has spent the better part of the last decade building one of college football's most powerful recruiting machines.

Kirby Smart has the facilities, the fan base, the championships and, most importantly, the money.

But Bulldogs fans might want to pay attention to Georgia's governor's race. The next person in the governor's mansion could have an indirect impact on the economic environment surrounding the state's most valuable football program.

And if Keisha Lance Bottoms wins, some Georgia fans might start worrying about the NIL budget.

There is another complication: the possibility of a governor who is more interested in seeing Georgia Tech succeed than Georgia.

In this entirely fictional nightmare scenario, Bottoms is portrayed as the ultimate Yellow Jackets superfan. Every Georgia touchdown is a personal inconvenience. Every Kirby Smart recruiting victory is a reason to call a press conference.

And Kirby's coaching methods? A potential public safety investigation.

"Bottoms Questions Whether Georgia Practices Are Too Physical."

"New Administration Wants Answers About Kirby Smart's Player Safety Standards."

"Georgia Tech Supporters Demand Investigation Into Why Georgia Keeps Winning."

In this imagined universe, even Smart's driving habits become a political talking point. Bulldogs fans could find themselves defending everything from practice intensity to the speed at which their head coach gets to the recruiting office.

But the real concern for Georgia supporters is economic.

Bottoms has campaigned on policies including a $15 minimum wage and higher public-sector pay. Those proposals are not a college football spending plan.

Still, in the highly scientific world of completely made-up sports economics, higher costs for businesses could eventually mean less disposable income for the average Georgia football supporter.

A family already spending hundreds of dollars on tickets, parking, concessions and merchandise might suddenly decide it has better things to do with its money.

Instead of buying another Georgia jersey, somebody might actually pay their electric bill.

Instead of donating to an NIL collective, a business owner might decide to keep a little more money in the company.

And instead of helping Georgia land another five-star offensive tackle, a local restaurant might decide it needs to cover payroll first.

Georgia's recruiting operation is not exactly operating on pocket change. The Bulldogs compete nationally for elite prospects, and that requires an enormous financial commitment from supporters, businesses and donors.

If the broader Georgia economy slows down, that money could become harder to find.

Nobody wants to explain to a five-star quarterback that his NIL offer got reduced because the local car dealership is worried about its operating expenses.

That is not how you win a recruiting battle with Alabama.

Republican candidate Rick Jackson has campaigned on cutting Georgia's income tax and reducing costs. Whether those proposals deliver the economic growth supporters expect is another question entirely.

But from the perspective of a Georgia fan, the theoretical appeal is obvious: More money staying in people's pockets could mean more money available for tickets, donations and the next recruiting-class arms race.

Georgia football is not going to collapse because of one governor's election. Smart has built a program with national resources, a massive following and a recruiting footprint that extends well beyond the state.

But the Bulldogs' financial advantage is not completely immune to the economy around them.

And if Georgia fans are forced to choose between paying higher household expenses and helping fund the next championship roster, the answer probably won't make Kirby happy.

The governor's race is about much more than football. But in Athens, practically everything eventually becomes about football.

So Dawgs fans might want to keep an eye on the results.

They can debate taxes, wages and economic policy after the game.

Right now, the only number some Georgia supporters care about is how much money is left for NIL.

Rick Jackson winning might not guarantee another national championship. But some Bulldogs fans would certainly prefer not to find out what a Bottoms administration means for the recruiting budget — or how many Georgia practices might suddenly become subjects of state government scrutiny.

#2812. Sixers play with their food a bit, but take care of business vs. lowly Bulls

And there's a blowout, for those that were still asking for one.

The Sixers picked up their fourth win in a row, handling the Chicago Bulls 126-107 Monday night to improve to 7-1 on the season.

VJ Edgecombe was everywhere from the start of this one, shooting 9-of-12 from the field for a season-high 21 points along with five assists and three rebounds.

Tyrese Maxey had his best night as a passer, putting up 11 assists while still leading the Sixers with 26 points on 10-of-15 shooting. LeBron James had another splendid all-around night, going for 15 points, seven rebounds and nine assists shooting 6-of-13 from the floor.

Jaylen Brown quietly shot the ball well on the night to put up 25 points and 11 rebounds on 9-of-15 shooting. Joel Embiid meandered his way to 15 points and eight boards while Caleb Wilson led the Bulls with 24.

A pedestrian start for both teams, but one the Sixers used to get out and run early. After Edgecombe threw a hit-ahead pass, he ran up the floor a couple of times for two transition buckets of his own to prompt an early Bulls timeout.

The Bulls, or rather center Jalen Smith to be more specific, took advantage of a laid back Sixers defense coming out of the timeout, picking up two cutting baskets and drawing a foul on the second. A Brown three was a nice response, but their defense kept biting on Josh Giddey's drives, opening Smith up for another layup at the basket.

The pick-and-roll between Embiid and Lebron has yielded good looks so far, which is exciting because you can see them refining it as they get more minutes together. James hit Embiid with a very late drop pass, setting the big fella up for a layup he was also able to draw a foul on. As Edgecombe continued to run out after misses for transition baskets the Sixers pushed their lead back up to a comfortable margin.

The Sixers did put Isaac Okoro at the line and let up an open three coming out of a timeout of their own, but Maxey got right to the basket to prevent any sort of run. On the next possession Maxey found Brown wide open in the paint for his fifth assist of the quarter. The Sixers assisted on 12 of their 13 made field goals and led by seven after the first.

Anfernee Simons came around a screen and buried a three for his first points of the game. Brown hit a three from the coach's stripe a couple possessions later, but the Bulls started walking into some open baskets that kept them hanging around. They gave up a pair of threes being slow to close out and gave up two more baskets on open cutters which kept Chicago within a possession or two.

This was far from Adem Bona's worst shift of the season but there were some struggles. It took two possessions for him to complete a rolling dunk off a pocket pass. On top of letting up an offensive rebound by being out of position, the Bulls scored five of their first seven field goals of the quarter at the rim. Embiid and LeBron checked back into a two-point lead that was overtaken by a Buddy Hield three.

Embiid getting stripped on one end led to a Zach Collins layup that capped off a 14-3 run for Chicago. After going without one his last three games, Dean Wade hit a corner three off a LeBron kickout to stop the bleeding.

Of all the Sixers not phoning this one in, Edgecombe was at the top of the list. His insistence on running down the floor continued to create easy baskets. After he got another much needed transition dunk, he found a cutting Wade with a beautiful bounce pass. The Sixers forced a travel on the ensuing possession, prompting a Bulls timeout.

For the first time all night, the Sixers came out energized out of a timeout. Edgecombe used the screens to get open at the basket on the ATO. LeBron threw another nice kickout to Wade for a corner three and bounce pass to Maxey for a dunk before Chicago's defense got back. As they had all night, the Bulls had a response. The rookie Wilson got open on a cut before drilling a three at the buzzer to keep Chicago within five at the break.

No one should complain about soft coverage on Giddey on the perimeter, but he walked into a three to cut it to a one-possession game to make the arena uneasy. The Sixers responded well with Brown and James both getting right to the basket. Brown threw a nice lob to James that got smoked, but Maxey getting to the basket for an and-1 layup was a much needed basket to calm things down. The Sixers ran out on a blocked shot to set up a fast break layup for James to force a Bulls timeout.

The effort in doing the little things has been what Edgecombe has excelled at this year, so it was nice to see him fill up the box score for a night. Coming out of the timeout he helped Embiid get out of a post-up with another cut for a basket at the hoop. The Sixers locked in a bit defensively after this, getting stops on five of their next six possessions including a turnover.

After making most of his impact as a passer, LeBron started to impose his will as a scorer with a couple more drives to the basket. His increase of energy may be due to the sip of a fan's drink he took after chasing a loose ball into the stands. Thanks to the reporting of ESPN's Khris Rhrim, we know the drink he took a sip of was indeed wine.

Edgecombe had a brilliant sequence that summed out how great he was in this one, getting all the way back to block a transition layup by Wilson, then getting back down the floor to get the ball in the paint and find Brown to get two more points the other way. Edgecombe tried to put Noa Essengue on a poster a few minutes later but had to settle for a trip to the free throw line. The one thing he wasn't able to do was hit the grenade swung to him as the quarter ended, so the Sixers had to settle for an 11-point lead after the third.

Maxey didn't really have to shoot a ton, so it was cool that the baskets he did make were impressively silly. He started the quarter by hitting his second highlight floater of the game. Brown followed that up with a midrange jumper and a trip to the line as he slowly put up a solid scoring night.

The Sixers struggled to come up with the killing blow, which was a little frustrating because when they did things well, it looked really good. Brown had a drive that the Bulls stopped by stepping up in the lane, but he spun and hit Maxey for an open stepback three. A minute later James drew a foul on a jumper that spun all the way around the rim before falling in and danced in celebration, but they weren't able to put themselves ahead by more than 15.

It seemed like the Sixers wanted to play Embiid as little as possible, which was fitting given their opponent and Embiid coming into this game questionable with a foot issue. Bona continued to make that difficult, picking up his fifth foul with over five minutes to go. Nick Nurse subbed in Wade at the five which was fine, but it did beg the question as to why Jabari Walker didn't see the floor at all.

The killing blow the Sixers were looking for came in the form of Brown's shotmaking. He came off a screen to hit corner three that forced another Bulls timeout, then hit another on the Sixers next possession that prompted a second timeout from Chicago within 30 seconds. The Sixers finally pushed their lead to 20 which led them to coast to victory.

The Knicks beat the Nets at Madison Square Garden Monday night, 103-90, extending their winning streak over their crosstown rivals to 15.

-- While the Nets entered the game riding the high of their first win of the season, the Knicks were hoping to bounce back after their second loss to the Philadelphia 76ers.

The last time Brooklyn beat New York was Jan. 28, 2023, just over one week before superstars Kyrie Irving and Kevin Durant were traded away.

-- The Nets jumped ahead early, finding their way to a 7-5 lead in the first three minutes of play. Despite working to overcome their turnover troubles early in the season, the Knicks committed their first of the game just 94 seconds in, which allowed for a three from Nets sophomore point guard Nolan Traore. OG Anunoby was the only Knick to score through the first three minutes until Mikal Bridges landed two free throws, tying the game at seven-all.

After that, the Knicks tightened their defense and found their way to the basket, scoring 10 straight points punctuated by back-to-back Jalen Brunson threes. Brooklyn was quick to tie it back up, but two shots from beyond the arc by Deuce McBride and a trio of free throws from Landry Shamet sent New York into the break up 27-21.

-- The back-and-forth play continued through the second frame. While the Knicks struggled to find the basket for the first three-and-a-half minutes, the Nets climbed to a three-point edge. Four uninterrupted points from Bridges — two free throws and a dunk — put the Knicks back out in front, and they maintained the lead through the end of the quarter, but Brooklyn kept the deficit low until Shamet landed back-to-back threes.

Brunson attempted to add three at the buzzer but was fouled by former Knick Julius Randle, earning two free throws. He missed the first, but his second shot gave the Knicks a 51-44 as the half came to a close.

-- Both teams found themselves in turnover trouble through the first 24 minutes of play, coughing it up a combined 15 times (Knicks had seven). Despite only shooting 36 percent — compared to Brooklyn's 40 — New York found game-changing success at the free throw line, going 15-for-16.

Karl-Anthony Towns, who recorded five double-doubles in the first six games of the season, headed to the locker room without a single point, though he recorded 10 rebounds and three assists in his 17 first-half minutes.

-- New York's energy quickly evaporated in the third. Towns finally got on the board, landing two driving layups and two of his three free throws through the first four minutes, but the Nets responded with a 13-0 run through the middle of the frame spearheaded by Randle, Day'Ron Sharpe, and Michael Porter Jr. Shamet finally broke the streak with a three, adding a second 90 seconds later to keep the Knicks in the game, but it wasn't enough. After outscoring New York 35-24 in the third, Brooklyn ended the quarter ahead by four, 79-75.

Shamet's 20 points through the first three quarters led all players at that point.

-- Then, as they often do in the fourth, the Knicks reappeared. Josh Hart drove New York to a 10-point lead in the five-and-a-half minutes of the frame, scoring a 25-foot three-pointer, assisting two Anunoby threes and a layup from Tyler Kolek, and adding a running layup as the Knicks outscored Brooklyn 16-2 to start the frame. Traore kept cut into New York's 10-point lead with a 24-foot jumper, but Anunoby and Towns responded quickly with two free throws and a field goal, respectively, to open up a 9-0 run.

As the Knicks continued to gain momentum, the Nets crumpled, turning the ball over six times through the first 8:30 and scoring just five points in the same span before Randle got the Nets moving again on two free throws with 2:23 left to play. Another foul shot from Randle and a three from Traore cut the Knicks' lead to 13, but the deficit proved too much to overcome, and the Knicks walked away with the 103-90 victory.

-- Overall, the Knicks shot 41 percent from the field, 39 percent from three, and 83 percent from the free throw line, compared to Brooklyn's 38 percent, 34 percent, and 70 percent, respectively.

-- Despite the rocky start, Towns finished with yet another double-double, scoring 11 points and adding 16 rebounds. He also had five assists and four turnovers.

Jose Alvarado, who missed four games with an ankle sprain before returning to the court Monday night, played nine minutes but didn't score.

-- In his first game against his former team since joining Brooklyn's squad in July, Randle recorded his first double-double as a Net, notching 21 points and 11 rebounds. He was the only player on Brooklyn's roster to break 20 points against the Knicks.

Shamet, who played for Brooklyn during the 2020-21 season, posted a game-leading 22 points, tacking on one rebound and one assist in 29 minutes of play. He also went 6-for-8 from the field, 4-for-6 from beyond the arc, and 6-for-6 from the free throw line.

The Knicks are set to host the Chicago Bulls Wednesday. Tip off is scheduled for 7:30 p.m.

Across the river at the Barclays Center, the Nets will take on the Charlotte Hornets that same night, when they'll look to avenge their 110-103 season-opening loss.

#2801. Nick Sirianni: Eagles will stick with Tanner McKee, Sean Mannion despite offensive woes

The Eagles have lost six in a row and rank 30th in the NFL in points per game, but Nick Sirianni said Monday that he isn't making a change at offensive coordinator or quarterback.

Sean Mannion will continue to call plays, and Tanner McKee will remain the starting quarterback with Jalen Hurts out for the year.

Hurts played five games before going on injured reserve with blood clots; Johnson retired after three games; Jurgens played four games with the Eagles before a trade to the Ravens; Barkley has missed two games and been limited in others with injuries; Smith has missed four games with a hamstring injury; and Wicks has missed two games with an ankle injury.

The Eagles are averaging 17.1 points a game.

#2800. Nets disastrous fourth quarter spoils near upset vs Knicks, lose 103-90

The Brooklyn Nets broke one losing streak yesterday. They couldn't break another at Madison Square Garden this evening, losing to the New York Knicks for a 15th straight time.

For whatever it's worth, which can't be much, the Nets did flirt with their first win over their crosstown rivals in nearly four years. In a way, they were close, as Brooklyn led late and never trailed by more than nine entering the fourth. But in another, they looked as far off as ever, completely unraveling and playing their worst basketball when it mattered most.

You don't need me to tell you this, but the latter is what separates the winners from the losers in this league.

The Nets began tonight with the same five they fielded in their win last night against Indiana. And, Nolan Traoré picked up right where he left off, splashing a deep triple and assisting on a Day'Ron Sharpe jam during Brooklyn's third and fourth possessions of the game to help Brooklyn establish and early lead. By the end of the game, he'd finish with 17 points and four assists while shooting 5-of-6 from deep. He turned it over twice, but also grabbed a steal and blocked a shot.

The defense, however, wasn't so easily copy and pasted over from the prior game. Whether it was miscommunication on switches or doubling in the gap and living with the result, the Nets gave up several corner threes early in the contest. Shooting 6-of-14 from deep in the first, New York caught and overtook Brooklyn quickly, going up 27-21 after one.

"I think that when you buy into playing as hard as you can, there's always breakdowns, and it's about giving your second and third, especially your your third effort," Fernández said. "It's easy to give one or two, but we always say we want three or more."

While Julius Randle received a warm welcome in the Garden tonight after being introduced with Brooklyn's starting five, he looked rather uncomfortable on the floor early on, beginning the game 0-3 from the field with a turnover. He did, however, assist on a Mikel Brown Jr. ATO triple in the opening frame.

Oddly enough, it was the 20-year-old rookie in MSG for the first time, not the old fan favorite, who looked at ease early on, moving well around New York's defensive pressure both on and off ball. After sitting out the last game for back injury management, Brown Jr. put up five first quarter points on 2-3 shooting. With five seconds left in the frame, he also dished an assist after blowing past Landry Shamet and Duece McBride to find Mo Wagner in front of the cylinder for an and-one.

"I think Mikel is a rock star," Fernández said. "He's gonna keep taking steps. And right now, we always want him to be aggressive, but he has the responsibility to run the team, and that's a big deal."

But with 150+ career games on that floor, you knew Julius Randle would find his footing already. And in the subsequent quarter's first four minutes, he did, as Julius pitched in four points to help the Nets start the period with a 9-0 run.

Playing the Knicks as a Net for the first time, Randle downplayed the rivalry, saying that he didn't feel any different now coming into it from Brooklyn's side.

"No, not really," he said. "Honestly, not really. I try to keep the game the same and stay levelheaded, so it's fun, always fun competing, but not really."

The Nets even retook the lead for a moment until a wayward Traoré pass found its way to Mikal Bridges, who took it all the way down the other way for an uncontested jam. For the fans still salty over his exit, it's worth noting that Bridges did little else worth mentioning beyond that point tonight. He finished just 1-7 from the field and played only 16 minutes.

Still, the Knicks controlled things for much of the second. Despite beginning the quarter 1-of-8 from the field while the Nets opened 6-of-13, New York benefitted from five extra free throws to stay afloat, even as Traoré made up for that turnover with another fine period. Nolan hit another triple in the second to stay perfect, adding 11 points and two assists in the first half…

However, it wasn't enough to overcome Brooklyn's woeful perimeter defense and the free throw discrepancy. Michael Porter Jr. had little-to-no interest closing out hard as the Nets gave up another bushel of corner threes in the second. The Knicks, despite having just 13 made field goals at halftime, went 15-of-16 from the line, while the Nets were just 4-of-6.

While the fan in you might want to pound your fist and chalk that up to an unfair "champ-friendly" whistle, the Nets weren't wise, even if innocent defenders, often fouling late in the shot clock and even the game clock, as Randle left his feet to give Brunson an extra pair right before the second quarter buzzer sounded. The Nets also fouled New York on three 3-point attempts.

So, Brooklyn trailed at the break by a 51-44 score. And early in the third quarter, they continued to lurk, as both teams traded buckets early on to keep the deficit intact.

The Knicks did piece together a 7-0 run at the heart of the frame, threatening to turn this into the blowout the 14.5 point spread advertised. That was, until Brown Jr. got back on the attack. He bolted through the New York defense for two quick finishes at the rim to ignite a 13-0 burst from Brooklyn, capped off by triples from Porter Jr. and Wagner, which gave them a small lead.

Brooklyn maintained that advantage, up 79-75 ahead the final frame. It was Brooklyn's first lead against the Knicks going into the fourth quarter since January of 2024.

It then evaporated in a flash, and became difficult to believe it had ever been there at all even quicker.

The Knicks began the fourth with a 9-0 jolt after the Nets missed two long threes and Wagner smoked a layup, which allowed New York to rebound, run, and shoot with space. Then, after a string of Brooklyn turnovers, it boiled into an extend 16-2 run. Like they had last summer, the Knicks looked like they owned the fourth quarter. The Nets looked like they were just renting space.

"I feel like we just wasn't connected as a group down the stretch," Brown Jr. said. "National champs, they played together for a long time, so we knew at some point they were going to make a run. That's just what great teams do. We didn't do our part on sustaining the level of connectiveness and just playing together on both ends of the floor."

Traoré hit his fourth triple to pump the brakes and make it a 91-84 game with 6:31 to go, but rather than swinging it, that shot got swallowed up by the New York momentum. The Nets kept missing shots around the rim and started losing all the 50/50 balls. With 3:50 to go, the Knicks had outscored Brooklyn in the period 23-5, and led on the scoreboard 98-84.

Shellshocked, the Nets could only let time trickle away by that point. Randle finished with 21 points and 11 rebounds, but went 1-3 from the field with four turnovers in the fourth. Porter Jr. finished with 18 points while shooting 4-11 from deep, but went 0-2 with zero points in nine fourth quarter minutes. Brown Jr. finished with 13 points, three assists, and two rebounds, but went 0-4 in the fourth with a turnovers. The team collectively shot 3-16 from the field in the final quarter.

While acknowledging the disappointment that comes with losing, Fernández opted to stay positive postgame.

"We played great for 39 minutes, and then the last nine were not good enough," he said. "I'm asking these guys to play as hard as they can, and the last two games, they've done it. There's a lot to learn from being organized and dealing with the lead, and obviously that's my responsibility to help them to be better right there.

"There's a lot of positive in this game to just throw everything out of the window think that we didn't do good things. It hurts because you wanted to win the game, and we're all competitive, but as we all know, if we keep playing as hard as we played in the last two games, there's going to be a lot of good things, and a lot of growth, because remember that it's not just a new group, but also a young group, and right now we want to see these steps. I think if you put too much negative energy into the group and into the young kids, then that that affects the growth. So, I'm proud of the group."

Final: New York Knicks 103, Brooklyn Nets 90

Julius Randle recorded his first double-double of the season tonight vs. NYK with 21 points and a season-high 10 rebounds. It is his first regular-season double-double in 23 outings, last recording one on 3/3/26 (MIN vs MEM).

With his 17th point tonight vs. NYK, Michael Porter Jr. reached 7,000 points in his NBA career. He is one of six players since his debut in 2019-20 to total 7,000 PTS, 2,500 REB and 1,000 3PM, joining Luka Dončić, James Harden, Jayson Tatum, Jaylen Brown and Lauri Markkanen.

Brooklyn gets a day off before going back home to host the Charlotte Hornets yet again, tipping off on Wednesday at 7:30 p.m. EST. After a brutal stretch to open the season, minus their first game, which of course came against Charlotte, this begins a winnable stretch of games for the Nets, with contests against Atlanta, Dallas, and New Orleans to follow.

#2799. The NFL, Caleb Williams shoe dispute takes center stage on Monday night

Monday night’s game between the Bears and Seahawks in Seattle comes with a subplot. Other than the ongoing Joe Buck and Troy Aikman drama.

The league has twice fined Chicago quarterback Caleb Williams for displaying an “unauthorized logo” (i.e., “the logo of a company that doesn’t pay us”) on his shoes. After the Week 6 game against the Falcons, the league fined Williams $11,941. After the Week 7 game against the Patriots, the league fined Williams $23,882 — twice the amount of the first fine.

Williams has said he will continue to wear the Caddix cleats, citing safety considerations. Unlike most if not all other NFL players who use Caddix footwear, Williams declines to cover the identifying markings with tape.

While the controversy calls back to former Bears quarterback Jim McMahon’s battles with the league over his Adidas headband during a playoff game (after being fined $5,000, he went with “ROZELLE” for the NFC Championship and “POW-MIA” for the Super Bowl) and to Bears linebacker Brian Urlacher’s whopping $100,000 fine for wearing a VitaminWater hat to Super Bowl XLI media day, Williams’s choice of footwear is rooted in the basic belief that the shoes promote player safety.

As to the refusal to cover the shoes with tape to hide the Caddix markings, it’s unclear whether he’s concerned about undermining the performance of the shoe or whether he’s simply trying to prove a point.

The NFL is clearly trying to prove a point, by fining him repeatedly. And while both prior fines are pending on appeal, a third fine is inevitable unless Williams bends.

Regardless, the next chapter arrives tonight. Neither of the fine letters threaten Williams with preventing him from playing if he doesn’t tape over the logos and markings. If the league decides to do that, Williams will have a pretty big decision to make.

Coach Ben Johnson was asked about that possible outcome on Saturday. “He’s all about the team, and I know he’s not going to hurt the team,” Johnson said.

The question of whether Johnson would be “hurting the team” is a matter of perspective. Williams wouldn’t be “hurting the team” by refusing to play; the NFL would be “hurting the team” by refusing to let Williams play in his preferred shoes.

Either way, both sides have been stubborn. It seems that a compromise could be reached, somehow.

#2794. The referee who became a role model after bouncing back from Diaz error

If anyone can talk about the highs and lows of being a referee, it is Darren England.

Three years ago, when acting as the video assistant referee (VAR), a blunder in a game between Tottenham and Liverpool stalled his career for months.

Luis Diaz scored for Liverpool, but his goal was flagged as offside. In a lapse of concentration, and despite the VAR image showing Diaz was onside, England said "check complete". The goal remained disallowed.

The South Yorkshire official suddenly found not only himself in the full glare of the media, but his family too.

"Refereeing is about low points and high points," England tells BBC Sport. "It's a rollercoaster of emotions.

"That was a low point. The lowest point, of course."

Today, the 40-year-old's career is revived. He is considered one of the most-trusted referees in the Premier League - both on the field and as a VAR.

Throughout 2026, England has regularly been given some of English football's biggest matches - including Manchester City's 1-0 win over Chelsea in the FA Cup final.

"So we flip it," England says, moving the conversation along to the game at Wembley. "That was a huge high for me, the pinnacle as a referee."

And on Tuesday, England has been promoted to a VAR in the Champions League for the first time, as Galatasaray take on Stuttgart.

Darren England made it to the Premier League as an assistant referee before becoming a referee, working his way back up from the National League [Getty Images]

The game has changed immeasurably in the 11 years since England swapped his flag for a whistle.

England says referees are now "dressed like RoboCop" as they carry so much additional equipment, such as communication devices.

The biggest change has been the introduction of VAR, which had only been in the Premier League for a few months when England refereed Southampton v Wolves in January 2020.

"It's certainly not changed the way I make decisions," England insists. "If I play on on a penalty decision, some people think the perception is 'oh you're waiting for VAR to get involved'.

"No, I've played on because I don't think it's a penalty.

"But I would rather be driving home from a game now thinking, 'OK, I misread it live, I've had the opportunity to go to the screen and we've corrected it'."

England underlines this, rejecting the notion that referees "don't care about football" when they get a decision wrong.

"It couldn't be further away from the truth," he says. "It's a myth that we go home, we switch off.

"It spoils your weekend if you make a decision that's had a big impact in the game.

From the VAR audio of the Diaz incident, it was clear England and his assistant VAR, Dan Cook were immediately aware they had made a huge mistake.

But the game was only 34 minutes old. They would have to get through the next hour.

"Once I realised I'd made the error, it's a really difficult place to try to forget that and move on," England says.

"I can't just physically stand up and walk out and leave it alone. A lot of resilience was needed - a lot of experience as well."

England described how the VAR hub is a "high pressure" and sanitised environment, with "mental fatigue" taking its toll.

There is no match commentary, just the conversation of the officiating team through their headsets.

"You don't have the atmosphere of the crowd," England says. "You hear some of the crowd sometimes, but it's just a noise.

"When you've had a busy match, you're constantly checking everything. You can come out of the hub sometimes and mentally you're exhausted."

What followed was a period of intense media scrutiny which England - and his family - were not prepared for.

The story dominated newspaper headlines, radio phone-ins and social media coverage for days.

Liverpool issued a statement that said "sporting integrity" had been "undermined".

Photographers gathered outside his children's school to try to get a picture of him for the newspapers.

One story highlighted the value of his home, while family photographs were taken from his wife's Facebook account.

"The aftermath obviously was really difficult to deal with," England says. "It was challenging because it's the goldfish bowl of the Premier League.

"But when mistakes happen, then you're in the public eye and criticism's inevitably going to come your way.

"That was difficult because it affected my family as well. We had people outside my girls' school, journalists and things like that.

"That then affects you not as a referee, but as a human being."

After the Diaz mistake, England was immediately removed from selection in the Premier League and began a process of rehabilitation.

It would be almost three months before he refereed a top-flight game again, and he did not return to full rotation until February.

It was a longer road back to the VAR room - six-and-a-half months before he was the video official in the Premier League again.

He was eased back in by the Football Association and given a couple of FA Cup ties with Michael Oliver alongside him as the support VAR.

"I did a lot of work with a sports psychologist," England says. "The support, not just from Pro Ref but more importantly family and friends, was really crucial.

"It's about perspective as well. There's a danger that we can think we're saving lives at times, but we also realise how important it is.

"I remained as focused as I could be, working hard, trusting myself, because for all that decision in the Liverpool-Tottenham game, I've made hundreds of other decisions that are correct."

All that focus has paid off, with England the VAR for a decision which was dubbed the 'biggest VAR call ever' as West Ham had a stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal disallowed on review in May.

England said he "absolutely understood the magnitude" of that decision but "kept calm" under pressure.

Six days later, England took charge of the FA Cup final.

"We're quick to always focus on mistakes and the low points, and how we deal with that," England adds.

"It's one of the targets when you start becoming professional that you want to referee the FA Cup final.

"You only do it once and it's a real honour."

VAR has added a huge amount of additional scrutiny on officials, not just from the press.

England says he will get quizzed by parents on the school run about decisions over the weekend - and not just his own. And then there are the fans online.

"If you want to go searching for good feedback on social media and you're listening to phone-ins, you probably won't find much," England says.

"That can have an impact on how you perform on the field.

"I don't have social media, I made a decision not to. But other people have different preferences and I respect that as well.

"But you have to manage your time accordingly, to be aware that you can never really switch off from football."

To dive or not to dive? Football's big dilemma

Wenger's 'daylight' offside trial unlikely to be extended

Is a double drop from Premier League becoming more common?

England's rise from his "lowest" point has been confirmed by his refereeing appointments.

But it has also been made clear by the respect of his colleagues - which BBC Sport saw first-hand at a referees' training camp at Loughborough University.

Hugh Dallas, the Professional Referee Group director, was at the front of the room, preparing to lead a discussion about decisions from the previous weekend. He paused for a moment, then beckoned forward a referee who, he said, had "become a role model".

That was England, who had recently taken charge of his 100th top-flight game. He was greeted with warm applause as he was handed a Premier League presentation box containing a plaque and a medal.

It is a journey that has taken England from his first match in the village of Royston, five miles outside Barnsley, to the top of the game - twice.

England, who qualified as a referee aged 15, is one of a few to come from inside the game, alongside the likes of Farai Hallam and Sam Allison.

He was working at Barnsley's academy, coaching during training in the week and matches on a Sunday, while refereeing on a Saturday.

Eventually, he had to choose between the two as a professional career - refereeing won.

England first made it to the Premier League as an assistant. Then, in 2015 at the age of 28, he decided to start again in the National League as a referee and work back up.

Within four and a half years, he would take charge of his first Premier League fixture.

"I had the chance of potentially going to tournaments (as an assistant), or do I back myself as a referee?" England says. "Thankfully, it paid off."

Referees only get the chance to referee the FA Cup final once - the exception being Anthony Taylor who took charge of the match twice [Getty Images]

England's progress has been closely monitored by Uefa, which has moved him through the levels as a VAR.

After 10 Conference League appointments, and six in the Europa League, this week he is elevated to the Champions League.

"We work extremely hard, and we continue to work extremely hard to stay at that level," England adds.

"Players in the Premier League, they're getting better and better. So we have to keep on improving as well."

After the honour of taking charge of the FA Cup final, does England have any other goals in his career on the field?

"When I don't have targets, that's probably time to come off the field," he says.

"I want to do all the finals that we can do. So obviously, the Carabao Cup, the Championship play-off final.

Three years ago, refereeing an FA Cup final and being a VAR in the Champions League seemed a world away for England.

Now, he's earned the right to have those targets.

#2792. Knicks 103, Nets 90: Scenes from ShamWow, Clarkson, and Kolek sparking life into a dead game

The Brooklyn Nets came into Madison Square Garden looking up from the bottom of the conference with a 1–5 record. They're the league's youngest team, and it shows on the court. And they'd played yesterday in Indiana. Their game against the Knicks (3–4) was either going to be a gimme or a trap. For much of the night, it smelled like the latter.

The home team decided to hurl a ton of three-pointers (44 of their 75 shots came from deep), sleepwalk through three quarters, and let Landry Shamet carry them for much of the night. Meanwhile, Brooklyn got inspired play from rookie Mikel Brown Jr. and won the third quarter 35–24 to take a four-point lead into the fourth. In the final frame, the Knicks came alive (with a special appearances by Tyler Kolek and Jordan Clarkson), outscored the visitors 28–11, and pulled out a 103–90 win.

In the first quarter, the Nets took a four-point lead, which the Knicks deleted and flipped into a nine-point advantage. So far this season, OG Anunoby (18 PTS, 3-7 3PT, 2 STL, 38 MIN) has been up and down, and perhaps Mike Brown was hoping to inject some excitement into his wing by calling his number early. Anunoby attempted two three-pointers (making one) and converted a cutting layup (dimed by Karl-Anthony Towns) to get New York on the scoreboard.

The game featured a fair amount of jostling, but the refs let it go. Midway through the frame, Landry Shamet (22 PTS, 6-8 FG, 29 MIN), Andre Drummond (9 RBS, 4 PTS, 13 MIN), and Miles McBride (6 PTS, 16 MIN) subbed in. Jalen Brunson (19 PTS, 4-11 3PT, 6 AST, 33 MIN) made three of his first four attempts from the yard before Jose Alvarado (back from a sprained ankle) relieved him at the three-minute mark. Cap and Deuce combined for five treys in the first.

Brooklyn shot so poorly that the rims seemed magnetically opposed to their attempts. Twice or thrice, the ball rolled around the cylinder before flying off to become a defensive rebound. Julius Randle (21 PTS, 10 RBS) and Michael Porter, Jr. (18 PTS, 4-11 3PT) are Brooklyn's marquee players, but neither did much in the first frame. The former missed all three of his shot attempts, and the latter scored five points on five attempts. On the whole, the Nets missed 13 shots and turned the ball over four times. At the break, they trailed New York, 27–21.

Mercury is in retrograde, and the second quarter proved it with a few rarities. Mikal Bridges (6 PTS, 1-of-7 FG, 16 MIN) attempted his first free throws, six whole games into the campaign. Towns (11 PTS, 16 RBS) played 13 minutes before taking his second shot, but grabbed his tenth rebound of the night with six minutes left in the half. And Mohamed "Free Mo" Diawara (0 PTS, 6 MIN) appeared after playing just one minute so far this season. The sophomore grabbed a rebound.

While the Nets don't excel at any conventional basketball skills, they do have teeth. Brooklyn played yesterday (beating the Hoosiers of Indiana), but your lyin' eyes would convince you that New York had the more fatigued fellas. Even the Garden crowd seemed mid-yawn for most of the second period. This borough buddy has a rotten record, but they took Boston into overtime this season, and the Knicks watched them score nine unanswered points early in the frame. A late-quarter bomb from Brunson steadied the boat but failed to ignite the team. Only when the half had nearly closed did Josh Hart (8 PTS, 7 AST, 6 RBS, +22) and Shamet—14 flippin points and counting!—connect from deep to give New York an eight-point lead. Then, after Randle made two free throws, he fouled Brunson on a foot-on-the-line jumper with 0.5 seconds left. Oh, Julius, I remember ye well. Intermission score: 51–44.

Rookie Mikel Brown, Jr. was having quite a MSG debut:

The score was a lot closer than the game felt. Our heroes had been outshot 40% to 36% from the field. They'd survived on threes and free throws while barely making any hay inside the arc. Ten of their 13 buckets came from downtown (shooting 40% there), and they'd taken 16 freebies to Brooklyn's six. Rebounds and turnovers were even at 21 and seven, respectively. Shamet led all first-half scorers with 14 points, while Nolan Traore had 11 for the villains. No points for KAT yet, and don't look now, but Bridges was having another bad shooting night.

The third quarter brought more of the same. Bridges missed again (1-of-7 thus far), but he wasn't alone. Brunson missed a long shot, and Day'Ron Sharpe and Traore blocked Towns and Brunson, respectively. With the offense a pasty, anemic color, Mike Brown sent in Jordan Clarkson (7 PTS, 11 MIN, +17) at around the 8:45 mark. Clarkson guarded Porter tenaciously and made a contested shot despite being hacked (no whistle), but he got dinged for two quick personal fouls and picked up a tech for complaining about that absent whistle. It's a bummer, because the fouls got him a quick hook just when some of us were starting to wonder if he, Shamet, or Towns might resurrect this lifeless game.

Meanwhile, Towns was taking the ball straight down the painted boulevard on repeated drives. He collected his first nine points of the night, going 3-of-4 from the field and 2-of-3 at the line. After two driving layups, he buried a three off Brunson's dime at 5:58. During that stretch, Cap added five points on two buckets and a free throw, but missed a three and had a layup blocked.

(For those watching the third quarter at home, Clyde dropped a "Posting and Toasting" at the 7:42 mark AND at 6:30. We hear you, GOAT!)

Mikel Brown scored on consecutive drives down Broadway, and a flummoxed Mike Brown called an exasperated timeout around 4:30. Those hoops cut Brooklyn's deficit to five. Porter hit from deep after the timeout to make it two, and Mo Wagner swished a triple for a one-point lead. When Porter dropped another bomb, that made 13 straight points for the bad guys. Whatever Mike said in the timeout didn't motivate.

Diawara was back in the game, but Shamet was the one whose three-pointer gave us some hope for salvation (which the misses by Drummond and Brunson that bookended his shot did not). Another bomb by Shamet on an inbounds play gave him a season high and narrowed the gap with a minute left. But Randle made shots at the stripe, Anunoby and Brunson were both blocked on drives, and Brooklyn's 19–6 run gave them a 79–75 lead at the break.

Needing a spark, it was another bench player to the rescue. Tyler Kolek checked in to start the fourth quarter and hit the ground running. He dished to Hart for a triple, then Hart found a trailing Anunoby for another bomb, and the game took a more favorable turn. The crowd rejoiced when OG swished another three, and although Randle bucketed on a drive, Hart returned the favor to Kolek by finding him wide-open under the rim.

Brooklyn's coach Jordi Fernández needed a timeout to get his young troops back in line. Out of the break, Randle coughed up the ball twice and Hart made good on a fast-break layup. When Clarkson hit from the corner, he capped a 16-2 run and goosed the lead to 10. Randle blew a layup and Fernández yanked him with seven minutes left, and Mike Brown swapped Kolek for Brunson. The Nets had scored just five points by the five-minute mark, and New York had stretched their advantage to 12.

The Knicks' energized defense had forced six turnovers (and counting), while Bridges continued to sit after getting pulled with 8:44 left in the third quarter. With three minutes left, Mike Brown sent in all his starters—except Bridges, electing instead to ride with Shamet. Fernandez kept his starters in, too, but the outcome was decided. The home team had won the frame 28-11 and that was the ballgame.

Chicago will visit on Wednesday, hoping to avenge last week's loss to New York. Mo's got a recap in the chamber for you. Rest up, Knickerbockers.

#2790. 'I don't like that': Jaylen Brown admits he dislikes what the 76ers have been doing this season

The Philadelphia 76ers have started the season in magnificent style, winning seven of their first eight games.

The latest of those victories came against the Chicago Bulls on Monday night, when the Sixers stepped it up in the second half again.

Jaylen Brown arguably had his best game yet with the 76ers, but he didn't seem fully satisfied with how his side performed against the Bulls.

The 76ers have shown the impressive trait of stepping it up late in games after slow starts.

In fact, in five of their seven wins so far this season, the Sixers weren't great in the first half but showed their class by going up a level after the break to secure those victories.

That is undoubtedly a great trait to have, but Brown has warned his teammates that this could come back to bite them in tougher games.

The former Boston Celtics star made it clear that he doesn't like these slow starts and urged his teammates to be at it from the first whistle.

When a reporter asked Brown if the ability to flip the switch in second halves gives the Sixers confidence, he replied: "No. I don't like that we have that.

"It's good that we have shown the potential, but we've got to keep that switch on. It doesn't work like that, where you just flip the switch and catch up to it. It can bite us against a better team, or on a night that we're not being as crisp on offence.

"So, there can't be a switch just because we're playing a lesser opponent or just because whatever the case may be. We have got to make sure that mentality is from the beginning to the end. Can't skip any steps."

Brown is spot on. The Sixers' ability to turn games on their head in the second half is definitely impressive, but they can't rely on that in every game.

The focus has to be on dominating the first and second quarters just as well as they do in the fourth. If they do that, they will become even bigger favourites to make the NBA Finals this year.
