#2788. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander drops season-high 43 points including dagger 3 to lead hobbled Thunder past Cavs

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander had a poor shooting night and played without several of his top teammates Monday.

It did not matter. The two-time MVP scored a season-high 43 points including a late go-ahead 3 that iced a 117-112 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers. The win snapped a two-game losing streak as the Thunder continue to adjust to playing without several of their best players.

Starters Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace are all sidelined with long-term injuries. The Thunder also played Monday without Alex Caruso, who's nursing a sprained right ankle.

OKC still had Gilgeous-Alexander, and that was a enough alongside a makeshift starting lineup for victory over the Eastern Conference hopeful Cavaliers. Gilgeous-Alexander shot just 40% from the field. But he hit the shots when they mattered most, most notably a late 3 that gave the Thunder the lead for good.

With the game tied at 112-112 in the final minute, Gilgeous-Alexander gained just enough separation from his defender, Sam Merrill, to pull up for a 3 from the left wing. The shot sank through the net for a 3-point Thunder lead with 32.6 seconds remaining.

The Cavaliers didn't score again, and the Thunder secured the win to improve to 5-2.

After the game, Gilgeous-Alexander spoke with NBC about the Thunder adjusting in the face of injury adversity after entering the season on the short list of favorites to compete for an NBA title.

"Just figuring it out," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "You never know what the future has in store for you. All you can do is play the cards you're dealt."

Gilgeous-Alexander tallied 43 points, 8 assists, 3 rebounds and 2 steals. He shot 14 of 35 from the field, 11 of 12 from the line and 4 of 8 from 3.

The 35 shots tied a career high and could be indicative of things to come with Williams and Holmgren sidelined. The All-Star tandem have been OKC's second- and third-leading scorers behind Gilgeous-Alexander for the past three seasons.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander put up a career-high 35 field goal attempts in what could be a sign of things to come for Oklahoma City.

Instead, it was Ajay Mitchell, Jaylin Williams and Kenrich Williams who joined Gilgeous-Alexander and Isaiah Hartenstein in the starting lineup Monday night. Mitchell finished second on the Thunder in scoring with 20 points and five rebounds, while Kenrich Williams add 12 points on 5-of-7 shooting.

It's OKC's trademark smothering defense that could suffer the most through injuries. Williams, Wallace, Holmgren and Caruso have all earned All-Defensive team selections in their careers and can't be replaced. The result Monday night was just seven turnovers committed by the Cavaliers.

But none of Cleveland's offensive stars broke out. Donovan Mitchell tied for the team lead with 17 points alongside 11 assists and five rebounds. Instead, it was a balanced team effort with seven players in double figures that kept the game close. A 58% (14 of 24) effort from the free-throw line ultimately doomed the Cavaliers.

The two teams will play each other again Wednesday night as they complete their season series in Oklahoma City and the Thunder continue to learn to play with a new-look lineup.

#2783. Georgia Football Could Be in Serious Trouble If Georgia Goes Blue on Tuesday

ATHENS, Ga. — Georgia football fans have spent years worrying about Alabama, Texas and the occasional quarterback controversy.

But Tuesday could introduce a completely different opponent.

If Georgia goes blue in the governor's race, Bulldogs fans might start wondering whether Kirby Smart's recruiting machine is about to face an entirely new set of challenges.

After all, Georgia football runs on money.

It takes money to recruit five-star prospects, retain elite players, build facilities and keep pace with the increasingly expensive college football landscape.

And it takes a healthy economy to keep the boosters, businesses and donors happy enough to keep writing checks.

That's why some Bulldogs fans could view Tuesday's election as more than a political contest.

It could be a referendum on the future of Georgia football's financial ecosystem.

Georgia has already spent years battling Alabama for SEC supremacy.

The last thing Smart needs is to start worrying about the economic policies coming out of the governor's mansion.

Keisha Lance Bottoms has supported policies such as a $15 minimum wage and increased public-sector pay. Those proposals don't directly dictate NIL spending, but critics could argue that increased operating costs might put pressure on some businesses.

And businesses are part of the ecosystem supporting major college football programs.

If sponsors and donors become more financially cautious, Georgia's recruiting operation could eventually feel some pressure.

Imagine telling a five-star defensive end that his NIL package is being reconsidered because the local business community is tightening its belt.

Alabama would never let Georgia hear the end of it.

There is another reason Bulldogs fans might be nervous about a blue Georgia.

Georgia Tech has spent years living in the shadow of its in-state rival. A political shift would not suddenly turn Atlanta into a recruiting powerhouse for Brent Key, but it could provide plenty of material for Georgia fans to worry about.

In the completely fictional nightmare scenario, a Tech-friendly administration starts asking uncomfortable questions about Georgia's football operation.

Are practices too physical? Is Kirby Smart pushing players too hard? Why does the head coach seem to have somewhere important to be every time he gets behind the wheel?

Suddenly, the Bulldogs are spending more time answering questions than preparing for Saturday.

It would be an absolute nightmare in Athens.

To be clear, a Democratic governor would not automatically destroy Georgia's economy or Georgia football's NIL operation.

The governor does not control private NIL agreements, and Georgia's recruiting resources extend far beyond the state's borders.

But college football is increasingly an economic arms race.

The schools with the strongest financial ecosystems have a major advantage. Anything that makes donors, sponsors and businesses more cautious could eventually matter.

That is why some Georgia fans may be looking at Tuesday's election through a very specific lens.

They don't necessarily care about the political implications of a blue Georgia when they walk into Sanford Stadium.

They care about whether Kirby Smart can keep landing five-star recruits.

And if the Bulldogs suddenly start losing NIL battles, don't be surprised if somebody in Athens starts blaming the governor.

Georgia football has survived plenty of challenges.

But a blue Georgia, a revitalized Georgia Tech and a financially stressed NIL operation?

That might be more than even Kirby Smart wants to deal with.

#2780. Pistons vs. Hornets final score: Cade Cunningham powers second-half surge in blowout win

The Detroit Pistons played great basketball throughout the night, but the Charlotte Hornets just kept hanging around. The Pistons were shooting better than 60% from the floor and 50% from three, and yet a Dennis Schroder layup made it a two-possession game with just under five minutes left in the second quarter. Then Cade Cunningham took over, then the Detroit Pistons took over, and suddenly a squeaker turned into a 124-91 Detroit win.

In that decisive 45-16 run, Cade Cunningham scored 14 points, and he did it in under three and a half minutes of game time. One of the league's best players finally had his first superstar quarter of the season, scoring 17 points and notching three assists in total in that decisive third frame. He finished the night with 33 points, seven assists, and five steals. In those magical few minutes, he was everywhere in his bag. Patient mid-range pull-ups, slicing through the D for layups, catch-and-shoot threes. He went to the bench with 1:17 left in the third quarter, and you were left thinking he might hit 50 in the fourth. But he never needed to come back in the game again.

He saw the game was getting too close, and he decided to do something about it. He put the team on his back and said, "We're playing too well to not blow these guys out."

But the true blowout wouldn't have happened without all the other contributions up and down the lineup. The Pistons really have something on offense this season, and while the range of ball handlers and actions can lead to some self-inflicted wounds, it is designed to open up this offense and let it breathe. And, boy, did they take a big gulping breath versus the Hornets.

The Pistons shot 57% from the floor and 48% from deep, and that was dragged down a bit as a consequence of some extended garbage time. The Pistons also kept their defense in top form. They forced 25 Charlotte turnovers, and that led to 27 fast-break points.

Detroit was led by Cade, but Duncan Robinson continues to be lights out this season. He shot 6-of-9 from deep on his way to 24 points. His stroke was immediate and effortless. He's truly in the zone. Some of that shooting magic might be rubbing off on Kevin Huerter. The one-time bucket has struggled from deep for a few seasons now, including his short stint after a mid-season trade to Detroit last season. But he hit three threes tonight and is now shooting 38% from deep for the season. Even Ron Holland canned three threes tonight. Not to be overlooked is Ausar Thompson's expanded role in the offense.

It's not always perfect, but Thompson is getting more comfortable making decisions with the ball in his hands, and he's understanding how to make defense pay by using his strength and burst to get something close to the basket. Thompson was 5-of-7 from the floor for 14 points, and he added six rebounds and four assists.

The Pistons had plenty of lopsided runs last season in their sprint to 60 wins. But those were driven by a defense that would suffocate you and an offense that could do just enough. Last year, the Pistons could go on a 27-2 run over the course of 17 minutes of game action. Tonight, they went on the same run in just over eight minutes.

Detroit's defense remains the best in the league. Its offense is starting to catch up. That's bad news for everyone else in the NBA.

#2769. Five takeaways from No. 22 UCLA stunning victory over No. 5 Arizona

The No. 22 UCLA Bruins defeated the No. 5 Arizona Wildcats 84-75 at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, Nev. to open the season on Monday.

The Bruins will likely jump up the rankings as they appeared to more physical team in a matchup that looked more like a game during March than the season opener. UCLA head coach Mick Cronin will undoubtedly have plenty of areas for the team to improve upon based on their performance, but here were five takeaways from the impressive win that Cronin and his group accomplished to open the season.

The Bruins played tough, physical basketball from start to finish and they have the fouls to prove it. UCLA did everything they could to knock Arizona out of rhythm and that started with limiting the Wildcats senior center Motiejus Krivas to just eight points as he played with a cut on his chin he received from the start of the game. Any time Arizona tried to come back into the game, UCLA pushed back and if they keep this energy over the course of the season, then it's hard to imagine them not making it far in March.

Cronin should be happy with what he saw for the most part on defense, but he will likely do his best to find something UCLA can improve upon. The Bruins were plastered on to Wildcat jerseys and ripped away five steals and seven blocks as well as 29 defensive rebounds. Nothing came easy for Arizona and that was by design. The Bruins limiting Arizona to 37 percent from the field and 23 percent from beyond the arc was a recipe for success and it could have been even better if Arizona sophomore forward Ivan Kharchenkov didn't have a career night with 38-points.

Junior point guard Trent Perry was the calming presence on the court when they needed him the most. Perry saw limited action in the first half of the game after he racked up two personal fouls, but he was essential in stabilizing the Bruins on the court in the second half as Arizona constantly attempted their comebacks. Although Perry made just 4-of-12 from the field, he put up 21-points thanks to his perfect 11-points from the line. The young star has continued to improve from his time on the court last season and should continue to improve as the season goes on.

UCLA did what they needed to on offense as they powered their way to the rim and forced the Wildcats to defend every inch of the court. The Bruins had 16 offensive rebounds, which proved fruitful in them extending their lead over the course of the game with their leading three-point shooter being sophomore guard Jaylen Petty, who made 4-of-6 from beyond the arc. As productive as the Bruins were on offense, UCLA shot 34 percent from downtown, but there were some errant attempts with freshman forward Nikola Kusturica and senior forward Eric Dailey Jr. both shooting and missing all five of their attempts.

The Bruins made a statement win as they powered through the No. 5 ranked team in the preseason polls with a mix of new and old players being productive. Perry lead the team in offense with 21-points, but Petty's and sophomore forward Segej Macura's shooting opened up the floor for other players to make plays. Senior center Xavier Booker and Dailey Jr. both showed veteran savvy throughout the game to stabilize some of the erratic errors made by their young teammates. Of course, Kusturica also showed why he was one of the highest regarded additions to the team as he made plays on both sides of the ball and showed that he was talented enough to develop into a star for the Bruins.

#2768. Hawks escape six-man Pacers 108–104 after record-tying first half

The Atlanta Hawks escaped with a 108–104 victory over an Indiana Pacers team with just six available players Monday, surviving a late rally behind Nickeil Alexander-Walker's 34 points.

Alexander-Walker connected on nine of his 15 three-point attempts. CJ McCollum finished one rebound shy of a triple-double with 13 points, 12 assists and nine rebounds, while Onyeka Okongwu contributed 13 points and 10 rebounds.

Atlanta made 15 three-pointers before halftime, tying the franchise record for any half. However, its hot shooting gave way to a stagnant offense after the break, allowing the depleted Pacers to fight their way back.

The Hawks were also missing key players, with Jalen Johnson sidelined by a left ankle sprain and Kingston Flemings serving a one-game suspension. Still, against an Indiana team operating with such limited personnel, Atlanta made the finish considerably harder than it needed to be.

The opening quarter offered little indication of those later struggles. Atlanta shot 60 percent from the field and 70 percent from three-point range, establishing an early offensive rhythm.

Rookie Zuby Ejiofor also made his regular-season debut, connecting from beyond the arc for his first NBA basket.

The Hawks maintained control through the second quarter, although Indiana showed the persistence that kept it competitive throughout the night. An 11–2 Pacers run cut the deficit to single digits, but Atlanta continued making perimeter shots to finish its record-tying half.

After halftime, those shots stopped falling as consistently. Atlanta led by as many as 15 points, but Indiana put together a 7–0 third-quarter run to help trim the deficit to five.

The Hawks' ball movement stalled, leaving them with stagnant possessions against a more active Pacers defense. Indiana outscored Atlanta 23–19 in the quarter, setting up a competitive finish.

Atlanta continued leaving the door open in the fourth. Fouls gave the Pacers opportunities at the free-throw line, while a late 9–0 Indiana run made it a one-possession game.

The Hawks ultimately held on, but the result did little to erase concerns about their second-half execution. Alexander-Walker's shooting and McCollum's playmaking helped secure the victory, yet Atlanta struggled to sustain the offensive flow needed to put away its opponent.

Indiana deserves credit for its effort. Despite having only six players available, the Pacers continued competing, increased their defensive pressure and gave themselves a chance to win late.

For Atlanta, the victory was welcome, but the performance left plenty to address. A record-tying shooting half should have provided the foundation for a more controlled finish. Instead, the Hawks needed to survive a final push from a severely shorthanded opponent.

The Hawks next face the Washington Wizards on Wednesday, hoping to have Jalen Johnson and Jock Landale back in the lineup.

#2763. 3 takeaways as the Mavericks fall into a 115-100 trap against the Sacramento Kings

The Dallas Mavericks (4-3) fell to the Sacramento Kings (1-6), 115-100, in a Monday night matchup at the American Airlines Center. The game against the previously winless Kings followed the Mavericks' Friday night win in Game 1 of NBA Cup group play. Dallas was unable to overcome night in the freezer on offense against a Kings team that was desperately seeking its first win on Monday.

Kyrie Irving was ruled out early Monday evening due to left knee injury management. Santi Aldama, Tarik Biberovic, Sergio de Larrea, and Dereck Lively were also out for the Mavericks. Keegan Murray, Maxime Raynaud, and Dylan Cardwell were the notable players absent from the Kings.

Walter Clayton Jr. and Daniel Gafford led the Mavericks with 20 points apiece. Darius Acuff led all scorers with 25 points for the Kings.

Mavericks head coach Dusty May decided to go with a no-guard starting lineup, inserting Caleb Martin into the first five with Irving's absence. The game started slowly for both teams, with both squads struggling to get their offense going in the first quarter. Dallas played 10 of the first 12 minutes of the first quarter without a point guard in the lineup, and the offense struggled as a result. The Mavericks finished the first period down 19-18 in a game that was quickly devolving into a snooze fest.

The Mavericks entered the second quarter more inspired, finally getting shots to fall behind Daniel Gafford shots at the rim. Once Cooper Flagg got going, the Mavericks gave themselves a little breathing room from the Kings. Walter Clayton gave Dallas the offensive boost it needed in the second period, but the Mavericks were unable to string together enough stops to separate themselves from the Kings.

Morez Johnson Jr. was a bright spot in this quarter for the Mavericks, playing aggressively on the glass and imposing his strength, getting to the foul line on three occasions. Sacramento punched back behind a string of buckets from Malik Monk, and the Mavericks walked into the intermission with the same deficit they faced after the first quarter, down 54-53.

Clayton started the second half for the Mavericks after it was announced that Max Christie would not be returning to the game due to a hip injury. Dallas entered the third quarter as slowly as they played the first half, struggling to get the offense going in any capacity. The Mavericks continued to try to claw their way out of the hole they found themselves in, but entered the final quarter down 81-74.

Dallas continued to struggle throughout the fourth quarter, with Clayton being the only Maverick to see shots fall late. Darius Acuff and Malik Monk continued to take advantage of the Mavericks' defensive missteps, completely shifting the momentum in the Kings' favor. The Mavericks were ultimately unable to dig themselves out of the deficit they faced all game, falling 115-100.

Here are three takeaways from tonight's loss.

When it was announced that Irving would be out for tonight's matchup, concerns arose regarding how the Mavericks offense would operate in his absence. Naji Marshall struggled in his return tonight after missing the last three games due to an illness. Christie continued to make no impact before leaving the game with that hip injury. The Mavs tried to shoot themselves out of their offensive struggles, to no success, finishing 7-of-33 from behind the arc.

The Mavericks are going to need more from guys like Marshall and PJ Washington when Irving is out, or they will continue to struggle in games where Dallas decides to rest Irving. Clayton stepped up when the Mavericks needed offensive contributions, but the Mavericks cannot depend on a two-way player every night.

"Shots weren't falling, and it kind of got in our head," Gafford said in a televised portion of his postgame press conference. "They wanted it more than we did. The energy was a little low."

Morez Johnson Jr. set a career-high in points tonight, with 13 points, and added two rebounds. Johnson was a bright spot in tonight's game, holding his own against Domantas Sabonis and Precious Achiuwa. He played physically, grabbing two offensive rebounds to lead to extra possessions for the Mavericks. He was also able to exert his strength to get to the foul line, though he shot 3-of-6 from the charity stripe. The ninth pick in the 2026 NBA Draft played more comfortably tonight and kept his foul count low again tonight, a pain point for him in the first several games for the Mavericks. Coach May gave insight into how he has coached Johnson before tonight's game.

Johnson highlighted this tonight, fighting on the glass and playing physically in the paint. Johnson will grow as a player if he continues to do the little things like he did tonight.

Cooper Flagg struggled against the Kings following his 33-point performance against the Rockets on Friday. He finished with 17 points on 3-of-19 from the field. Flagg struggled to take over offensively in Irving's absence. He was able to get to the free-throw line at a high volume, but failed to see his shots fall all night long. Luckily, this will be one of the worst performances we see from him. Dallas was unable to provide any contributions behind Flagg, putting this one out of reach for the Mavericks.

The Mavericks are back in action Wednesday night as they travel to San Antonio to face the Spurs. Catch the action at 8:30 p.m. CT on ESPN.

Hurts played five games before going on injured reserve with blood clots; Johnson retired after three games; Jurgens played four games with the Eagles before a trade to the Ravens; Barkley has missed two games and been limited in others with injuries; Smith has missed four games with a hamstring injury; and Wicks has missed two games with an ankle injury.

The Eagles are averaging 17.1 points a game.

McKee has started the past three games, completing 63.2 percent of his passes for 639 yards with two touchdowns and two interceptions.

“Tanner’s our guy. We’re not making any changes there,” Sirianni said. “Again, how do we find solutions? That could be within scheme; that could be within how our schedule is, practice plays. Everything’s on the table for us in that aspect. But right now, this is where we are, and we’re trying to find solutions there. We’re looking at everything as far as what we can do differently as coaches.”

McKee’s backup, Joe Milton, only arrived in Philadelphia on Oct. 16, signing from the Cowboys’ practice squad.

#2754. Warriors predicted to part ways with ex-Celtics' $20M NBA champion amid ongoing health battle

Warriors predicted to part ways with ex-Celtics' $20M NBA champion amid ongoing health battle originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Over the summer, one of the most questionable moves the Golden State Warriors made, outside of not acquiring a superstar-caliber player to pair with Steph Curry, was undoubtedly signing Kristaps Porzingis. The veteran center has struggled to stay healthy throughout his career, yet Golden State brought him in as a potential starter.

The plan was for Porzingis to start and potentially rebuild his trade value. However, none of that has materialized. Porzingis was unable to participate in training camp because of a medical issue, which turned out to be an autoimmune condition that could potentially threaten his career.

"Golden State has started exploring trade routes for Kristaps Porzingis, who is now seriously contemplating his future in basketball as he deals with recurring symptoms from the autoimmune condition termed as POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), sources tell ESPN," ESPN's Shams Charania posted.

In fact, there is currently little reason to believe Porzingis will play for the Warriors again.

"Team sources continue to express an extreme level of pessimism that Porzingis will ever play for the Warriors again, but he could end up helping the organization in another way, because his contract, which is only guaranteed for $3 million next season, could still prove to be valuable in executing a trade," ESPN's Anthony Slater wrote.

Bleacher Report's Zach Buckley also believes Porzingis could become a valuable trade asset for Golden State.

"They should still be probing for upgrades, though. They need to give Stephen Curry more help, and with Porziņģis once again stuck in a worrisome health situation, he seems incapable of providing it. But his $20 million salary (and tiny $3 million guarantee for next season) could be a gear-greaser for that kind of get. He can't have much (if any) standalone value given the constant availability concerns, but teams with big plans for the loaded 2027 free agency class could want to get their hands on that contract," Buckley wrote.

It clearly does not look like Porzingis will suit up for Golden State again, and the Warriors could eventually look to trade him. This was always a possible way for his tenure with the team to end, but his health was not supposed to be the determining factor.

The Warriors are focused on building around Curry, and they cannot afford to rely on a player who may never take the court again. Eventually, Golden State will likely part ways with Porzingis.

A Bears win over the Vikings would give both team two losses and two NFC North losses as well as two NFC losses. It would move the tiebreaker to the Strength of Victory tiebreaker until the Common Games opponents gets to four games, and Chicago would move ahead of Minnesota on the SOV.

In addition to those two NFC North teams winning, the Green Bay Packers won on Thursday night to stick in the seventh and final Wild Card slot. All four NFC North teams are in a playoff spot.

1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1, strength of victory .456)

2. Minnesota Vikings (6-1, strength of victory .400)

10. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5, win over ATL, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 3-2 NFC)

11. Atlanta Falcons (3-5, loss to TB, 3-3 NFC record)

12. Arizona Cardinals (3-5, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 2-4 NFC)

13. Dallas Cowboys (3-5, 0-2 vs TB+ARZ, loss to ARZ)

#2751. San Antonio vs. Utah, Final Score: Two impressive Spurs quarters are plenty versus Jazz, 119-97

Behind its dogged dedication on both ends in the first and third periods, San Antonio ran its undefeated streak to five with a 119-97 win over Utah. After conducting a well-played first 12 minutes with balanced contributions, San Antonio held on to that advantage while fending off an extended Jazz run over much of the second quarter. The Spurs then left no doubt after that, as their starters ran the Jazz off the floor in a 35-20 third period.

Dylan Harper (17 points, 8 assists, 7 rebounds, and 2 steals) led the way for San Antonio (5-2) with seven players (and all starters) getting into double figures. Western Conference Player of the Week Victor Wembanyama (12 points, 11 rebounds, 5 assists, and 3 blocks) seemed content to ride shotgun, as Devin Vassell (11 points) carried the offense over many of the team's second quarter minutes, while newly 22-year-old Stephon Castle (16 points, 5 rebounds, and 4 assists) and De'Aaron Fox (12 points and 3 assists in foul-limited minutes) helped their fellow guards outshine their less experienced Jazz counterparts. Keldon Johnson (15 points and 7 rebounds) was forceful and effective off the bench.

Lauri Markkanen (22 points and 8 rebounds) carried the offense in comparison to Utah's (1-6) callow execution throughout the evening. Jaxson Hayes (9 points and 5 rebounds) and Mo Bamba (8 points and 8 rebounds) provided moments of punch before the Jazz succumbed to the superior Spurs.

All five starters shared well in scoring the team's first 14 points, and the Spurs collectively went up ten early on a sluggish Jazz squad. Utah scores came sparingly throughout the opening frame and their two recent rookie selections combined to go 0-for-8. The Spurs' team defense proved adept both at guiding dribble-drives into the corners away from the rim and crowding the airspace around shooters. San Antonio got in its own way by missing a handful of free throws. All of the impressive two-way execution also was dragged out over a series of referee stoppages throughout the first and yet, the Spurs still left it up 11.

Markkanen found his shooting touch to start the second and helped bring Utah's deficit into single digits. Despite their unrelenting effort to catch and surpass San Antonio, the hosts persevered through many tough minutes throughout the quarter. Vassell and Harper's exploits kept the Spurs afloat, while well-traveled veterans Josh Okogie and Mo Bamba bolstered Markkenen's production. After Wembanyama's tip dunk midway through the second, the non-Wembanyamas fended off Utah 22-15 to make it a 59-49 game at the half.

San Antonio came out of the break intent to prevent any further Utah runs with its trio of Castle, Fox, and Harper doing the bulk of the damage to inflate its lead throughout the third as high as 22. The Spurs, in particular, negated any further support outside of Markkanen in a 35-20 quarter.

"Momma There Go Those Young Men" Sequence: Putting the finishing touches on a San Antonio push over the middle part of the third, Harper nabbed a crosscourt pass, and looked destined to glide in for a lay-up before he lobbed a feather to Castle for a tomahawk jam.

Tarris Reed, Jr. (lithe AND bruising big man) playing time: 3 points and SEVEN rebounds in SEVEN minutes of action!

Wembanyama played nearly 15 feet off of Jaxson Hayes during the initial possession as the Utah center floated outside the paint.

Utah was content to cede Wembanyama the free throw line extended for a good chunk of his first half shot diet to moderate success.

San Antonio's wings helped offset Utah's frontline size in the first half by hitting the defensive boards in droves.

Aside from a quick shooting stroke, there wasn't much that stood out about Peterson. He looked like early-career Buddy Hield out there.

A tussle between Brice Sensabaugh and Harrison Barnes (13 points) was likely not on anyone's scorecard tonight.

Kornet looks heavy-footed when he's going from baseline-to-baseline, but he's playing that dunker spot fairly well.

Sequence of the Game #1: Three-plus minutes in, Wembanyama snagged an errant Jazz miss and, instead of bringing it up himself, floated a 60 foot pass gently into Fox's ready hands for a transition lay-up.

Sequence of the Game #2: Late in the first half, Luke Kornet altered a George three attempt and, moments later, Fox rewarded the center by feeding him for a reverse lay-up at the other end.

Sequence of the Game #3: As part of an opening 10-4 to start the second half, Wembanyama swatted away a George floater, came to a jumpstop short of the paint, and found a streaking Harper for a soaring slam. On the next possession, Harper snared what seemed like a sure turnover on a Wembanyama pass, faked a pass back to his big man, and lofted a floater gently into the net.

Peterson poorly closed out on a Vassell (pronounced by the crew chief as "VASS-ull") corner three and was assessed a Flagrant 1 foul and the Spur guard netted three points from the line. Fox 's straightaway three and Wembanyama's banker put the Spurs up six. Utah's rookie again figured in a referee-involved situation as a shooting foul committed by Castle on Peterson was challenged and overruled. Harper converted a transition lay-up to make it 18-4, and the ensuing foul put Utah in the foul bonus halfway through the stanza. George's second basket came 8+ minutes into the quarter. Will Hardy challenged a Utah foul on a Fox attempt and won it, and Markkanen got the Jazz into double digits 10 minutes in. San Antonio held Utah to its lowest quarterly output of the young season and led 27-16 after one.

Markkanen's pair catch-and-shoot threes at the start of the second quickly brought the Jazz within five. Fox picked up his third foul 50 seconds in. Harper found Johnson crosscourt for an open three and followed that with a triple of his own. Vassell rescued a stalled-out sequence with a late clock jumper. A transition three from Bailey brought Utah within one and their increased aggression drew San Antonio into the foul bonus halfway through the second. Kornet got his first block on a George three, scored a reverse lay-up at the other end, and then set-up Castle for a three to prevent the Jazz from taking the lead. San Antonio built back up its cushion culminating with Johnson's timely pair of lay-ups. Despite Utah's opening push, the Spurs ended the half having lost only one point from their first quarter differential.

Harper and Fox dual-wielded their impressive scoring abilities deep in the paint to start the third, and San Antonio got the lead briefly back up to 16. Coach Johnson called a Pop-like timeout after George scored mere seconds after a Castle make. Markkanen's fourth three stopped the Spurs' momentum briefly. Julian Champagnie missed a straightaway three, secured the miss, and knocked down the next try to push the San Antonio lead to 17. A pair of tips from Markkanen was not nearly enough to dent San Antonio's offensive onslaught. Wembanyama sandwiched a driving lay-up and a lob dunk around a block to make it 94-69 going into the fourth.

The Boston Celtics had high expectations for Mitchell Robinson after signing him to a three-year, $47.4 million contract in free agency. They expected so much from him to the point that they named him as their starting center heading into the 2026-27 season, displacing Neemias Queta, who broke out in a starting role for Boston at the five last season.

The 28-year-old big man knows that he has to get it together even as he's still adjusting to life as a member of the Celtics after spending the first eight seasons of his career with the Knicks.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"I gotta figure it out soon," Robinson told reporters, via Bobby Krivitsky of Forbes. "At the end of the day, it's still basketball. Things that I do naturally, I should just still be doing it, and I just haven't found my rhythm yet."

#2749. Seahawks-Bears score: 4-4. Seahawks blown out in Monday night horror show

All the good feelings the Seattle Seahawks (4-4) brought back after dominating the Kansas City Chiefs were immediately canceled out and then some after a disappointing 34-17 home loss against the Chicago Bears (6-2). Caleb Williams was as brilliant as Sam Darnold was worryingly atrocious. This offense is Jaxon Smith-Njigba or nothing. The run game struggled even with the return of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price. Seattle's vaunted defense had some wins and some devastating losses against the high-flying Bears offense, which looks like a Super Bowl caliber unit. Chicago had 363 yards of total offense, the most by any Seahawks opponent this season, while Seattle had a meager 252. As usual, JSN had 118 of those 252 yards.

Seattle won the Super Bowl last season and it should be cherished forever. This year's team is not a lock for the playoffs. It is not playing complementary football and the sloppiness is too hard to gloss over. It's a disappointing first half of the season and the longer term outlook on this team is significantly altered by the continued struggles of Sam Darnold. How can you have a contender when the quarterback play is this shaky? Whether Brian Fleury is good or not, Darnold is a problem. A big problem.

The Seahawks offense has threatened a blowout loss all season with their erratic play. It finally happened. The defense cannot bail you out forever.

The Seahawks started on offense, giving Zach Charbonnet the ball in his first touch since January 2026. Sam Darnold was rocked for a hurried incomplete pass on 2nd and 5, then Tory Horton was leveled by Cam Lewis on 3rd and 5 in a very legal and physical collision. Seattle had Chicago pinned at the 2-yard line, if not for Rodney Thomas ridiculously sliding for no reasons and driving the ball into the end zone. Poor decision and costly for field position reasons.

Chicago's opening drive against the league's top-rated defense was a thing of beauty. Caleb Williams led a 17-play, 80-yard drive that included three conversions on 3rd down, as well as a D'Andre Swift 4th and 1 conversion to keep the series going. Luther Burden capped off an 8:32 drive with a touchdown grab on a rollout throw by Williams. That was impressive. 7-0 Bears.

Jeffery Simmons made an immediate impact in his Bears debut, sacking Sam Darnold on the first play of Seattle's second series. However, Grady Jarrett's silly face mask grab of Jalen Sundell resulted in a free 15 and a new set of downs. Seattle still didn't get a first down on its own, with Darnold sliding and getting jarred by former Seahawks linebacker Devin Bush. Somehow, this wasn't deemed a penalty, and Seattle punted.

Luckily, Irv Charles showed everyone how its done and downed a Dickson punt inside the 5. The Bears went three-and-out after Caleb Williams was pressured into an overthrow of Kalif Raymond. Tory Taylor's short punt had a short return by Tory Horton, but Seattle was near midfield nevertheless.

When in doubt, go to Jaxon Smith-Njigba. A couple of quick screens to JSN gained 35 yards and Seattle was in the red zone in next to no time. Jadarian Price's first carry back from injury gained eight yards, a promising sign for his health and explosiveness. Unfortunately, the red zone series was ugly and featured nothing but Charbonnet touches that didn't get Seattle particularly close to the end zone. Jason Myers put Seattle on the board with a 27-yard field goal. 7-3 Bears.

The Bears went three-and-out again, then the Seahawks looked like they had a huge special teams play from Irv Charles. He deflected a Tory Taylor punt and somehow it took a friendly, untouched bounce for 45 yards. Seattle went three-and-out and punted it back to the Bears.

Chicago added to its lead thanks to a big play-action shot to Luther Burden for 23 yards. It took only three plays for Seattle to get into field goal range, where the drive stalled. Cairo Santos was true from 44 yards. 10-3 Bears.

Another three-and-out resulted in nervous energy from the Lumen Field crowd. The Bears had a chance to double up with points before the half and then to start the second half. Williams again was on target with explosive plays, as Rome Odunze broke free for 24 yards after a long time for Caleb Williams in the pocket. Interestingly enough, Ben Johnson dialed up a D'Andre Swift run on 3rd and 6 on the other side of the two-minute warning. Swift gained four yards and set up 4th and 2. Johnson called for the hard count, which was unsuccessful, and then kicked another field goal. 13-3 Bears.

A Jaylon Johnson PI penalty gifted Seattle some free yards in their one-minute drill. JSN broke Jaylon Johnson's ankles two plays later to get into Chicago territory. On 3rd and 10, Darnold dialed up a deep shot to JSN for a wide open 43-yard touchdown. Tyrique Stevenson bit on the slant and there was no safety help, so you know the rest! The only bad thing was a horrific missed PAT by Jason Myers. 13-9 Bears at halftime.

The Bears and Seahawks traded punts out of halftime, but Chicago punished Seattle for yet another limp three-and-out. A 10-play, 69-yard drive took over six minutes off the clock. D'Andre Swift punched it in from a couple yards out to make it 20-9 Bears.

Seattle took a preposterous 6:29 to move slowly, barely effectively, and not score any points. A very iffy pass interference penalty on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the first of his entire career, took away a completed ball to the Chicago 1. That put the Seahawks behind the sticks, and inevitably they settled for a field goal. Jason Myers' 33-yard kick was blocked. Brutal.

But wait! A twist on the next drive! Caleb Williams was almost picked off by Julian Love on an overthrow, then sacked by Mike Morris for the first of Mike's career, and a give-up screen on 3rd and 20 was fumbled by Colston Loveland. DeMarcus Lawrence forced the fumble and recovered the ball all at once!

Seattle turned that turnover into points, but not without referee help. Darnold was picked off on a terrible double coverage throw, but Clark Phillips was called for a hold of Jaxon Smith-Njigba and that took away the turnover. Two plays later, Darnold hit an open Cooper Kupp for a touchdown. Tory Horton kept the feet down in the back of the end zone for two valuable points. 20-17 Bears with 11:46 to go.

A really awful penalty committed by Mike Morris resulted in great field position for the Bears on the ensuing kick return. Seattle still had a chance to get the Bears off the field on third down in fringe field goal range. A delay of game actually saved the Bears from a failed 3rd and 4 conversion. On 3rd and 9, a screen to the speedy Kalif Raymond broke through for a 39-yard gain and it officially goes down as a run. D'Andre Swift scored on the next play. 27-17 Bears.

Sam Darnold got picked in an impossibly funny way. He was aloof and didn't realize the ball was picked by James Lynch. D'Andre Swift got the game-sealing hat trick after Nick Emmanwori selfishly committed a personal foul penalty when the Bears had 3rd and goal. 34-17 Bears FINAL.

DL Leonard Williams left the game in the third quarter with a stinger and did not return.

C Jalen Sundell left the game in the fourth quarter with an undisclosed injury.

The Seahawks wrap up their three-game homestand against the Arizona Cardinals (3-5) on Sunday, Nov. 8 at 1:25 pm PT on FOX. Unlike the first meeting, the Cardinals will have Gardner Minshew II at QB instead of Jacoby Brissett.

#2746. Sacramento Kings get first win of the season, Darius Acuff Jr. scores 25

The Sacramento Kings are no longer winless. For the first time this season, Sacramento will light the beam.

The Kings earned their first victory of the 2026-27 regular-season after defeating the Dallas Mavericks, 115-100, at American Airlines Arena in Dallas, Texas, on Monday, Nov. 2.

Sacramento entered the game against the Mavericks desperate for a win as panic was soon mounting for the team in California's capital.

#2745. NFL Power Rankings entering Week 9: Broncos are 6-2 but need to improve, perhaps with some pre-deadline trades

NFC East: Cowboys | Giants | Eagles | Commanders NFC North: Bears | Lions | Packers | Vikings NFC South: Falcons | Panthers | Saints | Buccaneers NFC West: Cardinals | Rams | 49ers | Seahawks

AFC East: Bills | Dolphins | Patriots | Jets AFC North: Ravens | Bengals | Browns | Steelers AFC South: Texans | Colts | Jaguars | Titans AFC West: Broncos | Chiefs | Raiders | Chargers

The Denver Broncos went 14-3 last season with an inordinate amount of wins in close games. Everyone said that was unsustainable and they were due for regression.

This season, the Broncos are 6-2 with an inordinate amount of wins in close games. Take that, regression police.

Somehow, the Broncos are again pulling off what should be impossible. On Sunday they came back from a 24-13 deficit in the fourth quarter to beat the Kansas City Chiefs, who have had their own fortunate run in close games. It was the Broncos' 15th straight win in games decided by eight points or less, tying the 2008-09 Indianapolis Colts for the NFL record, according to ESPN Insights.

One of two things has to be true: The Broncos are incredibly lucky in games that shouldn't be far off a 50-50 proposition and that's bound to flip, or they have some skill in winning close games that nobody else has possessed aside from Peyton Manning's Colts more than 15 years ago. Regardless of how they've gotten to their impressive record, Denver has overtaken Kansas City for the best chance to win the AFC West at 56.4%, according to DVOA.

"I think honestly, to answer that, I think it has to come from, well, we did it before," Broncos head coach Sean Payton said about winning close games, according to the team's transcripts. "Then there's a belief that can get stronger and then there's experience and then you're seasoned a little, but we still have a lot of things to fix. I honestly think that's where I believe it comes from."

If the Broncos decide they are on a heater in which the coin is repeatedly flipping on their side for a statistically improbable reason, they have some work to do before the trade deadline on Nov. 10. The offense, which has been inconsistent all season and was catching boos from the home crowd Sunday after three straight three-and-outs to start the second half, should be the focus.

Denver is just 30th in yards gained this season. A play-calling change from offensive coordinator Davis Webb to Payton hasn't helped much. The Broncos aren't getting a quarterback to replace Bo Nix but practically every other position group could be a candidate for an upgrade. The defense is good enough for a long playoff run, as it was last season. The variable is the offense.

Or maybe it just doesn't matter. The Broncos have beaten the odds for two seasons. They're 20-5 since the start of the 2025 season and 16 of those wins have been by eight points or less. They continue to laugh at the regression proclamations.

Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 8 of the NFL season, looking at the biggest need for each team before the trade deadline:

The Chargers' season is lost, so the obvious move is to trade veterans who can help elsewhere. Mack is clearly at the top of that list. He has started all seven games, has three sacks and can add immediate legitimacy to a defense from the edge. He's a likely future Hall of Famer and while he isn't quite the same player at age 35, he's still an asset. He's also no stranger to being traded, having been dealt from the Raiders to the Bears and then the Bears to the Chargers earlier in his career.

"You've got to be where your feet are man, ultimately," Mack said, via Eric Williams of Fox Sports. "That can be the most difficult thing when you're dealing with a lot of outside noise and stuff. Just trying to be where your feet are at all time. That's kind of been my thing in years past."

Biggest need: Get value for Jonathan Taylor

The way the Colts gave up on Sunday, they probably should have made Taylor inactive. Everyone knows they're going to try to trade him after shipping off guard Quenton Nelson and defensive lineman DeForest Buckner. The Colts need to restock their draft picks after a regrettable trade that sent two first-round picks, including their 2027 first, to the Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner. And, presumably, they feel some obligation to find a good home for Taylor, who has been a tremendous player for them through the years.

There will be plenty of teams, perhaps the Giants, Broncos, Packers and Vikings among them, talking about trading for Taylor, so the Colts should get a good return.

"And you know that day always comes for many players,'' Taylor said about the possibility of being traded last week, via Fox 59. "Whether you like it or not, the day may come. You may get lucky enough to stay somewhere forever, but you understand the business of it.

Others, like defensive tackle Grover Stewart and receiver Josh Downs, could be traded too. It's going to be a rough rest of the season for Indianapolis.

Biggest need: Hang onto Garrett Wilson and others

The Jets are in a great spot. If the NFL Draft was today, they'd have the fourth pick from the Colts (Sauce Gardner trade), their own pick at No. 6 and the 10th pick from the Cowboys (Quinnen Williams trade). That would be historic.

Unlike last season, when the Jets were willing to deal young players for a stockpile of picks, the right move seems to be holding onto some foundational pieces. The one that would generate a ton of interest is Wilson, who has mostly been wasted away with the Jets. But he's 26 years old, signed through 2030, and is a legitimate No. 1 receiver. Perhaps there's a minor move to be made, like trading cornerback Nahshon Wright, but the Jets already did their trading work with the 2027 draft in mind and now it's time to stand pat.

Biggest need: Trade Moro Ojomo, maybe Saquon Barkley, and many others

Howie Roseman might be the busiest general manager with the trade deadline coming up. He usually does well in trades — we'll ignore that he traded two third-round picks for two tackles and zero sacks from Jonathan Greenard so far this season — and he has plenty of assets to move.

Barkley is the most interesting figure, even as the team reportedly won't move him. A trade would make too much sense for the Eagles to not entertain any inquiries. Any team that gets him would be gambling because Barkley has been injured most of the season and his numbers are way down since his magical (and high usage) 2024 season. Multiple teams are in need of a playmaking running back. It'll be interesting to see if the Eagles' stance on Barkley changes in the next week. The bigger piece might be Ojomo, a good defensive tackle who is about to be a free agent. The Eagles could keep him and try to re-sign him, but they have a lot of money invested at defensive tackle. Tight end Dallas Goedert, edge rusher Nolan Smith and cornerback Riq Woolen are others who should be available for the right price.

It would be surprising if the Eagles aren't very active.

Biggest need: Find draft picks for some aging vets

Once the Titans traded defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Bears, it was a sign that any veteran was available. And the Titans have a few who don't fit in the long-term plans.

Given the hot streak running back Tony Pollard has been on, he has emerged as perhaps the most intriguing piece. Receiver Calvin Ridley is buried on the depth chart but some team could take a shot on him for a third-day draft pick. Safety Amani Hooker, who is 28 years old, has been tremendous. Edge rusher Jermaine Johnson II, in the final year of his deal, could be moved too. The Titans could have a ton of extra draft picks by the time the deadline is done.

Biggest need: Figure out what to do with Zach Sieler

Sieler has been a productive defensive tackle for many years, but he's also 31 years old. Still, the Dolphins haven't entertained trade talks for him, according to SI.com. Miami is in full rebuild mode and while Sieler helps the Dolphins now, a 1-6 team should be looking for the future, and trading a 31-year-old defensive lineman who still would have plenty of trade value makes sense. We'll see what the Dolphins do.

Trading offensive tackle Austin Jackson has also been speculated, and teams are always looking for line help. The stripped-down Dolphins roster doesn't have a lot of attractive veteran trade candidates, which makes the decision on Sieler that much more important.

Biggest need: Figuring out if they're buyers or sellers

A 2-5, last-place team should not be thinking about buying. But most teams don't have the luxury of playing in the NFC South, where 2-5 is just a game out of first place. There are pieces the Saints could trade and easily absorb the loss, like running back Kendre Miller and safety Justin Reid. Perhaps that's a way to straddle the line of competing for a division title and thinking toward the future. The Saints also should be getting running back Travis Etienne Jr. and rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson back from injuries as soon as this week, so that will feel like a pair of deadline acquisitions.

The Saints are very much in the race in a bad division. They're also early in a rebuild and their record indicates they're still in need of draft picks and young talent. That makes it a challenge to figure out what to do before the deadline.

Biggest need: Adding to the defense, maybe

At some point the Cowboys need to have an honest conversation about themselves, which seems impossible after team owner Jerry Jones proclaimed everyone is letting head coach Brian Schottenheimer down. Jones has talked about making big trades, and already made one in-season for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. A putrid defense that let Gardner Minshew tear it apart in the fourth quarter and overtime on Sunday needs a lot of help. But, is a team that has losses at home to a Buccaneers team led by an undrafted rookie quarterback and to a Cardinals team that came back from a 14-point deficit in the fourth quarter really a defensive piece away from contending for a Super Bowl? Probably not.

It puts the Cowboys in a weird place. They're not out of the NFC East race because the division isn't good. They're also not very good themselves. It's not even outlandish for the Cowboys to look in the mirror after that hideous loss to the Cardinals and admit they should be sellers. That would require self-awareness, which isn't abundant in Dallas.

Biggest need: Making a move on two defensive standouts

The Cardinals should be feeling good about themselves after a win at Dallas, their third upset road win of the season. They should also be realistic. The Cardinals aren't going to compete for a playoff spot. The progress is great but it's still a rebuild. That makes them an interesting seller.

The top trade candidate is probably edge rusher Josh Sweat, who came over from the Eagles after helping Philadelphia win a Super Bowl and hasn't had a ton of impact on a non-contending team. There's also a question about safety Budda Baker, one of Arizona's best players but is 30 years old and signed through only 2027. Both of those players could fetch valuable draft picks in a deal.

There's also question now if quarterback Jacoby Brissett could move; he was benched on Sunday and replaced by Gardner Minshew, who has been named the starter for Week 9 vs. the Seahawks. Minshew and Carson Beck are higher priorities now. But the biggest key is finding the best return for Sweat and perhaps Baker.

Like everyone else in the NFC South and NFC East, other than the Eagles, the Commanders should feel like they have a shot to be division champions. The Commanders are flawed, without question, but sit just two games behind the Giants in the division. It's not like New York is a lock to run away with it.

The biggest problem for the Commanders is the loss of receiver Terry McLaurin for the season. It leaves them thin at receiver, and the good news is there are a lot of veterans available at the deadline at various price points. The Commanders should be interested. They also should be interested in improving a secondary that ranks 27th in passing yards allowed.

The biggest question for the Ravens is this: Can Lamar Jackson return for the playoffs from a thumb injury suffered on Sunday? If the answer is yes, it's not outrageous for a team with a .500 record to see what it can do to keep playoff hopes alive until Jackson can come back. The problem is that it's hard to find any quarterback who can save a season (contrary to everything you see before the trade deadline, NFL teams aren't excited to trade away their backup quarterback). Still, the Ravens have to look. As much as the Ravens like Tyler Huntley, he's not the answer, especially now that he's dealing with a toe injury. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano is very, very unlikely to keep the Ravens in playoff contention.

However, if Jackson is done for the rest of the season with no hope for the playoffs, the Ravens probably have to turn the page and sell. It would hurt, but it would kickstart what could be a huge offseason of change in Baltimore. Because without Jackson, the Ravens' ranking of No. 22 here might be generous.

The Falcons are in a weird space. They're tied with the Buccaneers for second place in the NFC South, a half game behind the Panthers (3-4). They also are one of the most inconsistent teams in the NFL. They followed up beating the previously undefeated 49ers by losing to a Buccaneers team that didn't complete a single pass.

Atlanta is wildly inconsistent on offense, and that's why adding a receiver to go alongside Drake London makes sense. But the offense should be good enough, when it's not playing in a rainstorm like Sunday, to contend in the division. The defense needs help. And it could use it at almost every position aside from off-ball linebacker and safety. It's weird for a 3-5 team to clearly be buyers, but that's the 2026 NFC South.

A sub-.500 team that just fired its defensive coordinator also doesn't profile as a buyer, but the Panthers are in the 2026 NFC South. Their defense needs help, and firing Ejiro Evero doesn't solve all the problems. Being without cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, who are both on injured reserve, is tough to overcome. Getting some help there would be wise. A pass rusher would be nice too, considering Jaelan Phillips has been injured and isn't living up to his $120 million contract signed in the offseason.

It's not like the offense doesn't need help too, particularly the offensive line's depth because of injuries. Coming off an NFC South title and striving for another, the Panthers will be looking around before the deadline. There are a few areas that could use help.

The Texans made a big and questionable move in the offseason, trading fourth- and seventh-round draft picks, along with offensive lineman Juice Scruggs, to the Lions for running back David Montgomery. Scruggs has been more valuable this season than Montgomery, who has averaged 2.7 yards per carry and missed two games with injury. Woody Marks hasn't been much better. Houston has no running game and it's a big reason it is 2-5.

Do the Texans possibly trade for another running back? Do they trade for anyone at all? It's hard to give up the idea that Houston can still get back in the playoff race. It's a talented but underachieving team. But the Texans still have a 33.8% shot to make the playoffs, via DVOA, and can theoretically be a dangerous playoff opponent. Is that enough to ship off more picks, especially if it's for another running back?

Biggest need: Not being myopic about trading picks

A team two games under .500 now has a 57.4% chance to host a playoff game as a division winner, according to DVOA. The NFC South, everyone!

The Buccaneers might have been sellers two weeks ago, with veterans like receiver Chris Godwin Jr. and defensive end YaYa Diaby available, but that mentality likely changes after decisive wins over the Panthers and Falcons. Still, this is a 3-5 team and advanced metrics say the Bucs are pretty good as is (they rank a surprising fifth in DVOA). Tampa doesn't have a pressing need, though defensive help is always welcomed. The Buccaneers can stand pat, keep their picks and still be the favorite in the NFC South while not giving away any valuable picks for the future.

Biggest need: Remembering the long-term plan

It's hard for a franchise that hasn't had much success over the past few decades to have a level head over a solid start to the season. At 4-4, the Raiders can talk themselves into being playoff contenders. That makes it hard to be a seller. It would be an even harder thing to explain to longtime fans who are dying for a taste of success or a new fan base in Las Vegas that hasn't fully embraced the Raiders yet.

Realistically, the Raiders probably should be closer to sellers than they are to buyers. Could they find out if a team is willing to pay a heavy premium for Maxx Crosby like the Ravens (almost) did in March? It's not like the Ravens' concerns about Crosby's knee over the long term have vanished. However, ESPN reported the Raiders have no plans to trade Crosby. It also seems very unlikely the Raiders trade Kirk Cousins, but what if a desperate team is willing to overpay for a viable quarterback who already has 19 touchdown passes? Wouldn't they have to listen? It's not like Cousins is the future and they'll want to get Fernando Mendoza some valuable reps before the end of the season even if Cousins stays aboard. It seems foolish to be buyers when they're well behind the Broncos and Chiefs in the AFC West. And the big picture says that they should be quietly gauging the market on Crosby, Cousins and any others without long-term value, even if that would be unpopular to many Raiders fans.

Like the Raiders, it's fun for a team that has had almost no success to start 5-2. An uncompetitive loss to the Steelers on Sunday should put the Browns in a more realistic mindset. They can't keep living off last-minute wins, and their poor quarterback situation makes their level of success unsustainable. The five wins have already put the Browns in a bad spot to find a quarterback solution in 2027, but that's a conversation for next offseason.

The Browns can still be partial sellers without hurting their playoff hopes for this season. Receiver Jerry Jeudy is tradable and there are plenty of teams that could use him. Offensive tackle Dawand Jones, a backup who could provide depth elsewhere, can also be available. But with a promising young core, the Browns have to be careful to not get ahead of themselves despite a 5-3 record.

The Giants landing a running back is one of the easiest predictions of the trade deadline. They have plenty of injuries at the position, seem lukewarm at best on Cam Skattebo, but have a great chance to win a bad division.

How much do the Giants want to pay for a running back? Jonathan Taylor is the dream, but he won't be cheap. Perhaps Tony Pollard will be more reasonable, though he has played very well lately and that could increase the price.

The Giants will be looking at every possibility to help at running back, which could push them closer to a division title.

The Packers are one of a few teams in need of a running back and it's a different situation than the rest. If Josh Jacobs was a sure thing the rest of the season, the Packers might concentrate on more offensive line help or simply hold tight, knowing Micah Parsons is on the way soon.

But Jacobs' legal situation took a turn over the weekend after more allegations of abuse were reported. He denied wrongdoing, but the NFL can revisit the case. We have seen how poor the Packers' running game was without Jacobs. Green Bay doesn't want to be stuck again in that situation if Jacobs faces further punishment. Adding a viable starter would allow the Packers to move on from Jacobs entirely.

Biggest need: Receiver or cornerback, but probably nothing

A team that has among the oldest rosters in the NFL and is 6-2 before the deadline might generally be a big buyer to make a push with an aging team. Yet, it doesn't seem like there's one move that can put the Steelers on the same level as some of the NFL's elite teams.

Another receiver would be nice, but there's a lot of money tied up in DK Metcalf, and someone like Josh Downs would be redundant with the skill set of intriguing rookie Germie Bernard. Perhaps adding Jacksonville's Brian Thomas Jr. would make sense. Cornerback could help after trading away Joey Porter Jr., but the Steelers have been good at that position without him. An old team trading away valuable picks seems bad for the future. And a 6-2 team trading someone like edge rusher Alex Highsmith seems like the wrong move too. We might see Pittsburgh make a minor move or two but little else.

The Rams have already invested heavily into the 2026 roster, so what's the big deal in sending off more draft picks? For now, the Rams are playing coy, saying that players they could get back from injury, like Myles Garrett and Davante Adams, would serve as their deadline additions.

"Based on our situation, I mean the good thing for us is, what you look at is hopefully some of those trades will be guys getting back from injury that haven't played for us," head coach Sean McVay said, via the Los Angeles Times. "That's kind of the way we look at it."

Yet, it's hard to believe that because of the Rams' history. And while the idea of getting Adams back from a major hamstring injury is good in theory, he'll turn 34 on Dec. 24 and it's not a guarantee he returns to his normal level. The Rams are very thin at receiver behind Puka Nacua while Adams heals, and it's not like Nacua doesn't have a long injury history. Maybe the Rams stay put, but it wouldn't be a surprise if they talk themselves into a deal. Grabbing an exciting receiver might give the sluggish Rams a spark.

The Dolphins don't have a good pass rush but they still pressured Drake Maye often in Week 8. Maye overcame that with a strong second half to lead the Patriots to a win, but it's not like the line issues are going away. Guards Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker are on injured reserve. Getting a guard to help makes a lot of sense.

The Patriots have also had some trade speculation on the selling side. Cornerback Carlton Davis III could be dealt, according to Albert Breer of SI.com. Davis returned from a neck injury for Week 8 and played 96.9% of the defensive snaps, but it's possible the Patriots want to trade him for extra draft capital, which they could use to improve at guard.

Biggest need: Some help for Jaxon Smith-Njigba

It's surprising to see Smith-Njigba at a 36.3% target share entering Monday night's game, because it's rare for a receiver to get that many of a team's targets. But then you look around Seattle's offense and realize there's no other viable option. Smith-Njigba has 985 yards this season and Cooper Kupp is second on the team at 206.

The Seahawks decided to address their run game by adding guard Quenton Nelson instead of one of the name-brand running backs who might be available. Maybe that's their only big move. But for an offense that has been uneven most of the season, another receiving threat would help. It would help take pressure off turnover-prone Sam Darnold.

The idea that the Broncos could make a big move for Jonathan Taylor is dubious only because Sean Payton's history of using committees at running back without a standout workhorse. And the team has to be intrigued by rookie Jonah Coleman, who has played well and came up with two big plays to give Denver the lead in a huge win over the Chiefs on Sunday.

Perhaps Taylor or another big-time back could solve some issues on the offense. Or maybe it's a receiver or a tight end, after the Evan Engram signing in 2025 has been a dud. Even some depth on the offensive line isn't a bad idea. The Broncos are set on defense, so their focus can be how to add an impact piece to an inconsistent offense.

Biggest need: Defense, particularly at cornerback

The Lions' fan base wasn't happy when the Cowboys overpaid to get cornerback Joey Porter Jr. in a trade. They know that cornerback is an issue and it seems hard to believe the deadline will pass without Detroit doing something at the position.

Yet, there are other issues on a defense that has struggled most of the season, though it has allowed just 32 points the last two games. While the human element of linebacker Jack Campbell's neck injury is overwhelming, and his recovery is the biggest part of that story, there is a football side to it as well. Detroit will presumably be without one of the best off-ball linebackers in the NFL indefinitely. While the team's thoughts are primarily on their young star's health, the Lions also have to deal with the reality of perhaps adding a linebacker before the deadline.

Biggest need: Receiver, but don't forget about offensive line

This is no surprise: The Chiefs still need help at receiver. Their offense has been built around Kenneth Walker III to good results, but it's an incomplete unit. Rashee Rice is productive but not a dominant No. 1, Xavier Worthy hasn't broken out and there's not much else to speak of. Among the Chiefs' wideouts, Rice has 243 yards, Worthy has 230, Tyquan Thornton has 219 but he's on injured reserve and nobody else has more than 65. It's a team that is a perfect candidate to try to turn around Brian Thomas Jr.'s career.

But the Chiefs also can't ignore the offensive line. Guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched for the second time this season on Sunday. Offensive tackle Josh Simmons has been a problem and was put on IR. Receiver would be the more splashy move, but adding to the offensive line might be even more prudent.

Biggest need: Interior offensive line, and maybe Jonathan Taylor too

Trading for Jonathan Taylor, which has been rumored, would be a big headline in Minnesota before the trade deadline. Taylor would obviously help, but it's not like there aren't other issues on the offense. Quarterback might be one of them but Minnesota isn't going to make a difference-making move there.

The Vikings could add Taylor and still have trouble blocking for him. They're thin at guard after Donovan Jackson suffered a torn meniscus in Week 4. Their starting guards on Sunday, Joe Huber and Will Fries, rank 33rd and 41st among guards in Pro Football Focus' grades. But, an upgrade like Taylor could make everyone look better. It would be a fun trade for everyone.

Biggest need: More defensive help, this time on the back end

The Bengals got the win in overtime Sunday and a bump up in the rankings, but there were some troubling signs. Tennessee's offense was one of the worst in the NFL and it gained 440 yards and scored 36 points on the Bengals. Given Cincinnati's defensive issues in recent seasons, it was worrisome even in the win.

"I know we have the guys in there that are happy we won, but they're not satisfied with our overall performance," Bengals head coach Zac Taylor said, via the team's transcripts. "Each position group will go through that and find things we have to be better at."

The Bengals' line has been better with additions Dexter Lawrence II and Boye Mafe (Lawrence came up with huge plays in the win over the Titans), but the back seven could use some work. Help at cornerback or safety would be nice, and while the Bengals are trying to see it through with young linebackers Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr., they could use an upgrade there too. Cincinnati is a respectable 15th in defensive DVOA, but the difference between it making a deep playoff run or losing early on could be a defensive addition at the deadline.

Biggest need: Still defense, though the big move was made

The Bears' front office understood the assignment. Chicago traded two first-round draft picks to Tennessee for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. If there's a bigger move at the deadline from any team, it'll be a surprise. Simmons is exactly what the Bears' defense needed as a disruptor on the line, and he notched a sack in his Chicago debut on Monday night against Seattle. Chicago clearly feels like it's a contender now and was willing to sacrifice some high future draft picks for a shot at making a deep playoff run.

That doesn't mean the Bears should be done on defense, though any other move wouldn't be major. A mid-round draft pick for pass rushing help would continue to improve the defensive front. A reunion with Khalil Mack would make a ton of sense. But make no mistake: The Bears already made their all-in move.

"Super Bowl teams all have what we call a 'red-level' interior defensive lineman," Bears general manager Ryan Poles said of the Simmons trade, via the Chicago Sun-Times. "You need one.

"We've been searching, but sometimes the draft doesn't provide that to you. Free agency doesn't really [provide them]; it's very hard for guys to get out of the building when they have all of those things that we're talking about. [Simmons] was an opportunity that we had to jump on."

Biggest need: Offensive and defensive line help

The aggressive mindset that general manager James Gladstone wants to be known for will be put to the test. The Jaguars are one of the best teams in the NFL. Jacksonville has also dealt with two major injuries that need to be addressed.

Left tackle Anton Harrison tore his ACL in Week 5. Then defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton, who had been playing very well against the run this season, tore his quad Sunday and is done for the season. Walker Little has done a good job replacing Harrison, and perhaps that leads Jacksonville to look for offensive line depth rather than an impact starter. Replacing Hamilton with a high-end defensive tackle would be a strong move. Grover Stewart of Indianapolis might be a possibility, though the Colts might not want to trade within the division. If the Eagles trade defensive tackle Moro Ojomo, he could make a difference. It's time to see how aggressive Gladstone plans to be now that Jacksonville has one of the best teams in the NFL.

For once, finding weapons around Josh Allen isn't the top priority for the Bills. That has shifted to the defense. That group looked fine on Sunday, but that's because Lamar Jackson was knocked out after one play. Buffalo looked good against Baltimore's second and third quarterbacks, but the rest of the season has been rough. The Bills are 24th in yards and points allowed, and that's with an easy day against the Ravens included. Baltimore had 144 yards; Buffalo has given up at least 348 in every other game.

The Bills don't have the salary cap space to make a huge move on defense, but they should be looking into help at all three levels, with an emphasis on the back end. Only two teams are giving up more passing yards per game. Even if it's a mid-level move at cornerback or safety, the Bills know what they have to do. The Super Bowl window is wide open if the defense is good enough.

Biggest need: DeForest Buckner fills it, though maybe other moves are possible

The 49ers made a smart move to bring back DeForest Buckner in a trade with the Colts. Buckner might not be at his peak, like he was with his first go-around with the 49ers, but he's still a very good defensive lineman. The 49ers needed that. They also are hoping to get Nick Bosa back after the bye, which would be a big boost.

San Francisco has to weigh making improvements now for a team that has dealt with many injuries, particularly at receiver, vs. restocking with draft picks. The 49ers haven't drafted well in recent years and that has hurt their depth. That hasn't been a problem this season but it's looming. San Francisco also understands how a huge move can have a wide-ranging effect: A massive trade during the 2022 season for Christian McCaffrey boosted the team to a Super Bowl a season later and is still paying off. A trade for a receiver or defensive help would strengthen the 49ers' standing as the Super Bowl favorite, but they have to keep an eye on the future as well.

#2744. Ohio vs Akron Prediction: Is It the Bobcats' MAC For the Taking?

It's starting to get late in the season, and Ohio has taken over the MAC. It hasn't dealt with a slew of conference stars – it doesn't play Western Michigan, and Toledo is later – but it's the only unbeaten team in MAC action. It's hot, and Akron is not, but this is dangerous.The Zips are the only winless team in MAC play, but its good at home with enough of an offense to screw up the conference race.

Akron (1-7) has lost six straight, but three of its last four games are at home. Western Michigan is up next.

Ohio (6-2) has won five in a row, and its last road game of the regular season is next week at Miami University.

The two teams haven't faced each other since 2024, a 30-10 Ohio win. The Bobcats have won seven straight in the series since 2017.

Date: Tuesday, November 3, 2026Game Time: 7:00 PM ETTV: ESPN2Location: InfoCision Stadium, Akron, OH– Week 10 Schedule, Predictions– CFN Top 25 | Bowl Projections– Expert Picks: Week 10

Akron is great at moving the ball, and it throws well, and then it turns the ball over … and over, and over. Few teams in college football suffer more turnovers.The Zips have given the ball away six times in the last two games and 13 times in the last six. Ohio doesn't force a ton of turnovers, but it should get at least two. The Bobcat running game should be in control of the game throughout, but …

Akron will wing it around and keep pressing the Bobcat secondary.The Zips don't have a high-octane attack, but Brayden Raggow is pushing the ball, throwing for 275 yards in the loss to Kent State the last time out for an offense that should throw for at least 200 yards. If the defense can force a few turnovers – Ohio has given it away twice in three of the last four games – and find some sort of running game to balance things out, it has a chance. Akron's one win came when it ran for over 200 yards, while Ohio's two losses came when it gave up over 200 yards.

Akron will give it the old college try on a Tuesday night, but the defense doesn't have any sort of pass rush, and the line won't hold up as Ohio runs it 40 times to keep the game under control for the full 60 minutes.Akron will have its moments, but that 200-yard running game came against Robert Morris. The Zips won't get close to that.

#2743. D'Andre Swift's TD run gives Bears a 20-9 lead on Seahawks

They put together a 10-play, 69-yard touchdown drive after both teams opened the second half by going three-and-out. D’Andre Swift’s 1-yard touchdown run, and Cairo Santos’ PAT have the Bears leading 20-9 with 5:38 remaining in the third quarter.

Rome Odunze had catches of 23 and 22 yards to get the drive going.

Quarterback Caleb Williams is now 22-of-31 for 227 yards and a touchdown. Odunze has four catches for 87 yards, and Luther Burden has seven catches for 56 yards.

Swift has 16 carries for 39 yards and a touchdown.

Seahawks defensive lineman Leonard Williams was injured on a tackle of running back Roschon Johnson for no gain with 7:37 left in the third quarter. He is in the sideline medical tent, but the Seahawks have not updated his injury.

#2742. Monday Night Football: Jeffery Simmons, Caleb Williams lead Bears to 34-17 rout of Seahawks

Simmons had a dominate debut with the Bears, who acquired him from the Titans on Thursday. He made a team-leading six tackles, with a sack, a pass defensed and two tackles for loss, and the Bears limited the Seahawks to 252 yards.

The Bears rolled to a 34-17 victory over the Seahawks on Monday night.

Chicago is 6-2, and the defending champions fell to 4-4.

The Seahawks didn't help their cause, with three unnecessary roughness penalties in the second half, including two on special teams. Kicker Jason Myers missed an extra point and had a 33-yard field goal blocked.

#2741. Timberwolves 112, Bucks 100: Ball-ing and Bowling to the Rim

After a grueling week that included five games in seven nights and two back-to-backs, the Timberwolves got back to a normal scheduling rhythm as they kicked off the week against the Milwaukee Bucks. Minnesota took down Milwaukee in a preseason matchup as the Bucks have continued to try to find themselves in their post-Giannis era.
