An already depleted Timberwolves roster was down another rotation player in Terrence Shannon Jr., due to a hip contusion, as the injury bug has found its way to the Twin Cities. The border battle clash always provides a little extra fuel, even when the teams are in opposing conferences.

LaMelo Ball, looking frustrated from his recent struggles, came out flame-throwing as the Bucks played drop and allowed him free rein to shoot behind physical Rudy Gobert screens. Ball drove the offense, hitting nothing but nylon on the majority of his shots. He drove the offense for the beginning of the game.

After a half-hearted defensive stretch led to some Bucks triples, Jaylen Clark and Joan Beringer came in and slammed the door. Minnesota kept the defensive intensity up but struggled to put the ball in the hoop after Ball went to the bench, but they maintained a 29-18 advantage after the first 12 minutes.

LaMelo Ball continued to drive the offense as he scored half of their first-half points while being aggressive in looking for his shot. Sloppy rebounding allowed Milwaukee to get back into the game as they closed the gap throughout the quarter.

There were a few stretches where Minnesota lost focus, and it allowed the Bucks to crawl their way back. The sloppiness persisted, and Tyler Herro hit back-to-back threes to close the second as the Bucks sliced into the double-digit Timberwolves advantage and cut the lead to one point.

The Bucks killed the Timberwolves on the glass and created second-chance points. They led that category 16 to 5 at the half.

Ayo Dosunmu took the baton from LaMelo Ball to start the quarter as he was bowling his way to the rim and finishing with feather-like touch. Tyler Herro matched that output as he stayed hot from his close to the second quarter, as the Timberwolves offense sputtered on the other end. The Bucks were getting too easy of looks as the game went back and forth during the period. Trey Lyles also left his mark, scoring 10 points in the third quarter.

It was a close start to the 4th quarter before Joan Beringer and Jaylen Clark gave the Timberwolves a shot in the arm. The Bucks were on a cold streak that Minnesota couldn't seem to shake for much of the game before this point. Those two helped to get some separation and grew the lead to double digits.

Milwaukee decided that they couldn't score with Rudy Gobert out there, nor were they able to stop the Timberwolves' offense, so they deployed the hack-a-Rudy strategy. That somewhat worked for them, as they were able to get Gobert out of the game, but Minnesota battened down the hatches and knocked down a few triples to close out the game for a 112-100 victory.

The Timberwolves themselves were reeling after the Anthony Edwards injury as they did not know who was next up in the team's hierarchy. There were multiple quotes that emphasized this sentiment, but it was always clear who would need to step up with their pack leader sidelined: LaMelo Ball.

Ball struggled initially taking the reins of the team that needed him to have his playmaking take a step back so his shooting could take the shine. He struck that balance in this one. He came out of the gates against the Bucks scorching hot, and kept the pedal down for the entire game.

LaMelo had half of the team's points at halftime and found ways to get his shot off while also finding ways to beat his man off the dribble and take it all the way to the basket. He scored 34 points on 12/21 shooting while adding a 6/13 day from beyond the arc. The fouls almost caught up to him in the second half, but his shooting aggressiveness is exactly what this offense needed.

Ayo Dosunmu is a jack of all trades while being a master at diving at the rim and finishing with a soft touch. While LaMelo was focused on putting the ball in the hoop in this one, Ayo took his role as a facilitator, setting up his fellow Wolves with easy looks all around.

He scored 19 points, added 12 rebounds and 8 assists in a stat-sheet-stuffing night. He is the king of scaling his game up and down to fit whatever the team needs, and did that in the third quarter tonight. When LaMelo was struggling to get going, and the Bucks were fighting back, he calmly took the ball and used his patented straight-line driving and love tapping off the glass to stem the Milwaukee tide.

He is a key part of the Ant-less Timberwolves, and more games where he finds himself all over the court will do the Timberwolves well in this stretch.

#2740. Rajat Paliwal's 21st first-class ton: A century without knowing he was nearing one

NEW DELHI: Ravikant has kept Palam's Air Force Complex Ground ticking for the past 35 years. The chief ground staff member, he also doubles up as the scoreboard operator. But when cricket resumed after the COVID pandemic, he received an unusual request from the Services captain Rajat Paliwal: he did not want his name displayed on the scoreboard while batting.Ravikant, a little hesitant at first, agreed."Sab ka apna apna hota hai. Kaptaan sahab ka farman aaya aur humne maan liya (Everyone has their own superstition. He made the request and I accepted it)," Ravikant said.On Monday, the 34-year-old Paliwal smashed his 21st first-class century to rescue Services, who were reeling at 27 for three, and took them to 266 on the opening day of their Ranji Trophy Group C clash against Delhi. He remained unbeaten on 111 off 196 balls.With no name appearing against Batsman 2 (Paliwal) on the scoreboard, the veteran batter had no way of knowing how close he was to his century. He eventually realised he had reached the milestone through the reaction of Delhi's fielders, who began closing in around him."I got to know that I was getting closer to a century when I saw more fielders around me. I realised I had scored a hundred only through the reaction of the Delhi players," he told reporters at the end of the opening day.

"I started this practice sometime after Covid. Sometimes, I used to feel a little nervous and lose my focus. The scoreboard draws attention, so I have taken it out of the picture entirely to concentrate only on the game," he added.This was Paliwal's highest score of the season so far, and he described it as particularly special. When he walked out to bat, Services were staring at the possibility of being bowled out for less than 100. But Paliwal stood up for his team, as he has done for nearly a decade-and-a-half."This hundred is very special, especially because the team had lost four wickets for 44 runs and we needed this knock. This has come after a long time and at a critical juncture before a break, to set the tone for the next phase," he said.

Paliwal, who turns 35 in December, knows that his chances of breaking into the Indian team are now limited. However, he continues to draw inspiration from Jammu and Kashmir captain Paras Dogra, 41, with whom he remains in regular touch."Yes, I look at Paras as an example. He has crossed 10,000 runs in first-class cricket and has been remarkably consistent. Last year, he also won the Ranji Trophy title. His persistence and consistency are inspiring. Paras has been an inspiration in this regard. He became a Ranji Trophy champion in his forties. When you see him consistently performing at that age, you feel confident about yourself as well," he said."Yashpal [Singh] is another player who has influenced me a lot. He scored a lot of runs and played alongside me for four or five years when I started. We had some very good partnerships together," he added.

A bulwark of India's domestic cricket circuit, Paliwal believes that the love for first-class cricket in the country is far from fading. He cited his Delhi counterpart, Ayush Badoni, who has scored back-to-back double centuries, as an example of the continued appetite for the longer format."It's true that cricket has become much faster. Throughout the year, there is a lot of focus on T20 cricket because of the exposure, media coverage and attention it receives. But you cannot categorise players like that. If you look at Badoni, he has scored two double centuries on the trot. Badoni is my opponent, but I would like to appreciate him because it is not easy to score back-to-back double hundreds."Every player has individual priorities, and everyone approaches the game differently. Everyone has their own preferences and ambitions. Some want to establish themselves in this format, while others prefer the shorter formats. But I believe many players still try to perform in the longest format as well," he continued.

#2738. Sixers Bell Ringer: Widespread effort from starters lifts Sixers past Bulls

Bell Ringer Standings:Tyrese Maxey – 3.5Joel Embiid – 1LeBron James – 1Anfernee Simons – 1Jaylen Brown – 0.5

The Philadelphia 76ers had all five starters score in double-digits and three score more than 20 points in a 126-107 win over the Chicago Bulls on Monday night.

The Sixers were almost completely healthy for this one, with the only absences being Dominick Barlow (back) and Ariel Hukporti, who is out for the season. Taking on a struggling Bulls squad that came into Monday 1-5 on the season, they had a golden opportunity to get a comfortable win and maybe even get the starters some rest if they could put it to bed early.

Of course, it can never be too easy. After letting Chicago hang close in the first half, the Sixers finally started to put a little distance between them going into the final frame leading by 11. Philadelphia couldn't seem to fully shake loose until late in the fourth when they extended their lead to 20 with two minutes to play. It would have been nice to gain steadier footing early to get the starters some rest before that point, but I guess we can't be too greedy talking about a now 7-1 team.

Next up, the Sixers will hit the road for three games, the first of which will take them to Detroit to take on the Pistons on Wednesday night.

Until then, let's get to the Bell Ringer. It was a widespread effort, so we have a few options!

VJ Edgecombe: 21 points, 3 rebounds, 5 assists, 1 steal, 1 block

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

To anyone who says that VJ Edgecombe can't thrive in this Sixers' lineup, please watch the first quarter of tonight's game. It was the perfect example of a simple but effective synergy between the sophomore and his new-look squad — VJ fully utilizing his speed in transition to get out ahead with LeBron James and Tyrese Maxey getting their heads up to nail impressive passes to him in stride. Edgecombe took full advantage, shooting 5-for-5 from the floor (1-for-1 from long range) for a floor-leading 11 points in the first frame. And if it ain't broke, don't fix it. LeBron hit another cross-court dime to a pushing Edgecombe to help the boy from Bimini to 15 points on 7-for-7 field goal shooting by halftime.

This is why I never worried about Edgecombe's development in this lineup. Sure, there's only one ball… but when you have passers like James (and Maxey, though to a lesser extent) around you, there will always be opportunities for a speedy, athletic player that is constantly in motion off the ball. Tonight was the perfect example of how he can become borderline uncoverable. And if you move (and finish) like Edgecombe did tonight, one can imagine those opportunities will only become more plentiful as the Sixers continue to solidify their chemistry offensively.

Edgecombe finished Monday night with 21 points on 9-for-12 field goal, 2-for-4 three-point shooting. He also had three rebounds, five assists, a steal and a block.

LeBron James: 15 points, 7 rebounds, 9 assists, 1 steal

LeBron James hit not only one but several passes in this game that I watched on repeat. And he made them look easy. I'm talking multiple full-court bounce passes that hit blazing fast players like VJ Edgecombe perfectly in stride and a number of perfectly timed dimes in the half-court offense working off double (or even triple) teams. I'll be honest, I didn't watch LeBron play night in and night out before he came to Philadelphia… it is an absolute treat to watch the plays he makes for his teammates every single game, with the correct passes at the correct time to the correct players to make the most of each moment. By the time an opponent's shot is in the air, James is already positioning himself to grab the rebound and to be able to make a quick, accurate pass ahead.

It sounds like I'm overstating things, but I genuinely don't think it can be overstated what a facilitator he's been to start this season.

In addition to his nine dimes, LeBron found the time to sink some buckets of his own, chipping in 15 on 6-for-13 field goal shooting. He also pulled in seven rebounds and had a steal. His first triple-double as a Sixer still eludes him for now, but something tells me it won't be too long…

Tyrese Maxey: 26 points, 4 rebounds, 11 assists, 2 steals, 2 blocks

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

Philadelphia rained down MVP chants for Tyrese Maxey when he went to the line at one point tonight… and frankly, they're not crazy. Well, maybe they are, but not for this! Maxey continues to be an absolute baller to start this season, and notably it's coming in different ways and on both ends of the floor. Not only has Maxey's defense been incredibly impressive these first eight games… and not only has he been an absolute scoring powerhouse at times… but he's also taking some clear queues from LeBron James and hitting some monster passes as well.

With such a widespread scoring effort tonight, it didn't have to be all on Maxey's shoulders to chip in 40 points. But even without the overwhelming point total tonight (not that 26 is anything to be ashamed of), it's amazing just how many of the Sixers' points Maxey played a large part in, whether he scored them, assisted on them, or came up with the defensive play that led to them. First, he got his team going early. Then, he was scoring in bunches himself by the fourth.

Maxey finished Monday with a 26-point, 11-assist double-double. He shot 10-for-15 from the floor. He also had four rebounds, two steals and two blocks.

Jaylen Brown: 25 points, 11 rebounds, 5 assists, 1 steal

It was another night of Jaylen Brown just being Jaylen Brown. I'm sounding like a broken record across these Bell Ringers, but it's incredible how much Brown contributes each game in a somewhat quiet manner. It's not the high-flying dunks of VJ Edgecombe or the cross-court passes of LeBron James. It's not always one big spurt of scoring where Brown puts the Sixers on his back for a few minutes. It's just simple, constant contribution when he's on the floor, on both ends of the floor. You hear his name called by Matt Cord in the arena so often you almost stop hearing it. He just balls. Tonight, it was 25 points on stellar shooting, 9-for-15 field goal and 4-for-7 from beyond the arc, spread out pretty evenly throughout the entirety of the game. This level of performance has seemingly already become the accepted, unceremonious norm from Brown on the Sixers… and that's something worth taking note of.

Brown finished the night with a 25-points, 11-rebounds (5 offensive) double-double with 5 assists and 1 steal. He hit four triples, two of which game back-to-back late in the game which really felt like the dagger in this one (finally).

#2737. Caleb Williams' late push, Jeffery Simmons' dominance help Bears hold off Seahawks for big prime-time victory

SEATTLE — The Chicago Bears emerged triumphant in a big NFC matchup against the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night.

Despite a late score that pulled the Seahawks within three points, Caleb Williams stayed cool to get a late touchdown, while the Bears' defense did enough to stifle the spark in a 34-17 victory.

Chicago got things started early, silencing the crowd at Lumen Field with a methodical, 17-play opening drive that ended in Williams finding Luther Burden III in the end zone on a 1-yard touchdown pass.

Seattle's offense, meanwhile, spent the first half struggling, and Chicago's new defensive acquisition Jeffery Simmons played a role in that. He notched his first sack as a Bear in the Seahawks' second series of the game, bringing down Sam Darnold for a 6-yard loss. He finished with six tackles, two for loss and one pass deflection.

The Seahawks regained their footing enough in the second quarter. Chicago led 13-3, but in the final seconds of the half, Sam Darnold found Jaxon Smith-Njigba for a masterful (and much-needed) 43-yard touchdown that cut Seattle's deficit to 13-9.

The Bears didn't back down, though, breaking up a slow third quarter with another touchdown and blocking a Seahawks field-goal attempt early in the fourth.

Seattle bounced back on the next drive with when DeMarcus Lawrence forced and recovered a Bears fumble. That gave the Seahawks a chance that they capitalized on. Darnold found wideout Cooper Kupp in the end zone for a 7-yard score, and connected with Tory Horton for a 2-point conversion to pull the game within 20-17.

That bit of momentum didn't last long. Williams cooly led the Bears down the field for a touchdown, converting on third-and-9 (thanks to a delay-of-game call that actually might've saved the drive) on a 39-yard quick toss to Kalif Raymond that was officially counted as a rushing attempt.

D'Andre Swift then pulled through for a 5-yard touchdown run to push the lead back up to double digits.

A tipped interception on Darnold then dashed any last hopes of a Seahawks comeback, especially with Swift taking in another touchdown, his third of the night.

He finished with 69 yards on 27 carries, which wasn't efficient, but the three scores mattered more.

Seattle had one last futile drive, but turned it over on downs on fourth-and-4 from the Chicago 7. That was enough for the Bears to seal the victory.

Be afraid, NFC. There's a new sheriff in town. And it's Jeffery Simmons.

His strong debut, coupled with Caleb Williams' ice-cold control of the offense, led the Bears to a resounding road win against the defending Super Bowl champions.

A desperate 11-play drive that got to Chicago's 7-yard line ends in a turnover on downs for Seattle.

Chicago is going to improve to 6-2 while the defending champions will fall to 4-4.

If your fantasy team needed a big game from D'Andre Swift, congrats.

D'Andre Swift scored his third rushing TD, this one from 5 yards out and it looks like it'll be a happy plane ride to Chicago for the visiting Bears.

Fans are now streaming out of Lumen Field following the interception. It's late, it's cold, and Seattle is on the verge of a tough loss — not a lot of reasons to stay.

Defensive lineman James Lynch got the first pick of his career and the Bears are a few yards away from icing this game with another TD.

Down 10 points, Seattle has rushed the ball on two straight downs. The lone pass of this drive was a 6-yard completion to RB Jadarian Price.

That'll kill some momentum: D'Andre Swift sprints for a 5-yard touchdown and Chicago is back to a two-score lead.

It looked for a moment like Seattle had gotten the stop, but a delay of game call right before gave Chicago a repeat of third down. Williams then found Kalif Raymond for a 39-yard gain out of nowhere.

Mike Morris is flagged for a personal foul after tackling Zavion Thomas out of bounds. Another scrum briefly breaks out after the contact, as Morris clearly pulled Thomas around while making the tackle.

To make up for Jason Myers' missed extra point earlier, Seattle goes for two. Sam Darnold gets the ball to Tory Horton in the back of the end zone, and we've got a game.

After DeMarcus Lawrence's forced fumble, the Seahawks needed to convert the opportunity — and they do. Darnold takes the pressure but finds an open Kupp in the end zone for a massive play.

Near-disaster for Seattle is averted, as a potential pick in the end zone is erased after Clark Phillips II is called for holding on Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

Bears DB Jaylon Johnson goes down after helping take down Jadarian Price. Johnson is tended to for a moment but is able to walk to the sideline on his own.

We've got some spice here in the fourth quarter: Colston Loveland loses the ball, and DeMarcus Lawrence is there to take him down and recover the ball. Seattle gets the ball at Chicago's 25, with a massive opportunity to turn things around.

Seattle's defense nearly picks off Caleb Williams, and then hits him with a massive sack for a loss of 10 yards. Mike Morris is there to take down Williams.

Official attendance for tonight is 68,739 fans, which is just about a sellout.

That JSN interference call doomed the Seahawks' drive. They couldn't make up the yardage, and instead had to settle for a short field goal.

But Jason Myers' 33-yard attempt was blocked at the line.

Chicago's lead is still 20-9 with 14:09 left in the fourth.

#2733. Rapid Recap: Timberwolves 112, Bucks 100

After fighting for most of the game, the Milwaukee Bucks stalled late, letting the Minnesota Timberwolves ride a dominant final four minutes to a 112-100 win. The Bucks slump to 1-6 for only the fifth time in franchise history, extending their losing streak to three games. Tyler Herro led the Bucks in scoring, posting 21 points on 8/18 shooting. Jaime Jaquez scored 19 and added eight rebounds, while Myles Turner and AJ Green each added 13 points. LaMelo Ball led all players with a season-high 34 points on 12/21 shooting, while Ayo Dosunmu (19 points, 12 rebounds, eight assists) had a near triple-double.

Taylor Jenkins tweaked his rotation on Monday, dropping Ryan Rollins from the starting lineup in favor of Brayden Burries. Kyle Kuzma fired a bullet to an open Jaime Jaquez in the paint, who easily rolled it in for a layup to start the scoring. However, led by back-to-back long threes from LaMelo Ball, the Wolves rattled off 10 unanswered points to take an eight-point lead inside the first three minutes. Ball connected on his third triple of the game with just four minutes elapsed, putting the Timberwolves up 15-4 and forcing a Bucks timeout. Milwaukee quickly worked their way back out of the break, going on a 9-0 run behind triples from Jaquez, Burries, and Myles Turner; Burries showed the hustle to compete with bigger Wolves defenders on the offensive glass and consistently found teammates on the perimeter. The Wolves responded with a run of their own (12-3), scoring ten points and feasting in transition to lead 29-18 after one.

Impressively, Milwaukee quickly cut the Timberwolves' lead out of the break and even took the lead, with AJ Green connecting on a pair of threes, Rollins getting a driving layup to go, and Burries converting a pull-up. However, Ball caught fire once again, helping Minnesota take the lead right back; the Wolves' star PG scored 11 second-quarter points on 4/7 shooting, and his presence created so many good looks. However, the Bucks did one thing well: they took away Ball's passing game, with his first assist coming with 1:40 remaining in the third quarter. Anyway, Ball's and-one gave Minnesota a 45-41 lead with 2:51 remaining, but Milwaukee kept it tight, with Herro cashing back-to-back threes in the final minute to cut the home side's lead to one, 48-47, at the half.

Although Minnesota stayed in control for much of the third quarter, Milwaukee kept the game within arm's reach. Myles Turner's triple off a Kuzma kick-out gave Milwaukee a 50-48 lead to start, but Minnesota wrenched it back with an Ayo Dosumnu fast-break layup. Bones Hyland's three gave Minnesota a 68-63 lead with just under five minutes left. Milwaukee and Minnesota kept trading the lead as the game wore on. Trey Lyles gave the home side a nice kick off the bench, knocking down a few bombs late in the third to give Minnesota a 76-71 edge. The Wolves stayed ahead going into the final frame, though a tough Kasparas Jakucionis finish through contact cut their lead to just four at 80-76.

Minnesota slowly built its advantage as the fourth quarter wore on, with Milwaukee struggling with turnovers as they tried to bridge the gap; Joan Beringer intercepted a bad Jakucionis pass, another Jakucionis pass went out of bounds, and Turner lost the ball while trying to draw a foul. These mistakes let the Wolves slowly build a double-digit lead, punctuated by Beringer's put-back layup that forced a Jenkins timeout. Eventually, Milwaukee's offense flatlined as Minnesota picked up steam: Kuzma airballed a three and Kel'el Ware missed a dunk, while a Ball dagger pushed the T-Wolves' lead to 15, their largest of the game. Despite trying some interesting tactics to close the game—including hack-a-Rudy—the Bucks just didn't have enough.

#2731. Bears v. Seahawks Postgame: A Statement Victory in Big Jeff’s First Game

Chicago opened with a grinding 17-play, 80-yard drive that consumed 8 minutes and 32 seconds and ended with Caleb Williams' 1-yard touchdown pass to Luther Burden. It was the first time in 27 games that an opponent had scored on the Seahawks on the opening possession. Jeffery Simmons made an immediate impact in his Bears debut with a sack of Sam Darnold.

Observation: The Bears set the tone early by sustaining drives and staying physical against a defense that had been difficult to score on.Gooch Hot Take: That opening drive wasn't flashy—it was the kind of ugly, clock-eating football that tells a contender "we can hang with you for four quarters." Simmons already looks like the interior disruptor the Bears paid two firsts for. But let's be clear – that first touchdown drive was EVERYTHING the Bears want to be.

Seattle got on the board with a Jason Myers field goal. Chicago answered with Cairo Santos field goals from 44 and 38 yards to push the lead to 13-3. With 30 seconds left, Jaxon Smith-Njigba beat coverage for a 43-yard touchdown from Darnold (extra point missed), cutting the deficit to 13-9 at the half.

Observation: The Bears were efficient enough in the red zone area to take points when available. JSN remains the one consistent explosive piece for Seattle.

Upon Further Review preview: We're going to talk about the QB slide this week. Nothing Bush could do – literally flying through the air with his back turned – on that late Darnold slide. The TV crew thought it was a clear penalty – and maybe it was on the rules – the rules need to change. It's just ridiculous – and it isn't protecting quarterbacks.

It isn't even that it produces dumb penalties – because of course you cannot ask defenders to stop in midair. It is the fact that it encourages QBs to slide – which is an uber-dangerous play for them. When QBs become runners – they should just be runners.

Gooch Hot Take: Santos quietly outkicked Myers when it mattered. The Seattle punter kind of rocks – respect given. But the other Hawks kicker – the missed extra point on the JSN score was the difference between a one-score game and a more comfortable margin heading into the locker room.

That opening 17-play drive was the statement of the half. It wasn't explosive, but it was the kind of grinding, clock-eating football that shows Chicago can match Seattle's physicality for a full game.

Simmons is already justifying the early returns on the trade. One sack and consistent pressure in his first half as a Bear is exactly the multiplier the defensive line needed.

JSN remains Seattle's entire explosive element. When he's bottled up, the rest of the offense looks ordinary. The missed extra point on his score was a quiet but meaningful swing.

Santos is quietly having a strong night. Two clean field goals kept the Bears in control when the red-zone finishing wasn't perfect.

If Chicago continues to control the line of scrimmage and limit big plays outside of JSN, this is a very manageable second half. Seattle will need more than one or two explosive plays to flip the script on the road.

The Bears REALLY need to solve the final drive of the half. This is the second week in a row they've allowed a soft touchdown heading into halftime.

Chicago answered the half-ending JSN score by controlling the third period and pushing the lead to two possessions. The Seahawks were held scoreless as the Bears continued to win the physical battle and sustain drives.

The Bears opened the half with the ball and marched 69 yards in 10 plays over 6 minutes and 19 seconds. The drive featured a 22-yard completion from Caleb Williams to Rome Odunze and a 9-yard pass to Kalif Raymond that set up short-yardage situations. D'Andre Swift finished it with a 1-yard touchdown run, and Cairo Santos' extra point made it 20-9.

Seattle's best chance late in the quarter was erased by offensive pass interference on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, wiping out a gain that would have put them near the goal line and leaving them with second-and-long instead.

Chicago's second drive of six-plus minutes ended in a touchdown, matching the pattern from the opening series. They are controlling the clock and the line of scrimmage against a Seahawks defense that has been hard to move.

Williams continues to deliver timely completions under pressure. The connection to Odunze on the drive was another example of him extending plays and finding open receivers.

Seattle's offense remains limited outside of isolated JSN moments. The OPI call was a tough break, but the Bears' defense is generating pressure and forcing incomplete or short gains.

Jeffery Simmons continues to show up as a disruptor in his debut, contributing to the interior pressure that has helped limit Darnold.

Swift's short-yardage score perfectly complemented the long opening drive. Chicago is winning with sustained, physical football rather than relying on explosives, and that is the harder style for Seattle to counter.

The OPI wipeout of JSN's potential scoring chance was a quiet but significant swing. Seattle is not generating enough consistent offense to overcome those kinds of setbacks right now. I thought it was the right call – JSN clearly pushed off. The only surprise is that the refs actually called it.

If the Bears keep stacking six-minute drives and finishing them in the end zone, this game is going to get out of reach even if JSN makes another big play. The Seahawks need a quick answer early in the fourth or the physical edge Chicago has established will decide the night.

The final period featured the night's most debated moments and Seattle's closest push. Early in the quarter, Austin Booker blocked a Jason Myers field-goal attempt, preserving Chicago's two-score lead. On the ensuing possession, Colston Loveland caught a short pass, then fumbled after a hit from DeMarcus Lawrence, who recovered at the Chicago 25. Seattle converted the turnover with a 7-yard touchdown pass from Darnold to Cooper Kupp and a successful two-point conversion to Tory Horton, cutting the lead to 20-17.

Chicago answered with two more Swift rushing touchdowns (5 yards each), the second set up in part by a Kalif Raymond screen, to push the final margin to 34-17. A late interception sealed the outcome.

The late-third-quarter OPI on JSN that wiped out a near-goal-line opportunity remained a point of contention. It was the kind of contact that draws flags inconsistently depending on the crew and the moment.

The Loveland fumble was forced cleanly by Lawrence, but the timing—right after the blocked kick—flipped field position and briefly brought Seattle back within one score.

Earlier in the game, a potential late hit on Darnold by Devin Bush drew criticism as a no-call; the broadcast and social reaction suggested it met the criteria for unnecessary roughness on a sliding quarterback, though no flag was thrown. I don't agree; even if it is technically a foul, we need to get the game back to reflecting real football.

Delay-of-game timing on Chicago snaps and a post-play flag that forced a replay of a down also drew complaints about consistency.

Even with the turnover and the OPI debate, Chicago's response was decisive. Swift's three rushing touchdowns closed the game after Seattle got within three.

Simmons' early sack and continued interior presence set a defensive tone that limited Seattle outside of the one JSN score and the short Kupp touchdown.

The blocked field goal and the subsequent fumble were the swing plays of the fourth. Seattle capitalized on the turnover, but Chicago's ability to answer immediately with sustained scoring drives showed the difference in control.

This was the most complete performance of the season so far from Chicago. They won the physical battle against the team that had been the gold standard on that side of the ball.

Final takeaway: Chicago didn't just survive Seattle. They out-physicaled them, controlled the tempo, weathered the controversial moments and the one turnover, and let Swift finish the job. That's the profile of a team that expects to be playing in January.

But what did you think about the Bears win over the Seattle Seahawks? How did you feel about Big Jeff's performance in his first game as a Chicago Bear? Tell us in the comments below!

#2729. Thomaston girls soccer wins a Berkshire League championship thriller after 3 shootout saves

WOODBURY – If the Thomaston girls soccer team printed its own money, the currency would say: "In Brynn we trust."

Golden Bears junior keeper Brynn Beaudoin, the backbone of the team all season, came through again in a 2-1 victory over Housatonic in a Berkshire League tournament final that was decided in a penalty-kick shootout Monday night at Nonnewaug.

In the rubber match between the two teams, Beaudoin not only stopped three Housy attempts in the shootout, but earlier made the play of the evening by smothering a penalty kick by the Mountaineers' Georgie Clayton with 6½ minutes left in regulation.

"It's really just guessing," said Beaudoin, who had 13 saves for the night. "They're all amazing players. They can shoot very well, so you just guess and hope you're guessing right."

Thomaston coach Greg Blasko will tell you it's more than just a guessing game. Intuition and instinct play roles, too. When the game went to the shootout round, he liked his team's chances. In fact, that was the strategy once the game went to two 5-minute overtimes.

"As we were headed to overtime, that was the plan. Let's defend. Let's get to PK's. You've been practicing them. We've got a BL first-team All-Star goalkeeper. Why wouldn't we want to go to penalty kicks," Blasko said. "The plan came together."

Through four kicks by each side, the shootout was tied, 2-2. Hannah Zuklie and and Kaylee Boulanger converted for Thomaston, while Leila Wiles and Emma Wiles were stymied. For Housatonic, Lainey Diorio and Attie Bergin converted, while Lyla Diorio and Kenzie Lotz were stopped by Beaudoin.

On Thomaston's final attempt, freshman Kyla Lahey planted the ball in the upper left corner for her 31st goal of the season. On Housy's final attempt, Clayton's shot, with a slight assist by Beaudoin, hit the crossbar.

"I was thinking if I make this, our team would win," said Lahey of her final shot. "I knew Brynn would save it and she did. I always trust Brynn."

Lahey scored the first goal of the game with 10 minutes left in the first half by intercepting the ball and rocketing a shot through the fingers of Housy keeper Vi Salazar (nine saves). Three minutes later, the game was tied again after an own goal when Clayton's cross ricocheted in off Thomaston defender Emma Harkness.

With 6:40 on the clock in regulation, Clayton was tripped in the penalty box and awarded a penalty kick. Her shot was headed for the lower left corner, but Beaudoin dove to cover it and keep the game tied.

"She's amazing. I asked her to be a captain this year for a lot of reasons, but mostly just her leadership and commitment to the game," said Blasko. "She works really hard at what she does. She plays all year. We're fortunate to have her and we get her for another year, too."

Thomaston (16-2) has the third seed in the Class S state tournament, while Housatonic (16-2), the BL champion after winning the regular season, will be No. 7.

"I thought we dominated the second half and that's what we needed. We couldn't put them away, but we had it in their end most of the time, I thought," said Mountaineers coach Don Drislane. "I'm super proud of our girls."

Thomaston keeper Brynn Beaudoin made 13 saves, including one on a late penalty kick in regulation and three in a penalty-kick shootout.

"This means we're ready for the state tournament. We're ready for the next level." – Thomaston keeper Brynn Beaudoin.

#2728. Knicks bench comes alive in groggy win over Nets

For their second time in less than a week, the Knicks' bench picked up the slack for an inconsistent New York team Monday night.

Led by Landry Shamet, Jordan Clarkson, and Miles McBride, the reserves combined for 41 of the Knicks' 103 total points against the Nets, replicating a performance that saved New York against the Chicago Bulls on Oct. 28.

After not scoring a single point in Friday's loss to the Philadelphia 76ers, Shamet, who played for Brooklyn during the 2020-21 season, posted a game-best 22 points, tacking on one rebound and one assist in 29 minutes of play. He also went 6-for-8 from the field, 4-for-6 from beyond the arc, and 6-for-6 from the free throw line.

Clarkson added seven points and a block in 11 minutes, and McBride shot 50 percent both from field goal range and beyond the arc. Though he saw just five minutes of play time toward the end of the game, Tyler Kolek scored two, added one rebound and one assist, and finished the game plus-13.

"Our bench was fantastic," head coach Mike Brown said after the game. "I thought Landry came off and gave us a big lift on both ends of the floor. Jordan as well. And then Tyler — I thought Tyler's minutes were tremendous. He did a fantastic job running the team, getting us some easy looks, and then he was solid defensively."

In a back-and-forth game that saw the crosstown rivals trade leads the whole way through the first 36 minutes of play, the deep bench provided the boost the Knicks needed to get over their third-quarter slump that began before the half. In the 12 minutes after the break, New York allowed a 13-0 run from the Nets and got outscored 35-24.

"When we went into a little funk was at the beginning of the second," Brown said. "Us not scoring gave [Brooklyn] a little hope because they were able to shrink that lead and tie it up, even take the lead. When you give a young team confidence, now it's hard to turn the water off ... So I just started searching at that point and went to Tyler, went to Landry, tried JC, and then we found a group that caught a little groove and helped us take the lead back and create separation."

Brown gave special praise to Clarkson, who recorded a season-high 18 points in 17 minutes, as well as two steals, three rebounds, and an assist against the Bulls. He finished that outing with a game high plus-15 plus/minus.

"You have a veteran that's been there, done that, and he's willing to accept a role that most guys wouldn't accept, even guys younger that haven't proved as much as he's proven in this league," Brown said. "... That's the ultimate team player. I will say this about JC — I've been around some good teammates. He's got to be the best. He's the definition of ultimate pro."

A win by the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night would have moved them into the final playoff spot in the NFC. Instead, they were outclassed on their home turf by the Chicago Bears. Seattle still sits in eighth place in the conference and just one game out of a playoff spot, but that tiebreaker could come back to haunt them.

All four NFC North teams are in playoff spots right now and at least two games over .500 while the Seahawks are even at 4-4, a game back.

In the NFC West, the San Francisco 49ers were on a bye and moved into the one seed in the NFC anyway after the Minnesota Vikings lost. The Los Angeles Rams won to tie Seattle at 4-4, but the Seahawks have the tiebreaker on division record. The Arizona Cardinals won a wild game over the Dallas Cowboys and are just ag ame back of Seattle and L.A.

1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1, strength of victory .456)

2. Minnesota Vikings (6-1, strength of victory .400)

10. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5, win over ATL, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 3-2 NFC)

11. Atlanta Falcons (3-5, loss to TB, 3-3 NFC record)

12. Arizona Cardinals (3-5, 1-0 vs DAL+ARZ, 2-4 NFC)

13. Dallas Cowboys (3-5, 0-2 vs TB+ARZ, loss to ARZ)

First, you get to one team per division so the Falcons and Buccaneers are against each other. Tampa has a win over Atlanta, so they have the tiebreaker.

Tampa vs Arizona vs Dallas is a head-to-head tiebreaker where Atlanta and Arizona move on since they both have wins over Dallas. The Bucs are 3-2 in the NFC vs the Cardinals at 2-4, so Tampa is the 10 seed.

Then the Falcons go into a three-way tiebreaker with the Cardinals and Cowboys. It goes straight to NFC record where the Falcons are 3-3 and the Cardinals and Cowboys are 2-4. Atlanta is the 11 seed.

The Arizona Cardinals beat the Cowboys so they win the head-to-head tiebreaker in the two-way decision. Arizona is 12th and the Cowboys are 13th.

#2724. Seahawks vs. Bears post-game reaction: What we learned from a damaging Monday night defeat

The Seattle Seahawks are in trouble. By no means is the season over at 4-4, but the NFC is deep enough just through the North alone that Seattle has to worry about making the playoffs, forget about making it back to the top of the NFC West. Their 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears was their heaviest under Mike Macdonald since 2024, and the defense finally broke down after the offense spent the whole night spamming three-and-outs.

Myself and Bryce Coutts are here for post-game immediate reaction podcast, which will start at around 8:40 pm PT. You can catch it live or just watch it afterward when you're in a mood to listen to a lot of ranting.

Brian Fleury's magic lasted a week, he's back on the hot seat. Where was the sense of urgency in this offense? Why are they constantly burning early downs with runs to the weaker side of the offensive line? Why does the offense look so consistently labored? How is the offense this broken when the ball isn't being thrown to JSN? Fleury looks like he's not in a good position to lead this offense.

Sam Darnold was terrible and worse than the stats suggested. The one pick was kind to Darnold. The sack number could've been much higher if not for repeated undisciplined penalties by the Bears secondary. He had happy feet, inaccurate throws, basically everything we weren't seeing last week against the Kansas City Chiefs. This is not a quarterback playing with confidence or trusting what he sees, and the combo of his struggles and Fleury's struggles could be tied together.

It turns out the running game just isn't magically fixed overnight. Quenton Nelson is here, which is cool. Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are back. That's super cool. The run game stinks. That's not cool. Only 61 yards on 17 carries from running backs.

Even "The Dark Side" is fallible. Caleb Williams made some magnificent plays, but the Seahawks defense was not at their sharpest. They gave up a few preventable pass game explosives, and that screen to Kalif Raymond at 20-17 was a killer to concede. With Leonard Williams out with a stinger, the hope is it's not a major issue because the d-line gets much thinner when he's not in the lineup, and the defense is worse off. Nick Emmanwori was last week's darling and one of this week's worst performers.

The Seahawks special teams was horrendous. Penalties, missed kicks, blocked field goals, and poor kick returns galore. This was an unacceptable performance by a unit that was magnificent last year and has been way too inconsistent this year.

Seattle's postseason hopes are in jeopardy. While Seattle doesn't have another daunting stretch on the schedule, this team isn't playing well enough to trust that they're capable of comfortably winning against anyone right now. A lot of things need fixing and I'm not sure how much can be fixed this year.

The Bears confirmed their own belief that they're serious contenders after last week's trade for All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons. Wearing the No. 99 jersey once used by Hall of Famer Dan Hampton with the legendary '85 Bears, Simmons had a whale of a debut in navy and orange, racking up six tackles, two tackles for losses and a sack as Chicago's ninth-ranked defense seems poised to take a step up in class. Chicago entered the night with the league's second-ranked rushing attack – and only because the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' 324-yard output in Sunday's win during a Florida deluge skewed the Bucs into the lead. But they will remain there after the Bears RBs ran for all of 86 yards and 2.7 per carry – though a 39-yard lateral from Williams to WR Kalif Raymond made the final total (126 yards) look more respectable. And D'Andre Swift did wind up in the end zone three times.

Seattle got its top RBs, Zach Charbonnet (back from a torn ACL in last season's playoffs) and rookie Jadarian Price (back from a chest injury that landed him on injured reserve), on the field together for the first time. They're going to need time to grow after combining for just 52 rushing yards – and behind a reconfigured offensive line starting Nelson at left guard while Grey Zabel shifted to right guard and LT Charles Cross was missing entirely.

For a while, it appeared the PAT the Seahawks kicker missed and field-goal try that was blocked would loom large. Ultimately, that wasn't the case – but not a pretty night, from several aspects, for Seattle's typically solid special teams.

A quarterback who's had a notably uneven career is having that kind of season in microcosm. Behind his new-look line, Darnold was often under fire and consequently inaccurate, completing just half of his 34 passes for 188 yards, two TDs and another pick (his ninth in seven 2026 starts). Darnold doesn't need to be Seattle's leading man most weeks, but he's got to be more than a small-time character actor.

#2720. Karl's agent Ballack hits back at Bayern chiefs with strong defence of teenager

Amid a rather difficult spell since returning from injury, Lennart Karl has recently faced criticism from Bayern chiefs Max Eberl and Uli Hoeneß over his performances and behaviour off the pitch, with the latter suggesting that the 18-year-old needs to show more humility.

Speaking ahead of Saturday night's clash between Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund, former Germany international Michael Ballack came to the youngster's defence in his role as a DAZN pundit.

Ballack, who also serves as Karl's agent, made it clear that he considers the criticism of his client too harsh, pointing to his young age.

“Lennart is 18 years old. Where were you when you were 18? Just as he is finding his feet on the pitch, he is also trying things out off it. Social media is a major factor today, not just for the younger generation. Everyone is entitled to present themselves however they want," Ballack said.

“Of course, that does not mean getting everything right. Criticism is unfortunately inevitable. But you should not mix that up with his development as a footballer. And that is exactly what Bayern Munich are doing.”

Following Bayern's 6-1 win over 1. FC Magdeburg, Eberl said that Karl “needs to show on the pitch that he can get himself out of this slump” – comments Ballack found difficult to understand.

“For Max Eberl to now claim that Lennart is going through a dip in form, accompanied by references to missteps, just as his performances are clearly improving again, is difficult to understand in terms of timing and certainly questionable in terms of content,” he said.

According to Ballack, the fact that Karl managed to break through at Bayern at just 17 shows that he possesses not only considerable talent but also strong character.

“Lennart's development as a footballer has been outstanding over the past year. To establish himself at Bayern Munich at the age of 17 speaks not only to his exceptional footballing ability but, above all – and that is far more important at a top club like this – to his character. Lennart Karl has character. It is to be expected that this will rub some people up the wrong way once or twice during his career. I hope Lennart doesn't allow himself to be completely changed before he even turns 20. He has my full support," he said.

Karl eventually came on in the 84th minute of Saturday's 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund, replacing Michael Olise after the Frenchman picked up an injury.

#2719. Warriors' Draymond Green ejected after shove match with Dillon Brooks

SAN FRANCISCO ― There's no love lost between Golden State Warriors forward Draymond Green and Phoenix Suns guard Dillon Brooks.

The two have a history of trash-talking and getting into shoving matches with one another. They kept that tension going during the Warriors-Suns matchup on Monday, Nov. 2.

Green committed a foul against Suns center Khaman Maluach, wrapping him up in an intentional foul before throwing him to the ground. Green was initially called for a foul and then an ensuing technical foul for shoving Maluach to the ground.

Things got spicy and Green got a visit from his old friend, or foe, Brooks. Brooks took exception to Green's push on his teammate and ran to the pile, pushing Green.

Green retaliated as teammates, coaches and game officials had to separate the two players. Both Green and Brooks received double-technical fouls for the dust up.

It was Green's second technical, which resulted in an automatic disqualification. Green left the game at the 10-minute mark of the third quarter. He finished the game with four points, four rebounds, two assists and a steal in 17 minutes.

The Warriors went on to win the game, 116-113.

#2718. Bears DT Jeffery Simmons gets huge sack in Chicago debut en route to win over Seahawks

SEATTLE — Just four days after heading to the Chicago Bears, Jeffery Simmons immediately made an impact.

Simmons, who was acquired by the Bears on Thursday in a big trade with the Tennessee Titans, made his debut in blue and orange in a 34-17 win over the Seattle Seahawks on Monday night. And in the first quarter, the defensive tackle made a huge play, sacking the Seahawks' Sam Darnold for a 6-yard loss.

Unfortunately for Chicago, it didn't get to reap the rewards of the tackle due to a penalty. Grady Jarrett was flagged for a facemask that took place after the play, resulting in Seattle gaining 15 yards. But the sack counted in the books, giving Simmons his first big stat since changing teams.

Simmons finished with six total tackles, including three solo, in the massive win over Seattle. He also tipped a pass from Darnold that was collected by James Lynch for a game-sealing pick in the fourth quarter.

"It means a lot to me," Simmons said on the broadcast after the win, "to be able to play meaningful football."

The Bears paid up in order to get Simmons, sending Tennessee two first-round draft picks (a 2027 and a 2028) as part of the trade package. Chicago's defense has had its struggles, with the team allowing the most yards per attempt (8.7) in the league.

Despite the high cost, Bears general manager Ryan Poles said Friday that the team doesn't think of it as not caring about draft picks — or, as he calls it, the "F them picks" mentality. Instead, he touted Simmons' ability to make a difference both on the field and within the team's culture.

"I don't think it can be either or when you talk about a move this size," Poles said. "You need to have both. And that's what Jeffery does. We believe he's going to impact us at a high level on the grass but also in the locker room, too."

#2716. Luka Dončić shows how unbeatable Lakers can be in rout of Heat

LOS ANGELES — Luka Dončić has had himself a day.

Dončić, over a 24-hour stretch, dropped a staggering 87 points in consecutive Los Angeles Lakers victories, the latest Monday, Nov. 2 in a 138-117 domination over the Miami Heat. In the process, not only did Dončić outshine Heat star Giannis Antetokounmpo, he's proving that Los Angeles is close to unbeatable when he's besieging opponents with buckets.

Case in point: entering the night, NBA teams were averaging 113.7 points per game; the Lakers, by the end of the third quarter, were already at 111. For reference, that was four points off from tying the most allowed by the Heat through three quarters in their history.

One night after he dropped 45 in a win over the Toronto Raptors, Dončić toasted the Heat to the tune of 42 points on 14-of-24 shooting, scooping 7 rebounds and dishing out 13 assists.

It didn't matter who Miami sent at Dončić. Versatile defensive wing Andrew Wiggins started the game on Dončić, but Pelle Larsson and Davion Mitchell each got their turn. Later in the third, after Dončić was creeping toward 40 points, Heat coach Erik Spoelstra dug deep in the bench and deployed defensive-specialist guard Dru Smith. The Heat threw double-teams at Dončić, but that didn't matter, either.

Dončić zipped and lofted passes to open teammates who had been left neglected because of those double-teams. By the end of the third, he had already posted double-digit assists.

This is the bewildering thing about defending Dončić: even when you try to rush him, he stubbornly plays at his pace, parries away the additional defensive attention – almost teasing blitzing defenders and daring them to get close – only to pinpoint passes right into his teammates' shooting pockets.

This was an efficient Dončić. He did not need to strafe the rim with shots. He was under control. He was never flustered. And, at least on Monday night, he made his teammates better.

Antetokounmpo, by comparison, finished with 30 points on 10-of-17 shooting, adding 12 rebounds and 7 assists.

The Lakers improved to 6-2 and Dončić is now averaging 38.3 points per game, which is a full 4 points greater than the next closest player. They wield one of the top 3 offenses in the NBA. And as injuries have plagued some of the top teams in the West, like the Oklahoma City Thunder, there could be an opening for the Lakers to blossom into a legitimate title threat with Dončić as the unquestioned anchor of the team.

#2713. Luka Doncic's 42-point effort carries Lakers past Giannis Antetokounmpo and Heat

The clash between Luka Doncic and Giannis Antetokounmpo received top billing Monday night at Crypto.com Arena.

Doncic leads the league in scoring with 37.7 points per game for the Lakers and Antetokounmpo is fifth at 28.2 for the Miami Heat.

But this matchup didn't quite live up to the hype after Doncic continued his early season dominance in the Lakers' 138-117 win.

Doncic was masterful, producing 42 points, 13 assists and seven rebounds. He was 14 for 24 from the field and six for 15 from three-point range.

Read more: 'Like a supernova.' Luka Doncic's 45 points only eclipsed by his defense in Lakers' win

Antetokounmpo finished with 30 points, 12 rebounds and seven assists, but the Lakers surged in the third quarter, outscoring Miami 32-21 to cruise to victory.

Doncic was better, but he had more help. Austin Reaves scored 27 points and Walker Kessler finished with 15 points and 15 rebounds.

The Lakers (6-2) shot 57%, including 44% (19 for 43) from three-point range.

Doncic has been on a scoring tear for the Lakers, his play at such a high level that even coach JJ Redick has marveled at the guard's achievements.

In the third quarter, Doncic missed a three-pointer, but Jake LaRavia hustled to collect the rebound. He passed the ball to Doncic, who then made a three to give the Lakers a 93-74 lead. The play forced the Heat (2-5) to call a timeout as Doncic pointed at LaRavia in appreciation.

Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo, right, scores over Lakers center Walker Kessler in the second half. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times)

Doncic started strong like usual, with 16 points, five assists and four rebounds in the first quarter as the Lakers took a 37-30 lead. Doncic, who was called for a technical foul late in the first half — his second of the season — had 24 points by halftime.

In his previous four games, Doncic had scored 45, 37, 41 and 52 points.

Redick was asked before the game if anything stood out to him about Doncic's early-season surge.

"No, and I don't take it for granted," Redick said. "I think a lot of times you can just be agog at his offensive prowess. Like watching some of the tape last night, and even during the game, like I think our guys were like agog at his defense. And it was just awesome. It was inspiring. I really mean that."

#2710. Knicks Notes: Mike Brown not hesitating to sit Mikal Bridges; Jordan Clarkson providing spark

Mikal Bridges was 1-for-7 in the third quarter on Monday and the Knicks were struggling. Some NBA head coaches would stick with their veteran in that spot. It's easier to keep a player like Bridges - one who is signed to a large contract and was obtained for significant trade capital - on the court.

But in this respect, Mike Brown isn't most coaches. He didn't hesitate to bench Bridges in the second half of the Knicks' win over the Nets.

We're seven games into the season. Brown has pulled Bridges in the third quarter of three of those seven games.

"Yeah, he's just got to keep playing. Everybody goes through those ups and downs throughout the course of the season, and obviously, it's the beginning of the season right now, so he's got to find his way," Brown said after New York's win over Brooklyn. "Not just with him but with everybody, when you're in a funk you gotta find one or two things to hold your hat on. Mikal is one of the best runners in the NBA.

"In both directions - offensively and defensively. So he's just got to try to hang his hat on that as well as his cutting and trying to do the other little things - rebounding and driving and touching the paint and spraying it. Then this shot will come eventually."

Bridges is shooting 30 percent from the floor so far this year. If you've watched the Knicks during Bridges' tenure, you know that he can be up and down over the course of the regular season. And you also know he can deliver in big playoff situations. Brown believes Bridges will ultimately be fine.

"It's a matter of time in my opinion, before Mikal gets going," Brown said.

But if the Knicks head coach thinks someone else gives the team a better chance to win on a given night, he won't hesitate to sit Bridges.

After a sluggish three quarters, Brown turned to Jordan Clarkson and Tyler Kolek to start the fourth quarter. Clarkson, Kolek, Josh Hart, OG Anunoby and Karl-Anthony Towns sparked the Knicks early in the fourth.

It was the second time in the past three games that Clarkson helped turn things around. The veteran had 18 points in New York's comeback win in Chicago. But he has also basically been out of the rotation in three of New York's seven games.

"I think it shows his character more than anything else. He's someone that if he was on a different team, he could play 20, 25 minutes every night. He could score double digits. He could be that spark, that microwave off the bench. And he's here," Hart said. "He was willing to sacrifice and take a smaller role, be a part of something bigger than himself. So it shows its character.

"It shows his professionalism. To be able to go out and do those things. And when he's not doing it, he's out there coaching, not on the court, he's coaching guys up, talking to them, letting them know what he sees. So he's the ultimate professional. He's someone that you want on your team. And whenever he's given an opportunity, he'll go out and play well."

Brown also had effusive praise for Clarkson.

"You have a veteran that's been there, done that. and he's willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn't accept - even guys younger that haven't proved as much as he's proven in this league. And he's willing to accept it," Brown said. "So, in my opinion, if he's willing to accept it, which is what he did last year, and still try to uplift everybody, connect everybody while he's going through what he's going through, then everybody else should. That's that's the ultimate team player, I will say this about JC. I've been around some good teammates. He's got to be the best. He is the definition of ultimate pro."

Additionally, Landry Shamet led the team in scoring with 22 points off of the bench in 29 minutes. The veteran shot 4-for-6 from three, 6-for-8 from the field, and was a perfect 6-for-6 on free throws.

#2706. Warriors on a roll, get fifth straight win behind Steph Curry's 34-point night

SAN FRANCISCO ― The Golden State Warriors have rattled off five consecutive wins following their hard-fought 116-113 win against the Phoenix Suns on Monday, Nov. 2 at Chase Center.

Warriors guard Stephen Curry led the way with 34 points and seven assists, while backcourt running mate Brandin Podziemski dropped 20 points on 50% shooting in the game.

There was no love lost between these two teams, which saw each other on Oct. 24 when the Suns got the upper hand. In the rematch, it was the Warriors who came with energy and fight.

Warriors forward Draymond Green was ejected for the first time this season following a foul against Suns center Khaman Maluach when afterward Green committed a takedown on Maluach. Suns guard Dillon Brooks confronted Green about the push and the two began a shoving match before receiving double technical fouls.

Golden State trailed by 11 points at the time of the technical foul and proceeded to go on a run to fight back into the game before taking over, putting up 42 points in the third period to tie the game 93-93.

The Warriors received a major boost from Charles Bassey, who was effective off the bench scoring 17 points and pulling down 8 rebounds in 23 minutes. Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had 16 points on 3-of-10 shooting, grabbing five rebounds and five assists.

"Bass was great. What a big night for him," Kerr said after the game. "The rebounding, the scoring. You know he and Yaxel have a really good connection. The pick-and-roll game. He gives him a lot of threat. Yaxel sees the floor so well and he's so big that he finds him when he's behind the defense."

Golden State will host the Miami Heat on Thursday, Nov. 5, beginning at 7 p.m. PT (10 p.m. ET).

#2699. What's next for Connor Bedard, Blackhawks after massive five-year, $75 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks have locked in their franchise cornerstone for the near future. On Saturday, the Blackhawks announced that star center Connor Bedard has signed a five-year contract worth $75 million.

Bedard's $15 million average annual value makes him the third-highest paid player in the NHL for the 2026-27 season. Only Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million) and the newly-signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson ($18 million) are ahead of him.

"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat, but to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has already displayed elite offensive upside, even if his overall game still has work to do. Last season, Bedard posted a career high 75 points in 69 games. In 219 NHL games, Bedard has totaled 75 goals and 128 assists.

The biggest issues for Bedard are durability concerns -- he's played fewer than 70 games in two of three seasons and will miss the first month of the upcoming season with a shoulder injury -- and subpar defense. The defense is a common problem for young centers and should improve in the coming years, but Bedard has now suffered multiple shoulder injuries in his career.

With Bedard's long-term contract finalized, both he and the Blackhawks will try to take the next step toward greatness. For the player, that means refining his game in order to become the $15 million man most believe him to be. For the team, that means surrounding Bedard with an adequate supporting cast for the first time in his career.

First and foremost, Bedard needs to get healthy and stay healthy. After missing 13 games with a shoulder injury last year, Bedard suffered another injury that required surgery to fix, and he will miss roughly a dozen games out of the gate in 2026-27. Those issues may delay his jump into the NHL's elite tier of players.

Once back at full strength, Bedard will have to show improvement defensively. He oozes offensive ability, but if Bedard is going to be a true No. 1 franchise center, he has to thrive at both ends of the ice. With Bedard on the ice at five-on-five last season, Chicago surrendered 3.60 xGA/60, per Natural Stat Trick. That was the second-worst number on the team with rookie Anton Frondell bringing up the rear.

That doesn't necessarily mean Bedard was the Blackhawks' worst defensive player, but it does mean he often struggled when going up against the opposing team's best players. Stars -- especially those raking in $15 million per season -- are expected to drive play for their team regardless of circumstance. Bedard didn't do that last season.

Bedard also needs to show more growth in the face-off circle. To his credit, Bedard has already done that, going from 38.9% as a rookie to 47.1% last season. Still, Chicago would probably like to see Bedard closer to 50%, especially with him taking key draws in big moments. Maybe that number keeps rising as Bedard gets strong and adds more tricks in the dot.

If Bedard can round out his game without the puck, $15 million per season will be a very fair deal, especially as salaries explode across the league.

We've already seen what can happen when a restricted free agent has all the leverage in contract negotiations. The Ducks were essentially backed into a $90 million contract after the Philadelphia Flyers signed Carlsson to a massive offer sheet.

That risk was there for Bedard too, which is why Davidson deserves some credit for signing him at a more reasonable cap hit. Bedard still has work to do in order to reach that price point, but his ceiling is worth at least $15 million per season.

The Blackhawks can help their young star by putting more NHL-caliber players around him. Chicago tore it down to the studs in hopes of landing Bedard in the 2023 draft, and while that plan worked, it also created a roster full of holes around the No. 1overall pick. Over the last three seasons, Bedard has had little help.

Chicago already improved its defense this offseason when it acquired Bowen Byram from the Buffalo Sabres. Say what you will about the acquisition cost or his $75 contract extension, but Byram inarguably makes Chicago better on the blue line. That unit still needs work, but it's a step in the right direction.

The real issue is finding Bedard a quality running mate at the top of the lineup. Outside of Bedard, only one other player topped 50 points in 2025-26, and it was 31-year-old Tyler Bertuzzi. Chicago still has $14.1 million in cap space with which to add some firepower, but some upgrades will have to come internally.

It's conceivable that the Blackhawks' lineup will include seven players selected inside the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

That's an exciting proposition, and fans have reasons to be optimistic about the future. That said, none of those players have really established themselves as future stars, outside of Bedard. Frondell, Nazar and Rinzel seem like the best bets to get there soon, but that's based more on projection than anything tangible.

The first month of the season should be an excellent barometer for the Blackhawks as they assess those players. Bedard will be out of the lineup, and it'll be interesting to see who sinks and who swims until he returns. Once Chicago establishes exactly what it has in its young nucleus, Davidson can then go out and aggressively address needs via trades and free agency.

#2697. Biggest questions for World Series Game 5: How will the Rays get enough innings to avoid elimination (again)?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Tampa Bay Rays took their first step toward a baseball miracle with their 12th-inning comeback win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Tuesday's Game 4 of the World Series. That 4-3 victory means the Rays avoided the sweep and cut the Brewers' series lead to 3-1. That sets the stage for Wednesday's Game 5.

Tuesday's escape for the Rays was obviously an essential one, as it was an elimination game. The win also nudged the Rays' chances of winning the series from "all but impossible" to "merely a longshot." Across all of Major League Baseball postseason history, 42 teams have been down 3-0, and only one – the 2004 Boston Red Sox – has come back to win the series in question. That is, history suggests the Rays had a mere 2.4% chance of pulling off the miracle comeback when they were down 3-0. Now, though, they're down 3-1.

In all, 96 teams have been down 3-1 in a best-of-seven MLB postseason series, and 14 of them have clawed back to win the series. That particular data set says the Rays have a 14.6% chance of stunning the Brewers and winning this Fall Classic. Those aren't great odds, obviously, but they're much better than the odds the Rays were facing going into Game 4. Interestingly, teams down 3-1 have a .500 record in Game 5.

Speaking of which, that brings us to three questions for Game 5 – the answers to which will determine whether the Rays can cut the Brewers' advantage to 3-2 and send the series back to Milwaukee. Let's get to it.

Here's the big one. Rays manager Kevin Cash wisely managed Game 4 for what it was: a must-win contest. That means you worry about tomorrow when tomorrow comes and tactically do everything possible to survive the elimination game. Tomorrow, though, has now arrived, and Cash must figure out how to deploy his pitching staff for another elimination game after using seven arms on Tuesday. Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen will be going on short rest in Game 5, but what then?

The most notable Game 4 decision was using Nick Martinez, who had been slated to start Game 5, in relief. Martinez worked two scoreless innings out of the bullpen and threw 33 pitches. It'll be another all-hands-on-deck affair on Wednesday, but just who those hands will be after Rasmussen is another matter. Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay and amassed 74 pitches, which presumably rules him out for Game 5.

As for the traditional relievers, Cole Sulser, Steven Matz, and Garrett Cleavinger did not pitch on Tuesday and thus can probably expect to be used in Game 5. Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly did pitch in Game 4 but they didn't pitch in Monday's Game 3 blowout loss, which means they're presumably available. Ian Seymour also didn't pitch in Game 3, but his 32-pitch workload in Game 4 may rule him out. Tyler Wells and Cameron Booser have each pitched two days in a row, but desperate straits in October may mean they'll be called upon again. As for Rasmussen, he's made short-rest starts before, but he was basically an opener in those outings, the last of which was in 2022. This, then, is something close to virgin territory for him. No doubt, Cash won't lean on Rasmussen for a long start even if he's cruising, but they could use some bulk from him given the shallow and probably tired bullpen. This will be Rasmussen's fifth start of the 2026 postseason. Across his previous four starts, he put up a 2.19 ERA and 2.57 FIP with 27 strikeouts and five walks in 24 ⅔ innings.

In light of the maxed-out stakes involved, anyone who's even a remotely feasible option will probably tell Cash he's willing to pitch. As such, Cash's decisions on whom to trust and whom to assign the plurality of innings will be fascinating and perhaps determinative.

No such dilemmas are to be found for Pat Murphy and the Brewers, at least insofar as their Game 5 starter is concerned. Jacob Misiorowski, the 24-year-old NL Cy Young favorite and the hardest-throwing starting pitcher anyone's ever seen, on Wednesday will make his fourth start of these playoffs. Last time out, Misiorowski in Game 1 against the Rays went five innings and permitted only one run en route to picking up the win. "Miz" also enjoyed a velocity bump compared to his prior run of starts.

However, he was coming off 11 days of rest in that start, and for his Game 5 trip to the bump he'll be on the standard four days of rest. He's well into career-high-workload territory in 2026, so it remains to be seen whether the sizzle he showed in the series opener will be back for Game 5. The Brewers could use some length from him given how hard the bullpen worked in Game 4.

The Rays' best hitter and one of the richest power sources in all of baseball had to exit Game 4 in the 12th inning not long after reaching base on Joey Ortiz's throwing error. He did so because of an injury to his left foot. From afar, this seems like the kind of knock that would earn Caminero a few days off had it occurred in, say, June, but this is very much not June.

"Junior, he's fine and obviously in the lineup today. Really impressive that he went first and third right there, very instinctual play," Cash said on Wednesday.

"He's been dealing with some lower extremity injuries, but there's a lot of guys that are nicked up right now playing through a lot and know that Cammy will be ready to go today."

The heart of the matter is whether Caminero will be in top form less than 24 hours after sustaining the injury. That's worth pondering in light of his ongoing power outage. Caminero this postseason has a respectable .717 OPS, but he has only one home run in 48 at-bats. That's after hitting a whopping 42 homers during the regular season and averaging one every 14.7 at-bats. It's quite possible that the Rays will need some customary thump from the hard-hitting 23-year-old if they're going to extend the series. That we shall see.
