#2672. Five ways the NBA's injury outbreak could impact trade season: OKC has work to do, Rockets are in control

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At a bare minimum we're still six weeks away from the unofficial start of NBA trade season. It's still October, and a bit less than one-third of the league is still not trade-eligible because they signed new contracts in free agency. The moves usually don't begin until Dec. 15, when the bulk of those players become trade-eligible.

The strategizing for those moves, however, is a never-ending process, and even though we've only seen nine days worth of games, the entire league landscape has already been turned on its head by one of the earliest injury outbreaks in NBA history. Let's do a quick roll call: Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, Jaren Jackson Jr., Tyrese Haliburton, Kawhi Leonard, Anthony Edwards and Paolo Banchero are all out with injuries that should sideline them for weeks or months at best and all season at worst. Their teams suddenly have to figure out how to manage without their best players... but everyone else has to figure out what those absences mean in the long run.

Again... we're barely a week into the season. The market could change drastically again in eight days or eight weeks. We're more than three months away from the deadline. But so much has already happened that it's worth taking a step back and figuring out what this could mean when the deals eventually start coming. Here are five ripple effects the early rash of injuries could have on the trade market.

Think about the trades Oklahoma City tends to make. They're almost always from a position of strength. They traded Paul George to the Clippers when they had them at their mercy during Kawhi Leonard's free agency. They didn't proactively seek out Alex Caruso. They were looking to move Josh Giddey when the perfect role player fell into their laps. They got Jared McCain with a spare first-round pick because Daryl Morey thought he was selling high. The only notable, recent occasion in which the Thunder have added a notable veteran based on an immediate need was Isaiah Hartenstein, who came in free agency. The Thunder typically don't have needs. They develop players to address them before they arise.

Well, because of injuries, the Thunder suddenly do have needs. The bare minimum here is a versatile, forward-sized defender. They tried to steal Spencer Jones from the Nuggets over the summer for this exact purpose. At the time, they likely viewed Jones or Jones-esque defender as a luxury. Now, someone like that is a necessity. Oklahoma City's formerly endless rotation of All-Defense-caliber point-of-attack stoppers is now down to Caruso, who's already sporting an ankle sprain. Their playing style is enormously reliant on this archetype for turnover generation and transition offense.

There are half-court offensive questions as well. We all saw what Victor Wembanyama did to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander without Williams in the Western Conference Finals. Ajay Mitchell is healthy now. He wasn't in that series. How his next few months play out will tell the Thunder whether or not they have to upgrade the offense as well. They can't expect to score on Wembanyama if their offense devolves into nothing but Gilgeous-Alexander mid-range jumpers. Eventually, Alex Caruso is going to miss a playoff 3-pointer.

So for the first time since perhaps the Kevin Durant era, the Thunder, and their endless reserves of assets, go into a trade deadline with obvious needs and an imperative to address them. This roster gets more expensive by the year. The Thunder can't afford to waste a season. Their financial limitations are significant, but Sam Presti is the NBA's best general manager. If there is a way to keep the Thunder up to speed with Wembanyama and the Spurs, he's going to find it.

Oklahoma City's vulnerability trickles down to everyone else. We entered the season assuming a Thunder-Spurs conference finals rematch was inevitable. The Thunder are weakened. The entire rest of the West is one Wembanyama ankle sprain away from 2027 becoming their best chance for the foreseeable future. The Lakers, the Nuggets and the Timberwolves suddenly have far more reason to be aggressive than they did 10 days ago. The problem is that all three of them are working with limited means of improvement:

Minnesota is obviously dealing with the trickiest situation of the three since Edwards is already hurt. They can't justify a win-now move until they have a better sense of how healthy he'll be in the spring. And yet, with Rudy Gobert in his age-34 season and the Thunder more beatable than ever, they might have to roll those dice. Can they really justify holding onto Donte DiVincenzo's contract considering he might not return from his torn Achilles this season, for example? He's someone they hope to keep as a long-term bench fixture. He's also the only notable salary Minnesota can use to add someone who can help now, when the West seems winnable.

The Lakers are starting two minimum-salary wings, and their backup center minutes have been atrocious. The Nuggets are winless against teams besides the Pelicans. These are talented yet flawed teams staring down a future in a conference that features two younger, deeper and better juggernauts. This is an opportunity that may not repeat itself. The ones who take it will be in far better shape than the ones who don't.

The Rockets have the same newfound sense of urgency that the Lakers, Nuggets and Wolves do... under a completely different set of internal circumstances. They have a sizable draft pick surplus. They have salaries of every size to trade. They're also undefeated, including a win over San Antonio that underlined their meaningful advantages in that matchup Alperen Sengun is one of the few bigs in the NBA that tends to enjoy attacking Wembanyama. They have the perimeter defensive depth to handle San Antonio's guards. The Rockets, of those four non-Thunder or Spurs West contenders, probably should feel the best about their ability to win the title right now, with what they already have.

That puts the Rockets where the Thunder usually sit: a position of strength. There's an obvious need to fill when it comes to adding another shot-creator, but their ability to trade for basically anyone across the salary or asset spectrum with the leverage to tell any trade partner "no thanks, we're good enough as is" gives them control of the board. They can outbid just about any rival suitor for just about any theoretically available player if they so choose, effectively giving them right of first refusal over most of the trade landscape unless the Thunder or Spurs are prepared to take on contracts bigger than we'd presently expect.

So much of what's happening in the West starts with Oklahoma City. Those same ripples aren't felt in the East. There, teams are much more concerned with themselves than their competitors.

Take the Raptors. They have RJ Barrett on an expiring contract and a clear need for more shooting. With a healthy Kawhi Leonard, Barrett's individual creation might be a luxury. With him injured, it's a necessity. The Thunder can't really evaluate Barrett's fit on the Leonard-centric version of their team until Leonard returns, and they can't consider whether or not there's a way to flip Barrett into more shooting until they know how important he is to their actual roster.

The Pacers are adapting to playing with a center that cannot shoot 3s. That's a fairly traditional basketball problem, but it's still new to a team that reached the Finals on the strength of its shooting. The Haliburton-Ivica Zubac tandem has only played 52 minutes together thus far, and with Haliburton sidelined, it'll be awhile until Indiana gets a bigger sample than that. Those two are going to be fixtures for the Pacers, but Indiana is still relatively liquid from a draft pick perspective and has serious questions to address on the bench. A clearer idea of where that duo is deficient, if anywhere, would help the Pacers figure out what sort of bench help to target.

And then there's Orlando. Poor, poor Orlando. For the third straight season, Paolo Banchero has suffered a meaningful injury in October or November. In each of the last two seasons, Franz Wagner took on a bigger role while Banchero was out and eventually got hurt himself right around Banchero's return. The Magic are running out of bullets to fire. They've traded most of their picks for Desmond Bane and they've changed coaches by hiring Sean Sweeney. They're headed for a financial crisis with Anthony Black hitting restricted free agency next summer and their total payroll getting dangerously close to the second apron.

The West trade market changed drastically by virtue of what happened to the Thunder. The opposite is true for the East. These teams haven't gotten new information. They're awaiting information they assumed they'd be getting in the early weeks of the season but will instead come further down the line. If the rumors start coming in earlier than expected, you should therefore assume that the West is the conference driving most of that activity.

So we've identified why the West contenders are going to be eager to improve. The East isn't there yet, but give it time. In a conference with no clear favorite, there are usually plenty of teams looking for reinforcements. Here's the problem: we don't know where they're going to get them. The NBA has never had fewer obvious sellers than it does right now.

We're in a post-lottery reform world now. Nobody wants to lose. That's not just true in a single-year setting. There are going to be fewer and fewer teams that proactively initiate multi-year teardowns now that there are slightly more plausible paths to building from the middle. Contenders get stripped for parts every offseason because of the aprons. Teams that might have rebuilt in the past are instead going to attempt to be opportunistic about adding players whose teams can no longer afford them.

Now you throw in all of these injuries. Not only does that create an excess of potential buyers, but it also freezes the potential sellers market because there are inevitably going to be teams that outperform their on-paper talent because the schedule just got a bit easier and teams that should be above them in the standings instead fall short because of absences.

There are only four teams we can confidently call sellers right now: the Kings, Pelicans, Nets and Bucks. If you want an idea of how confident these sellers are in their ability to extract value for their veterans, look at Shamit Dua's reporting on the Pelicans. New Orleans still reportedly wants two first-round picks worth of value for Herb Jones... who is averaging less than 18 minutes per game to start the season.

New Orleans has been notoriously averse to trading its players away under Joe Dumars, but remember, the Nets functioned as buyers this offseason when they added Julius Randle. They have historically held their veterans until they've been offered a premium, most notably Kevin Durant, Mikal Bridges and Cam Johnson. That's something to keep in mind as they consider Michael Porter Jr. offers. The Bucks and Kings are so early into rebuilds that their plans, for now, are a bit of a mystery.

All of this together suggests that the teams that are willing to trade veterans expect to get significant returns for them. There are simply more teams that want to add right now than there are teams that want to subtract. We'll get closer to equilibrium in January and February, but for all of the reasons we've outlined, we'll probably be further from it as a whole than we've been at any point over the last several years at least.

#2669. Key MLB offseason dates: When does free agency start? What else will happen before potential lockout?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 MLB season is complete and the Brewers are World Series champions. They defeated the Rays to clinch the first title in franchise history. We were assured a first-time champion this season and the Brewers won it. The Rays will try again for their first title next year. With the World Series now complete, the 2026-27 offseason has officially begun, and several significant events are right around the corner.

Of course, this all comes with a disclaimer. When the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. That could take days, weeks, months, who knows? It may affect spring training and even the 2027 regular season, or they may find labor peace before the spring. Regardless, the likely lockout will all but certainly affect some of the calendar. MLB free agency will still begin in early November, but transactions will all come to a halt the minute there is a lockout.

Here now are the important dates and deadlines for the coming weeks and months.

As of 9 a.m. ET, eligible players (i.e. those with at least six years of service time) are free agents. Free agents cannot sign with a new team just yet. They have to wait five days for that. The first five days of the offseason are an exclusive negotiating period during which free agents can only talk money with their most recent team. Very few players re-sign during the exclusive negotiating period. Edwin Díaz returning to the Mets four years ago is by far the most notable in recent memory. Once players get this close to free agency, they typically test the market. Also, trades involving 40-man roster players resume on this day for the first time since the summer's trade deadline.

This year's Gold Glove winners will be announced during an ESPN broadcast at 8:30 p.m. ET. The Cubs and Blue Jays lead the way with five Gold Glove finalists each. In addition to the nine individual positions in each league, there is also a utility Gold Glove and a team Gold Glove.

Most contract option decisions are due on this date. Some contracts specify a different date (the Yankees had to make a decision on Zack Britton's 2022 club option in November 2020, for example), but the vast majority have to be made within five days of the end of the World Series. Club options are controlled by the team, player options and opt-outs are controlled by the player, and mutual options are kind of pointless. They're a way to shift money to the next year's payroll more than anything.

Some option decisions are no-brainers, like the Braves picking up their $17 million club option on Ronald Acuña Jr. or Luis Severino picking up his $22 million player option with the Athletics. This offseason's notable contract option decisions include Michael King (can opt out of two years and $58 million with Padres), Bo Bichette (can opt out of two years and $84 million with Mets), and Luis Robert Jr. (Orioles hold $20 million club option).

The qualifying offer is a one-year contract worth the average of the top 125 salaries, or $23.15 million this offseason, according to the New York Post. To be eligible for the qualifying offer, a free agent must have spent the entire 2026 season with one team and have never received the QO previously. The Mariners can make Randy Arozarena the QO, but the Dodgers cannot do the same with Tarik Skubal because he was traded during the season.

The five-day exclusive negotiating period ends and free agents are truly free. They can negotiate and sign with any team as of 5 p.m. ET on this date. That said, much like the regular season, MLB's free agency is a marathon, not a sprint. We (probably) won't see a rush of signings on Day 1 because MLB is not a salary-capped league (not yet, anyway), and free agents aren't worried about getting left out in the cold when cap space runs out.

Rookies of the Year on Monday, Managers of the Year on Tuesday, Cy Youngs on Wednesday, and MVPs on Thursday. The awards will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast at 7 p.m. ET each day. Awards finalists will be announced Nov. 2. The All-MLB Team, Comeback Players of the Year, and Relievers of the Year will also be announced on Nov. 11.

Generally speaking, the GM Meetings are used to handle off-the-field matters like rule changes, but when you put all 30 GMs in one place, deals inevitably get discussed and sometimes completed. The Angels signed Travis d'Arnaud and the Braves traded Nick Allen to the Astros at last year's GM Meetings, for example. Also, the groundwork is often laid this week for deals that are completed at a later date.

If Silver Sluggers are your thing, this is the date for you. Four years ago, a utility player Silver Slugger was added, then three years ago, MLB and Louisville debuted a team Silver Slugger. Finalists will be announced Nov. 2.

The deadline for free agents to accept or reject the QO is 4 p.m. ET.  Players who accept the QO sign that one-year, $23.15 million contract and remain with their team (and cannot be traded until June 15 without their consent). Free agents who reject the QO are attached to draft pick compensation. Their former team receives a draft pick if they sign elsewhere, and their new team has to forfeit a draft pick(s) and, in some cases, international bonus money. Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are among the free agents who will surely reject the QO and sign more lucrative contracts this offseason.

That is a fancy way of saying this is the deadline for teams to add eligible minor leaguers to the 40-man roster to protect them from the Rule 5 Draft. Generally speaking, college players drafted no later than 2023 and high school players drafted no later than 2022 are Rule 5 Draft eligible this winter, as are players signed internationally no later than 2022. Among the notable Rule 5 Draft-eligible prospects this offseason are Dodgers righty Christian Zazueta and Nationals righty Travis Sykora. Those two and many others will be added to the 40-man roster on this date. The deadline is 6 p.m. ET, specifically.

It should be noted that there are usually several minor trades in the days leading up to the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline as teams get their 40-man roster in order. Four years ago, the Rays traded Xavier Edwards to the Marlins in the 40-man roster management move at the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline.

The now triannual owners meetings cover big-picture business matters and are rarely a source of hot stove news or rumors. Three years ago, the owners voted on and approved the Athletics' proposed relocation to Las Vegas at their November meetings. With the collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1 and talks with the MLB Players Association ongoing, the owners will likely use this week as one last strategy session.

This is the deadline for teams to offer contracts to their pre-arbitration and arbitration-eligible players for 2027. Contracts do not have to be signed yet. An offer just has to be extended. Players who do not receive a contract offer before the deadline are considered "non-tendered" and immediately become free agents. Notable players are non-tendered every offseason as teams determine that their salary outweighs their performance and the trade market turns up nothing worthwhile. Adolis García and Nathaniel Lowe were among the players non-tendered last offseason.

Specifically, the CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET, and it is very likely the owners will lock out the players at that time. It is possible MLB and the MLBPA will agree to a new CBA before this date, sure, but it would be a major surprise. All major league transactions get put on hold during the lockout. There will be no trades or free agent signings involving 40-man roster players, or even any negotiations. Here is our timeline of CBA talks and proposals. Because a potential lockout would bring so much uncertainty, any events and deadlines listed after this date are subject to change. We'll put asterisks as a reminder.

These are the extra draft picks given each year to teams that fall in the bottom 10 in revenue and/or market size. There is overlap between the two groups, so there are typically 14-15 competitive balance picks awarded each year, not 20. Competitive balance picks are MLB's only tradeable draft picks. Last offseason, picks were included in the Shane Baz, Brendan Donovan, and Caleb Durbin/Kyle Harrison trades. Five years ago, the assignment of competitive balance picks was pushed back until after the lockout.

Voting results for the Hall of Fame's Contemporary Baseball Committee for Managers, Executives, and Umpires will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame has restructured its veteran committee three times in the last 14 years, and this year's Contemporary Baseball Committee will consider "candidates whose primary contribution to the game came since 1980." The 16-person committee will consider eight candidates on the ballot. This has nothing to do with the CBA and the announcement will take place as scheduled.

This is typically when all hot stove hell breaks loose. The Winter Meetings are the busiest period of the offseason and feature plenty of trades, free agent signings, and rumors. It is three-plus days of nonstop hot stove action. Historically, the biggest moves of the offseason are completed at the Winter Meetings. GMs can talk face-to-face with agents and other GMs to get things done. Last year, Pete Alonso, Edwin Díaz, and Kyle Schwarber signed during the Winter Meetings while Jose A. Ferrer and Harry Ford were among those traded. The Winter Meetings were canceled during the last lockout. It seems likely they would be canceled again during a potential lockout this offseason.

In an effort to curb tanking, MLB and the MLBPA agreed to a lottery to determine the top six picks of the annual amateur draft as part of the current CBA. The 18 non-playoff teams each have a shot at the No. 1 pick, though the worst teams have the highest odds. Here are this year's odds for the No. 1 selection in the 2027 Draft (via Baseball America):

Teams that pay into revenue sharing cannot pick in the lottery in back-to-back years, so the Giants (No. 4 pick in 2026) are not eligible for the lottery this year. The Pirates, meanwhile, cannot get a lottery pick this year because teams that receive revenue sharing can not pick in the lottery in three consecutive years. They had the No. 6 pick in 2025 and the No. 5 pick in 2026. The Giants and Pirates cannot pick higher than No. 10 overall in 2027.

The lottery determines the top six draft picks. Picks 7-18 are the remaining non-playoff teams in reverse order of the standings. Picks 19-30 are the 12 postseason teams ordered by their finish, with the Wild Card Series losers coming first and the World Series winner picking last. The draft lottery was not yet a thing during the last lockout. It's unclear how MLB would handle it during a potential lockout this offseason.

By rule, players selected in the Rule 5 Draft must remain on their new team's MLB roster all season in 2027; otherwise, they must go through waivers and be offered back to their original team. Teams don't often find difference-makers in the Rule 5 Draft. They usually look for middle relievers, platoon bats, and lottery tickets. Most Rule 5 Draft picks don't stick and wind up back with their original team. Last offseason's notable Rule 5 Draft selection was Blue Jays righty Spencer Miles, who gave them 95 ⅔ innings with a 2.63 ERA. The Rule 5 Draft was canceled and not held during the last lockout. There is a minor-league phase that still took place, however, because that phase does not involve 40-man roster players.

This is the deadline for teams and arbitration-eligible players to submit salary figures for 2027. The player files what he believes he should be paid while the team files what it believes the player should be paid. This date is only the filing deadline, and the two sides can still agree to a contract of any size even after filing salary figures. The vast majority of arbitration-eligible players agree to a contract before the filing deadline and avoid this headache. MLB Trade Rumors released their 2027 salary arbitration projections a few weeks ago. The entire arbitration process (submit filing figures, hearings, etc.) was pushed back until after the lockout five years ago.

The 2027 international amateur signing period opens at 9 a.m. ET. The annual signing period used to run from July 2 to June 25, though MLB and the MLBPA agreed to push the start of the 2020-21 and 2021-22 signing periods back to the following January because of the pandemic, and now the January start is permanent and the signing period is neatly confined to a single calendar year. These are non-40-man roster players and the international signing period opened as scheduled during the last lockout.

The 2027 Hall of Fame class will be announced during a live MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame ballot will be revealed on Nov. 16, votes are compiled over the following weeks, then the results are announced in January. Newcomers to this year's ballot include Jon Lester and Buster Posey. This is Omar Vizquel's tenth and final year of eligibility. This is also Year 6 on the ballot for Alex Rodriguez and Year 4 for Chase Utley. Among holdovers, Utley was closest to getting in without actually getting in last year. He received 59.1% of the vote, well short of the 75% needed for induction, but he's made huge gains in his three years on the ballot and is trending toward induction.

Inevitably, a few arbitration-eligible players and their teams will be unable to come to terms on a contract, and wind up in front of an arbitration panel. Each side states their case -- hearings can be contentious because the team will outline the player's shortcomings and explain why he deserves a lower salary than he believes -- and the three-person panel picks either the salary the player filed or the salary the team filed on Jan. 8. Nothing in between. Again, teams and players can work out a contract of any size prior to a hearing, even after filing salary figures. Skubal and Kyle Bradish were among the players to go to an arbitration hearing before the 2026 season. Hearings were pushed back until after the lockout five years ago, and in some cases they took place during the season.

Spring training camps open across Arizona and Florida in the middle of February. Each team sets its own reporting dates for pitchers and catchers and then position players, though they'll all be up and running by the second full week of February. All 30 teams are scheduled to play their first exhibition game on Feb. 19. If the lockout extends into February, the start of spring training will be delayed. During the lockout five years ago, MLB announced spring delays one week at a time, piece by piece.

March 24 is the exclusive Opening Night game on Netflix (teams TBA). The other 28 teams will begin their seasons one day later. There's Rivalry Weekend, a special series in Las Vegas and more. Of course, if the lockout extends in March, Opening Day and other games will be pushed back. Five years ago, the regular season started a week late and teams picked up the existing schedule. A new schedule was not drawn up. Missed games were made up with doubleheaders and on mutual off-days throughout the year, with a few extra days tacked on to the end of the season as well.

#2668. Why is Ashton Jeanty not getting carries? Another Raider emerges as Vegas' top RB in Week 8

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is not how Ashton Jeanty was supposed to develop when the Las Vegas Raiders made him the No. 6 overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft. The former Heisman Trophy finalist projected as an eventual superstar, but to reach that heralded potential, he needs to improve upon his play in 2026. Not only is Jeanty on pace to regress statistically from his promising rookie year, but he is also experiencing a role decrease.

The Raiders got into a shootout with the New York Jets in Week 8, yet Jeanty carried the ball just twice in the 38-33 win. He saw a greater workload as a receiver with three catches on four targets than he did as a rusher. The five total touches were the fewest of his young career.

Jeanty's downturn in opportunities is a trend. He opened the season with a fantastic effort against the Miami Dolphins and amassed 102 rushing yards, 45 receiving yards and two touchdowns across 29 touches. Since then, his carry total has diminished on a weekly basis. It reached a new low on Sunday when Mike Washington Jr., conversely, set a career high with 38 snaps.

The road game at MetLife Stadium also marked the first time this season that Washington started over Jeanty.

"That's my call," Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said postgame of the snap distribution at running back. "Ashton's still going to be a big part of our team. He had a huge catch. He's going to be a huge part of our run game going forward. We just wanted to give Mike a few more opportunities today. I think both of those guys are going to be a huge part of our rushing and passing success moving forward."

It is more than just the reduction in opportunities that contributes to Jeanty's underwhelming sophomore NFL campaign. He is not nearly as efficient of a runner as he was last year, either. Jeanty averages 0.6 fewer yards per carry in 2026 than in 2025. His success rate is nearly identical to a year ago, but the overall yardage simply is not there. And he is on pace to come up shy of last season's five rushing touchdowns despite playing on a much higher-scoring offense.

It's possible the offensive revitalization (and the coaching behind it) is the crux of this downturn. Jeanty remains the same highly skilled ball carrier who was nearly untackleable at Boise State, but this is now his fifth consecutive year with a new play caller dating back to his freshman year with the Broncos.

His running style seems to clash with Kubiak's system, and he now plays for a coach who has a history of splitting carries rather than utilizing a bellcow back.

"We won," Jeanty said to ESPN. "It doesn't matter how I feel about how [many] times I get the ball. Whatever it takes for the team to win, I just want to win. That's all."

This week's dramatic reduction in carries did not have anything to do with the comments Jeanty made ahead of the game about the Jets' defense, Kubiak said. During a locker room media availability at the Raiders' facility, Jeanty took a dig at individual players on the opposing team.

"I think we can definitely get the run game going, get back on track and just really get after these guys," Jeanty said. "Couple guys out that don't really want to tackle, but I'm not going to say names."

That remark was widely received as being in poor taste. Former Jets coach Rex Ryan was among those who called Jeanty out for taking a dig at the New York defense.

Rex Ryan on Raiders RB Ashton Jeanty saying that there are a couple of Jets who look like they don’t want to tackle: pic.twitter.com/zoXmTnwQpK

Jeanty said after the game that the coaching staff gave him advance notice that he would receive fewer touches in Week 8 than in previous games, but he said he did not know whether the comments were the reason behind that decision.

While Kubiak said Jeanty's two carries were not the result of discipline, the timing of that role reduction and his comments about the Jets' defense do indicate that they could be related. It is also entirely possible that the coaching staff simply felt Washington gave them a better chance to beat New York as a ball carrier. Even if it was a one-game situation, a rebound in opportunities next week may not take Jeanty all the way back to his Week 1 workload or that of his rookie season. There is enough of a sample size beyond this one game to suggest the Raiders would prefer to use him more sparingly.

Kubiak did not say whether Sunday's roles — with Washington as the early-down back and Jeanty entering on third downs and passing situations ‚ would continue. Instead, he said that the staff would review the film and that it has "two runners that we believe in."

Barring any changes, Jeanty will be more of a receiving threat than a rushing threat. That is a job he can specialize in, as he proved in Week 1 when he scored two receiving touchdowns and in the seven following games when he crossed the 50-yard mark four times. But it is not remotely what he was drafted to be. As one of the top running back prospects of the decade, if not the absolute best, Jeanty figured to become an every-down featured back.

As Washington continues to carve out a job of his own, this could also trend more toward how Kubiak deployed Kenneth Walker III and Zach Charbonnet during his tenure as the Seattle Seahawks' offensive coordinator. He essentially used them as co-starters and schemed up opportunities for Walker to thrive in space while using Charbonnet on inside runs, in pass protection and as a red-zone weapon. Jeanty would fit the Walker mold with Washington playing more a la Charbonnet.

The best-case outcome is that Jeanty improves his per-snap efficiency, makes the most of a smaller workload and flirts with the same rushing numbers that made his 2026 season a promising one. Paired with the clear year-over-year uptick in production as a receiver, that would make him a well-rounded and highly impactful running back.

But if Jeanty keeps picking up only 3.1 yards per carry, he may cede further touches to Washington and settle in as a passing-game specialist. That would be a monumental disappointment given the investment the Raiders made in him at the draft.

Welcome to the best and busiest month for sports. October obviously features the NFL and college football, but did you know that there's at least one football game on the schedule every day this month? Also, the NBA season tips off on Oct. 20, and the NHL just dropped the puck on its season. And October has treats for WNBA (playoffs), Formula 1 (United States Grand Prix) and horse racing (Breeders' Cup) fans as well.

But very little surpasses October baseball, especially in a winner-take-all matchup. And that's exactly what's teed up on Thursday when the Atlanta Braves host the rival Philadelphia Phillies in a win-or-go-home Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park.

For Game 3, Aaron Nola (7-12, 4.67 ERA) will get the ball for Philadelphia, while Grant Holmes (10-6, 3.44) is likely to serve as the bulk pitcher for Atlanta.

#2664. Week 8 overreactions: Time for Vikings to bench Kyler Murray? Colts should fire Steichen?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For much of the first seven weeks of the season, the predominant question around the Minnesota Vikings was: "Can they really keep winning this way?"

And the answer was yes, six times over. Sure, Minnesota's 10 touchdowns were the fewest by any 6-0 team in more than 100 years, but wins are wins, and Minnesota was stacking them.

This week, that ended. The Lions grounded out an impressive 19-15 win, a crucial result in the cutthroat NFC North. Jahmyr Gibbs had 168 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown, and Jared Goff gutted through a tough day overall to throw the game-winning touchdown to Jameson Williams.

There were major, uncomfortable questions during the Vikings' winning streak. Those questions just came to the forefront even more with a loss, and the Vikings must find answers immediately. The most important question revolves around the most important position.

I gave Murray a lot of grace early this year. He was on a new team and in a new system. He suffered a concussion moments into his Vikings debut. It was about as inauspicious a start as possible, and even as he struggled after he returned, I was willing to give him some time to figure it out.

That time is over. Murray was dreadful again Sunday: 17-for-29 for 210 yards, one touchdown and one interception, with three sacks taken. He also ran four times for 35 yards, which was a team high (more on that in a bit). His touchdown pass was a miraculous Justin Jefferson catch.

JUSTIN JEFFERSON OH MYMINvsDET on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/DUTDY0f59E

But Murray was so wildly inaccurate that he often didn't even give his teammates chances to make otherworldly catches or routine catches. According to TruMedia, five of Murray's 29 passes (17.2%) were off-target. He missed Jefferson up the seam on what would have been a touchdown. He missed Jefferson on a rollout, firing the ball several feet above his superstar wide receiver. He dirtied a ball when Jefferson was open on a slant, a play that left Jefferson shrugging as if to say, "What happened?"

Then, there are far too many throws that have an extremely low likelihood of being completed anyway. He throws a ton of perimeter passes that are 50/50 balls at best, and usually, they're closer to 10/90 balls because Murray is so inaccurate on those, too.

He also rarely finds or takes easy answers. His 3.20 average time to throw is by far the highest of his career, even though he is also having the slowest time to pressure this season. Only three players — Caleb Williams, Malik Willis and Drake Maye — have a longer time to throw, on average. But Murray isn't the playmaker or physical force Williams or Maye are.

It's a huge surprise to see Murray play this poorly. Even at his worst in Arizona, he was an average or slightly below average quarterback by most metrics. But this season, he has been so much worse than he's ever been.

Murray's mobility and pocket management have declined, too. He can still move as a runner, but his sack rate and sack-to-pressure rates are way up.

Simply put, it's time for the Vikings to look elsewhere, whether that's in-house (Carson Wentz is the backup) or via a trade. Frustration is bubbling up — Jefferson declined to speak to the media after Sunday's game — and in his postgame press conference, Kevin O'Connell mentioned multiple missed opportunities.

#Vikings HC Kevin O’Connell on getting Kyler Murray comfortable in the offense:“I don’t necessarily believe it’s going to be one tell all thing. I think it’s how we continue to put together the plan of where he’s most comfortable in his alignment, then marrying the offense from… pic.twitter.com/Cf3RjlWVc1

O'Connell can only do so much, though. Murray hasn't been close to good enough for a team with a championship-level defense, and Minnesota simply can't keep the status quo much longer.

The Colts played one of the worst excuses you'll see for a football game Sunday, falling to the Jaguars 42-7. Indianapolis' first-half drive chart was as follows:

Trevor Lawrence threw for 210 yards and three touchdowns on 14 attempts, a ridiculous 15 yards per attempt — the highest rate by any quarterback in any game (min. 10 attempts) in the last two seasons. The Jaguars also averaged 5.5 yards per carry, and only one of their 33 carries went for negative yards.

The trick play goes awry and the Jaguars get it back!INDvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/AinguLvhQi

Yes, the Colts traded away Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner this week and fired GM Chris Ballard the week before. Yes, the season has gone off the rails. But the Titans traded Jeffery Simmons this week and took the Bengals to overtime. The Colts, on the other hand, didn't look interested in playing. This wasn't acceptable in any way, shape or form, and it falls on Shane Steichen.

One issue in the Colts’ locker room right now is a lack of players with the standing to check their teammates and keep it real. Jonathan Taylor is trying, but he isn’t naturally a vocal leader. I commend his effort here. pic.twitter.com/xbXVJwHlSQ

Speaking of Taylor, the Colts reportedly aren't actively shopping him, but not trading him would be a massive mistake. Indianapolis is facing a multi-year rebuild. They have no competent quarterback and likely no way to find one in the draft due to the Sauce Gardner trade. Taylor is reportedly commanding significant offers. The Vikings would be a great fit, as their running game continues to stink.

Indianapolis must move their star running back, and it must move on from Steichen, too. If not, it's a damning mismanagement by Carlie Irsay-Gordon at an absolutely critical junction early in her ownership.

Just kidding! But boy, a 27-6 loss was a rough dose of reality for the Browns, who haven't won a regular-season game at the Steelers since 2003.

Speaking of a rough dose of reality for the Browns, Watson was once again pretty poor Sunday. Though the passing box score stats look good (27-for-39, 324 yards), he took eight sacks. He has now taken 22 sacks in his last four games, a completely unsustainable number. This has been an issue throughout his time in Cleveland, and after a better start to the year avoiding sacks, he has fallen back significantly. He has had a negative EPA per play in three of his past four games, too.

But the Browns don't have a better answer. Shedeur Sanders had major sack problems last year. The offensive line is in rough shape. Watson may be back on his downward trajectory, but Cleveland is still 5-3, and Watson has had some good moments in clutch time. All five of the Browns' wins are by four points or fewer. Plus, there's not a better alternative. If there were, Sanders would be starting.

Baker Mayfield did not complete a single pass in the Buccaneers' 16-0 win over the Falcons on Sunday, a game played in an absolutely downpour. Let's take a little history lesson.

Mayfield only attempted three passes. The week before, he only attempted 11 (completing seven) in a 43-13 domination of the Panthers. Tampa Bay ran for 258 yards in that game.

The Buccaneers cannot win this way forever, clearly. But they don't have to be that far off. The offensive line has really come together after a rocky start, and Bucky Irving looks absolutely excellent. The bigger factor here is the defense, which held Michael Penix Jr. to 8-for-24 passing for 125 yards and four(!) interceptions.

WIDE OPEN JACOB PARRISH ‼️📺: #ATLvsTB on FOX pic.twitter.com/LcZ3BpvEul

Penix was absolutely atrocious, but this isn't a one-off occurrence. Tampa Bay absolutely dominated Carolina with a relentless pass rush the week before, and this defense has been stupendous all season:

It's not like the bar is that high in the NFC South, and the Buccaneers' defense is the best single unit in the division. If Mayfield can avoid making multiple back-breaking mistakes per game, the Buccaneers will join the 1992 Chargers as the only teams to make the postseason after starting 0-4.

The Bengals needed a six-touchdown day from Joe Burrow to beat the lowly, Jeffery Simmons-less Titans 43-36 in overtime. It's a score and a storyline all too familiar for Cincinnati, which has had defensive issues for years.

But even after Sunday's poor performance, Cincinnati's defense is only 16th in EPA per play. Why? Well, the Bengals have the third-highest sack rate in the NFL and the fourth-highest rate of 0 or negative yards gained. They are the league's best fourth-down defense. The defense has forced 11 turnovers, too, a top-10 number.

Listen, it's not necessarily the way you want to live. The Bengals are 25th in yards per play allowed and 30th in explosive play rate allowed. But this passing offense is truly elite. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins both had 10+ catches, 140+ yards and a touchdown, and as I wrote last week, the latter is only getting better.

Plus, the defense has an absolute game-changer in Dexter Lawrence, who has been the best defensive acquisition of the offseason. He saved the game late in regulation.

Dexter Lawrence takes down Cam Ward for a sack in the final minute 💪TENvsCIN on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/V2ju4flSe1

An elite offense plus a play-making defense? Again, it's far from perfect, but it might be enough.

The Broncos deserve a ton of credit for rallying from a 24-13 deficit in the fourth quarter to beat the Chiefs 28-24. Bo Nix came up clutch, leading touchdown drives on both of Denver's final two possessions, and the defense had a huge goal-line stand to seal the deal. It was an absolutely crucial win for the Broncos, who erased Kansas City's head-to-head advantage from Week 1.

But this comeback doesn't happen without the help of Andy Reid. His offense's final three drives finished as follows: punt, missed field goal, turnover on downs.

The missed field goal and the sequence leading up to it will be the main talking point, but let's go chronologically. Early in the fourth quarter, up by 11, Patrick Mahomes threw a 5-yard pass to Emmett Johnson on third-and-6. Really, though, Johnson gained almost 5 yards. It set up fourth and inches. According to the CBS broadcast, Reid was upset that the officials took so long to figure out the spot — he thought it was going to be fourth-and-a-full 1 yard, or maybe more — which forced him to punt. Had he known the spot earlier, he might have gone for it.

This is a bad look. Reid should have gone for this regardless. He had Mahomes, his superstar quarterback, playing at a high level. Though the Chiefs did not run the ball well Sunday, all 22 of their rushes to that point had gained at least 1 yard. This is another spot where the Chiefs' inability to run a quarterback sneak — Mahomes hasn't attempted one since 2019 — loomed large. Teams must have a way to gain 1 yard, or, in this instance, a few inches, reliably.

But the even worse decision came with just under three minutes left. Up three and facing a third-and-2 at the Denver 30, Reid called an awkward rollout that was immediately stymied. Mahomes took a 6-yard sack — an uncharacteristic and untimely error — to set up fourth-and-8. Then Reid trotted out Harrison Butker for a 54-yard field goal attempt in the rain. He missed (very) wide right.

Then late in the game, the Chiefs couldn't punch it in, and their lack of urgency was befuddling. After Kenneth Walker III got down to the 4-yard line with about a minute left, Walker ran 3 yards on a play with 35 seconds left. Then Kansas City didn't take a timeout until there were 15 seconds left, making run plays risky and eliminating any room for error. Mahomes threw an incompletion on second down, and Walker went nowhere on third-and-goal. That forced Reid to use his final timeout. The false start pushed it back to the 6, and Mahomes got sacked. A little more urgency would have kept the playbook more wide open.

#2662. Jacob Misiorowski wraps breakout Brewers year with World Series title and a reminder that best is yet to come

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- When the Brewers took the field for Game 5 of the World Series, they did so with their ace on regular rest. All that stood between them and their first World Series championship was a win with the best possible formula that they could draw up on the lineup card.

If there was any question, it was if Misiorowski could channel some of his early season magic. In the playoffs, he hadn't been bad, but hadn't been nearly as dominant as in the regular season. He also hadn't gone more than five innings in a start.

He stepped up, as championship-caliber athletes do. He was forced to leave the game late in the sixth inning due to calf cramp, but the Brewers already had a 4-0 lead (the eventual final score) and handed things off to their elite bullpen on cruise control. Misiorowski came through with 5 ⅔ innings of scoreless ball, allowing only two hits. He stifled the Rays until the game felt like it was elementary. Only two pitchers have ever recorded a scoreless start of 5+ innings with two or fewer hits allowed in a potential World Series clincher: Misiorowski and some guy named Tom Glavine in 1995.

And behind their ace, the inevitable Brewers are World Series champions.

"It's awesome," Misiorowski said on the field after the Brewers clinched. "It's awesome for this team, it's awesome for the city of Milwaukee. I just made it work. It didn't matter how we won tonight, just that we won."

There were questions in the aftermath of Game 4 about whether Brewers manager Pat Murphy should have brought Misiorowski in for the bottom of the 12th to close things out. There shouldn't have been. It wasn't Game 7. The Brewers were up 3-0 in the series. Losing Game 4 meant they had full-strength Misiorowski waiting to close the door in Game 5. Unsurprisingly, he did exactly that, despite likely being on fumes from his 2026 workload.

In 2025, Misiorowski only worked 141 ⅓ innings between the minors, majors and playoffs. That was a career high in his professional career. In 2026, he finishes with 193 ⅔. It's a monster leap, and it's why the Brewers held his workloads in check down the stretch. They needed something left in the tank to achieve the ultimate goal. That was the plan all along: for him to do exactly what he did in Game 5.

And we're only scratching the proverbial surface here. Remember what a phenom Misiorowski was in the regular season, especially early in the year? He was the must-see player in the sport. Even with his workload monitored, he finished the season with a ridiculous 1.80 ERA (leading the majors) and 252 strikeouts (again, leading the majors) in 174 ⅔ innings. He also led the majors in WHIP, strikeout rate and had the lowest hit rate.

Between his rookie season and this year, "The Miz" ratcheted up his strikeout rate, plummeted his walk rate, improved his efficiency and, early in the year before workload became a concern, worked much deeper into games. As a rookie, he was a talent to dream on. As a sophomore, he was the dream. He's already as decorated as any pitcher the Brewers have ever had (with the Brewers, that is).

Now, let's keep a few things in mind. Misiorowski is:

After the Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS, Murphy remarked on how they don't have a bunch of Hall of Famers, an indirect shot at Los Angeles' star-studded lineup, but there's an argument that Misiorowski has a strong foundation right now (so does Jackson Chourio, by the way).

Given the improvements that Misiorowski made from Year 1 to Year 2 in the majors, there's every reason to expect that next year he'll be just as good, only he'll have built up more stamina for late in the season.

Could he go 200 innings in the regular season next year and lead the Brewers to back-to-back championships while winning a second Cy Young? I don't see why not. That would have sounded like a pipe dream to Brewers fans if we got in a time machine to the aftermath of last year's sweep at the hands of those dastardly, mega-payroll Dodgers. But, you see, Misiorowski just had a dream season. With a guy with his level of talent, the only answer is to dream bigger.

Many weeks in such an unpredictable league as the NFL, the football world witnesses something so historically improbable that it is difficult to believe. There were two such occurrences in Week 8, with the Dallas Cowboys enduring as miserable a fourth-quarter and overtime sequence as any in the last 25 years of franchise history and Joe Burrow delivering a stat line that no other quarterback has posted since the merger.

The highs of Burrow's career day and the lows of the Cowboys' blown lead exemplified everything that makes the NFL such a successful entertainment product. What more could fans seek than late-game drama and excellence from the greatest football players in the world?

Of course, there are two sides to every outcome. The Arizona Cardinals celebrated at the Cowboys' expense. The Tennessee Titans were left bewildered by the quarterbacking they witnessed from their opponent.

Here are the biggest winners and losers from Week 8 in the NFL.

Brian Schottenheimer left his offense on the field on fourth-and-1 from his own 32-yard line in the first quarter, and the Cowboys turned the ball over on downs. That was the first sign that Sunday was not going to be their day. Coaching and offense failed them in that moment, and the defense failed them the rest of the afternoon in surrendering 33 points to the Cardinals in a stunning three-point overtime loss. The same defense that has not held a single opponent under 20 points all year, that is.

At home against a Cardinals team that might finish the year at the bottom of the NFC West, the Cowboys blew a 10-point lead with 3:54 to play in regulation and gave up a game-ending field goal in overtime. They were fortunate to even get to the extra period, because it took an Arizona missed extra point with six seconds remaining for regulation to end level at 30-30.

Arizona is now 5-0 all-time at AT&T Stadium. This loss for the Cowboys stings as much as any of the previous four. The most painful part might be that the 30 points they allowed in the second half and overtime came with backup quarterback Gardner Minshew on the field for Arizona. Or maybe it is the unfathomable splits in two-score games, where since 2000, the Cardinals were 1-174-1 when trailing by 14 or more points in the fourth quarter and the Cowboys were 69-0 at home when leading by 14 or more in the fourth (according to ESPN Insights). If they cannot close out a game against that kind of opponent, then the Cowboys essentially cannot be trusted against anyone.

Ideally for the Cincinnati Bengals, they would not have needed Burrow to shoulder such a heavy load against the Titans. Their opponent, after all, entered Week 8 with just one win. It was one of those situations, though, where they should have felt fortunate to have such a premier quarterback on their side, because most signal-callers are not capable of playing hero to the degree Burrow did in a 43-36 overtime triumph. The three-time Pro Bowler became the second quarterback in NFL history with 450 passing yards, five passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown in the same game and the first such player in 75 years.

Joe Burrow today (passing + rushing):- 472 total yards- 6 total touchdowns📺 CBS & @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/OSGgAriSWT

To be clear, Burrow would have been a major reason why the Bengals lost had they come up short. He threw three interceptions. However, the Cincinnati defense mostly stood tall after those turnovers and limited the damage to just one field goal. In essence, Tennessee only gained one net point off of turnovers, because one of its ensuing possessions resulted in a safety.

The five touchdowns matched a career high. The 462 passing yards were his third-most in a game.

The last thing the Baltimore Ravens could have expected when they reinserted Lamar Jackson into the starting lineup was that Joe Fagnano would wind up spending more time under center than any other quarterback on the roster. A pair of injuries thrust the undrafted rookie into action, however, as the Ravens lost Jackson to a thumb injury and backup signal-caller Tyler Huntley to a toe issue. Fagnano was the Ravens' emergency third quarterback and shockingly made his NFL debut in the second quarter of the 36-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills.

To lose Jackson on his very first play back from a sprained ankle is the most cruel luck possible for a Baltimore offense that desperately needs him to stay healthy. The unit has not scored more than 13 points in any of its last three games, all losses. A team with Super Bowl aspirations now stands at .500 and in last place in the AFC North, and with Jackson out for at least four weeks as he undergoes surgery, it will be difficult to turn things around.

The moral of Sean Payton's tenure with the Denver Broncos is that if his team is in a close game, it is destined to win. The Broncos' 28-24 victory over the Kansas City Chiefs marked their 15th consecutive win in one-score games dating back to last season, which tied the NFL regular-season record. They are also now 5-0 in games decided by seven points or fewer this year alone, which matches the best record through Week 8 since 2000.

It takes immense clutch fourth-quarter efforts to stay unbeaten in tight situations, and the Broncos displayed plenty of timely play in their latest triumph. They trailed the Chiefs by 11 points with just under nine minutes to play and scored a pair of touchdowns to take the decisive lead. They received a bit of help in the way of a Harrison Butker missed field goal, but they also stepped up on both sides of the ball on their own and ended the game with a fourth-and-goal sack of Patrick Mahomes.

The Broncos’ win probability fell to 10.2% early in the fourth quarter and was just 11.9% with 2:44 left in regulation in their comeback win over the Chiefs.Denver’s chances of winning the AFC West are now 64%. With a loss, they would have been 24%.Powered by @awscloud pic.twitter.com/yTc9UFmuQx

That was far from the first time the Broncos grasped victory from the claws of defeat during the 15-game streak. At this point, it is hard to say it will be the last.

Who needs completed passes? The 1974 Bills did not, and neither did the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 8. Those are the last two teams to win a game without a single completion. Baker Mayfield went 0-for-3 in the Buccaneers' 16-0 shutout victory over the Atlanta Falcons. The run game did all the work with Bucky Irving racking up 170 yards and the game's lone touchdown and Kenneth Gainwell adding 139 yards. Mayfield scampered for 14 of his own.

Tampa Bay is now on a two-game winning streak with a total of 59 points in that span. Mayfield completed only seven throws for 64 yards in the previous victory.

The quarterback on the other sideline had an even worse day. Michael Penix Jr. completed just eight of his 24 attempts and threw four interceptions. Two of those picks came in the first quarter when Alex Anzalone came down with both of them, and by halftime, Penix had more turnovers than completions. He ended the day with more interceptions than in any game of his college or professional careers.

Mostly to blame for the offensive disaster was the torrential downpour that persisted throughout the contest in Tampa Bay.

This is how bad the rain is coming down here. Could be a long nasty game in Tampa. #Falcons pic.twitter.com/Hu4nc0C0cp

It took two months for the obligatory reminder to arrive: The 1972 Dolphins are the only team in NFL history to complete an undefeated season. They will continue to stand alone. The Minnesota Vikings lost on Sunday, and thus there are no unbeaten teams left. The NFC North leaders entered the week at 6-0 and as the only perfect squad in the league and left it with a divisional loss to the Detroit Lions. They fell, 19-15, in another one of their patented defensive battles.

Could the Vikings make a play for a quarterback at the trade deadline? This loss exemplified how the lack of a proficient offense could halt them from maximizing Brian Flores' elite defense.

The bye week would have been a sensible time for the Los Angeles Chargers to move on from offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel after they finished their first six games as the NFL's lowest-scoring team. Instead, Jim Harbaugh stuck by his assistant, lauded his talent and then promptly watched as his unit managed a meager nine points in Sunday's 24-9 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Harbaugh has to own the fact that he could have made a play-caller change and that by not doing so, the offense continued to sputter.

Justin Herbert threw two more interceptions to return to sole possession of the league high. The rushing attack posted a mere 64 yards. The unit failed to hit double-digit points for the second time in as many games.

As he sits at 0-7 and enters the season's third month as the NFL's only winless coach, Harbaugh is now under perhaps the strongest microscope of anyone in his role. He had an opportunity to fire a scapegoat during the bye, and if he does not think that making a change would be in the offense's best interest, then the focus intensifies on his own inability to correct the group's woes.

The AFC North is a battle. The Pittsburgh Steelers took a critical step toward potentially winning one of the NFL's most competitive divisions with a 27-6 win over the Cleveland Browns. History made it a safe assumption that they would handle business against their rival, and they only strengthened the longstanding trends that favor the home team in this series.

In games between the Steelers and Browns, the home side has now won 11 consecutive games dating back to January 2022. That is the longest such active streak in any series. Pittsburgh has also now won 24 of its last 25 regular-season home games against Cleveland. The Browns – who had -1 yard of total offense through the first quarter on Sunday – own just two total wins at Acrisure Stadium, which opened in 2021.

#2660. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2658. Jaylen Brown insists he never demanded Celtics trade, pushes back on 'false allegations' from Brian Scalabrine

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The messiest drama in the NBA resides in the Northeast corridor, where new Philadelphia 76ers star Jaylen Brown has yet to reach the stage where bygones can be bygones with his old team, the Boston Celtics.

Brown was floated in trade rumors early in the offseason as the Milwaukee Bucks were trying to trade Giannis Antetokounmpo before ultimately getting dealt to Philly in a stunning in-division deal for Paul George. His old running mate, Jayson Tatum, said he was shocked by the move, which Brown finds hard to believe.

Tatum tried to bury any notion of beef between he and Brown, insisting "this ain't f--kin Shaq and Kobe," but Brown is less eager to move on and said it might not be beef but could be "lamb chops and gravy" between the two former teammates.

Amid all of that, former Celtics player and current Celtics TV analyst Brian Scalabrine tried defending Tatum by claiming on his radio show that Brown asked for a trade and actually gave Boston a list of demands this offseason and wanted to be traded if they weren't met.

Brown's reps called that "10,000% a lie" and Brown was asked about it after the Sixers' win on Wednesday night and elaborated further, via the Philly Voice.

"Yeah, I mean, I guess it is what it is. I saw that. I saw Scal, he made some comments. Never had any issues with Scal. I love Scal, but I guess he's doing what he has to do," Brown said. "I can understand why he feels the need to do that, but I have no interest [in] letting any false allegations [follow] me to my next chapter here in Philadelphia. Never. I never demanded a trade. Never made a list of ultimatums. None of the sort. None of that is true, but as of now, I'm going to just stay focused on what's in front of me here in Philadelphia. I've got a tremendous opportunity, and I'm looking forward to that. So, I'm going to just leave the questions for another time, but during the season, I'm going to just focus on what's in front of me."

This seems to put this weeklong saga to rest for now, but with the Celtics visiting Philadelphia in less than two weeks on Nov. 10, it won't be long before the questions pick up again about what exactly happened that led to Brown's departure.

The reason the questions persist is the Celtics' process for trading Brown felt sloppier and more hurried compared to the more surgical, calculated approach that's been the hallmark of Brad Stevens' tenure in charge in Boston. Brown's name surfaced in the Antetokounmpo talks and then never went away, with reports emerging that Boston was shopping him around the league to anyone who would listen.

Doing that after Brown put together an All-NBA campaign in 2025-26 raised eyebrows, and there has been an assumption around the league that something happened behind the scenes to sour the team-player relationship to the point of no return.

Brown indicates he'll address that at an appropriate time but not during the season. Until then, the speculation will continue about what went down in Boston.

#2656. Andy Reid backs decision to trust Harrison Butker despite Chiefs kicker's struggles

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Kansas City Chiefs have a kicker problem. Harrison Butker missed yet another kick on Sunday, a 54-yarder that would have extended Kansas City's lead over the division rival Denver Broncos to six points but instead set up the game-winning touchdown drive by Denver.

The Chiefs led by three points when they drove down to the Denver 30-yard line and faced third-and-2 from there. Patrick Mahomes dropped back to pass, but he was sacked for a six-yard loss, which turned what would have been a 48-yard field goal attempt into a 54-yarder, and Butker missed his kick wide to the right.

The kick is no good and the Broncos will take over down 3 👀KCvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/VRZzs9NNwG

It was the third significant miss in two weeks for Butker, whose job already appeared to be on thin ice after the Chiefs signed former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad earlier this week. Tucker had been out of the league since 2024 after he was accused by multiple women of sexual misconduct, as originally reported by The Baltimore Banner. After the game, Andy Reid defended the decision to send Butker out to try the deep field goal attempt.

"Those are hindsight. It ended up being what it was," Reid said, via FOX 4 Kansas City. "But it's within Harrison's range."

Here's the thing, though: 54 yards isn't really within Butker's range anymore. It may have been during his prime, but these days, he is not nearly consistent enough from that distance to justify trying that kick.

Here's what we wrote just last week, for example, when Butker missed a pair of field goal attempts in the Chiefs' loss to the Seattle Seahawks:

Through 2023, he made 89.1% of his total field goals, and 28 of 40 (70%) from beyond 50 yards. Since then, though, Butker has made just 82.2% of his kicks, and only 8-of-18 (44.4%) from beyond 50 yards. He missed one of those 50-plus-yard kicks short by several yards in this game, making him just 1-of-5 from 50-plus this year, and he missed another from 45 yards out, pushing it wide to the right.

Whether you agree with the decision to kick the field goal or not, it's clear that the Chiefs can't trust Butker in big spots anymore. And that means his time with the Chiefs could soon be coming to an end, whether Kansas City turns to Tucker or somebody else.

#2655. Victor Wembanyama on 60 Minutes: Spurs star explains why 'villain' label didn't bother him during NBA Finals

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama's 2025-26 season -- his third in the NBA -- affirmed his status as the league's next megastar. Wembanyama led the Spurs to the 2026 NBA Finals before they lost to the Knicks in five games, and he earned the first of what figures to be many Defensive Player of the Year awards and All-NBA honors.

Wembanyama has entered the 2026-27 season with sky-high expectations. The 7-foot-4 Frenchman is the favorite to win NBA MVP honors, and the Spurs are the favorites to win the 2027 championship.

For the better part of his first three years in the league, Wembanyama was a beloved figure, doing things no one else could do on the court to create jaw-dropping highlights that got passed around social media and group texts.

However, as the Spurs moved through the postseason, some of the love from fans started to get lost. There were moments that started to earn him a "dirty" label, including when Wembanyama clocked Naz Reid with an elbow in the second round of the playoffs against the Timberwolves. Wembanyama then irked Knicks players (and their fans) when he shoved New York star Jalen Brunson in the NBA Finals.

Once viewed as a conquering hero, Wembanyama became a villain, particularly in New York.

In a sit-down interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim that will air this Sunday night on CBS, Wembanyama was asked about that switch. He noted that he was unbothered by having a "villain" label because he was solely focused on what he was doing on the court.

60 MINUTES: Last year in the Finals you were portrayed-- as a villain. Correct me if I'm wrong, I didn't get the feeling that bothered you.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: No, it didn't because I'm not paying attention to this-- during the Finals. I don't think any player on either team really is.

While Wembanyama insists he ignored the chatter off the court, he doesn't seem to want that villain tag to last. Wembanyama added that last year's playoff run was a learning experience of toeing the line between being competitive and going to far -- which he noted he crossed on occasion.

60 MINUTES: I wondered if you didn't show, "Hey, this is part of my character too." Edgy Wemby, whatever it is. But you showed a new side of yourself.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA: It showed my limits more than anything else. Going out there, you need to play basketball. You don't need to beat the s--- out of people. [laughs] If you wanna win, at least.

Wembanyama is one of the league's most openly introspective and reflective stars, even at just 23 years old. He seems to recognize that he allowed himself to get too caught up with the physicality of playoff basketball and seems determined to better understand how to play up to that line without crossing it in the manner he did at times in his first taste of the postseason.

TUNE IN: The full interview with 60 Minutes' Jon Wertheim and Wembanyama will air Sunday, Nov. 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET, after NFL football, on CBS and stream on Paramount+. In the preseason, 60 Minutes followed Wembanyama in his native France, where he runs an annual tournament combining basketball with another one of his passions: chess.
